email_papers.title: Cross-modal Steering Vectors Exist Across Both Image and Text Generation
email_papers.abstract: Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one? We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying cross-modal steering: 1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality. Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal. We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities. Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text). Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design. This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept. Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one?
We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying
cross-modal steering
:
1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality.
Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal.
We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities.
Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text).
Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design.
This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept.
Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior.

Introduction
Despite the complexity of modern generative models, such as LLMs and diffusion models, many high-level concepts can be controlled through surprisingly simple interventions: adding a linear direction, or
steering vector
(
Subramani et al., 2022
)
, to a model’s intermediate representations. Steering vectors have been used to modulate a wide range of behaviors in both language models
(
Li et al., 2023
;
Todd et al., 2024
;
Turner et al., 2024
;
Dunefsky & Cohan, 2025
;
Bayat et al., 2025
)
and image generation systems
(
Bau et al., 2019
;
Goetschalckx et al., 2019
;
Spingarn et al., 2021
;
Park et al., 2023
;
Gandikota et al., 2024
;
Konovalova et al., 2026
)
, providing a lightweight and causal means of controlling model outputs. Yet steering in these two modalities has largely been studied separately. Here we ask: are steering directions themselves modality-specific, or can a direction discovered in one modality also control generation in another?
Consider a steering vector extracted entirely from text that, when added to a model’s hidden states, reliably causes it to write more formally. If the same model also generates images, what happens when that very same vector is instead added to its generated image tokens? Could it induce a corresponding notion of
visual formality
, such as more formal clothing or design? And vice versa: could a direction extracted purely from images steer how the model writes?

Together, our results show that modality-specific representations can nevertheless contain shared causal directions of control, revealing a form of internal structure that is neither fully modality-specific nor captured simply by representational alignment. Beyond offering a new lens on how vision and language interact inside unified models, cross-modal steering points toward modality-agnostic approaches for controlling multimodal generation.
2
Cross-Modal Steering: Methodology
2.1

Our approach
We adopt one established approach for both language and vision: we find steering vectors via a dataset of minimally different inputs, and add them to representations at either a subset of layers or whole ranges of layers. Crucially, finding and applying the vector need not use the same modality: for cross-modal steering, we construct a vector entirely from examples in one modality and then apply that
same vector, without any adaptation or target-modality data
, to representations of the other modality during generation.

Related Work
Unification and Alignment of Modalities.
Approaches and tasks for connecting vision and language differ widely, from
multimodal language models
(

(

, to the many variants of recent unified multimodal models
(
Team, 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Deng et al., 2025
)
.
Across all, it is widely studied how vision and language representations interact and align
(
Merullo et al., 2023
;
Neo et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025a
)
, ranging from modality gaps studies in CLIP models
(
Liang et al., 2022
)
to circuit analyses and vocabulary space projections in multimodal LLMs
(
Nikankin et al., 2025
;
Krojer et al., 2026
;
Feucht et al., 2026
)
.
Only few works have studied internals of unified models, via attention patterns and embedding geometry
Serra et al. (2025)
, transfer of knowledge edits
Gao et al. (2026)
and steering vectors
Wang & Li (2026)
.

Conclusion
In this paper we have shown cross-modal steering vectors in both directions (
txt
→
\to
img
and
img
→
\to
txt
).
We also characterized and provided intuition how such cross-modal steering can manifest in the other modality.
As unified multimodal models become more capable and mature as a field, we see potential for methods that leverage this unified nature for model control.
If we identify a promising (steering) intervention to make models safer
(
Arditi et al., 2024
)
, it should automatically transfer to visual capabilities; likewise, if we want to regularly update knowledge in the model, such knowledge edits should transfer to visual capabilities
(
Gao et al., 2026
)
.
We encourage future work to expand our findings to other families of unified models and novel concepts.
Scientifically, we see unified models as a fruitful testbed for developing modality-agnostic interpretability tools and theories of multimodal interactions, as exemplified by our study of cross-modal steering.

Experimental Details
Concepts.
Our concepts are chosen from those commonly studied in either the language or vision community. Emotion (sad/happy) is commonly steered in language models
(
Turner et al., 2024
;
Zou et al., 2025
)
, and age (young/old) and expression are canonical targets of latent-direction editing in image generation
(
Shen et al., 2020
;
Gandikota et al., 2024
;
Baumann et al., 2025
)
. Cleanness and chaos are semantic concepts that describe the state of a whole scene. In text a single word expresses them, while in an image they are spread over many objects, which makes them an interesting test of whether one direction can capture both. The visual concepts describe basic properties of objects in a scene, such as their size, depth, spatial position or color. We expect spatial (left/right) to be the hardest concept to steer, since spatial relations are a well-documented failure mode of image generation models and VLMs
(
Chatterjee et al., 2024
;
Kamath et al., 2023
)

article.headline: 图像与文本之间可共享引导向量
article.lede: 在统一多模态模型里，从一种模态提取的引导向量能零样本迁移到另一种模态，且双向生效。
article.problem: 以往对引导向量（steering vector）的研究基本在语言模型和图像生成两个社区各自进行，很少有人检验同一方向能否跨模态起作用。作者把「模态是否统一」这一宽泛问题操作化为跨模态引导：向量在一个模态上被找到，再原封不动地加到另一个模态的 token 上，观察它是否仍能因果地改变生成结果。相比表征相似度这类相关性证据，引导干预本身带有因果性。
article.method: 作者在若干共享参数、同时做语言与图像生成的统一多模态模型（UMM）上做实验，覆盖三种模型。他们用最小差异输入对构造引导向量，做法是取正负样本隐状态的均值之差；向量只在单一模态的样本上提取，之后不加任何适配、也不接触目标模态数据，就直接施加到另一模态的生成过程上。这样共形成四种设置：向量的提取模态与应用模态两两组合；此外还比较了单层与全层的施加方式。所测概念包括情绪、年龄、表情、整洁与混乱，以及物体大小、深度、空间位置、颜色等视觉属性，共七个概念。
article.results: 在情绪、物体大小等多个被引导的概念上，引导向量都能双向零样本迁移，即文本到图像和图像到文本；即便是「正式与口语」这类高度偏向单一模态的概念，向量在另一模态中也常引发可解释的一致效果，例如更正式的服装与设计。几何上，尽管文本与图像表征之间存在明显的模态间隔，跨模态迁移性强的向量在同一概念下倾向于指向相近方向；作者报告该相关分析每个模型、每个迁移方向使用 21 个点（7 个概念 × 3 个层范围，空间概念因在多数设置下无法引导而被排除）。各概念的峰值触发率等具体数值论文正文摘录未给出具体数字，需查阅原文图表。作者也指出空间（左与右）是预期最难引导的概念。
article.why_it_matters: 如果控制手段天然跨模态生效，那么一次安全干预或知识编辑就可能同时覆盖文字与视觉输出，而不必为每个模态单独训练控制器。这也为「模态无关」的可解释性工具提供了一个可操作的实验范式。
article.limitations: 结论建立在三种统一多模态模型和七个概念上，作者自己就呼吁把发现扩展到其他模型家族与新概念；空间关系这类概念在多数设置下根本引导不动，说明迁移并非普遍成立。几何分析每格仅 21 个点，且评测依赖评判模型与人工验证，迁移效果的稳健性与判定标准仍待更多工作检验。

email_papers.title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
email_papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/

Abstract
Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page:
https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/
.
1

Introduction
Transferring knowledge from large pretrained models to robotics has become a primary approach to general-purpose robot control
(
Firoozi et al., 2025
;
Ma et al., 2026b
;
Shen et al., 2026
)
. Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt vision-language backbones for end-to-end visuomotor control
(
Kim et al., 2025
;
Black et al., 2025b
;
Black et al., 2025a
;
Ma et al., 2026a
;
GigaBrain Team et al., 2026
;
Yuan et al., 2026a
)
, whereas world action models (WAMs) jointly model future visual dynamics and actions to utilize the physical and temporal priors of video generative models
(
Ye et al., 2026
;
Kim et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026a
;
Yuan et al., 2026b
;
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Cai et al., 2026a
)
. Both approaches rely on post-training with robot manipulation trajectories: although effective within their training distributions, their generalization is bounded by the scale and diversity of collected robot data. By contrast, frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) acquire stronger emergent capabilities from massive-scale pretraining data, and this training scale remains costly to replicate with embodied data alone.
Without robot-specific post-training, frontier MLLMs provide an alternative approach through their spatial understanding and embodied reasoning capabilities
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Rao, 2026
)
. GPT-6-Astra
(
OpenAI, 2026
)
, for example, can generate end-effector (EEF) commands directly from camera observations and language instructions
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Jia et al., 2026
;
Lou et al., 2026
)
. Combined with an agent harness that supplies its prompt, observation interface, and tools, the model serves as the core of an agent that controls the robot in closed loop, as formalized in Section
3
. Beyond direct control, recent studies explore a harness with policy in which the agent invokes a post-trained policy for action execution
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Xu et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026a
)
. Such a harness combines the agent’s task planning, progress monitoring, and error recovery with the closed-loop visuomotor control that the policy learns from robot demonstrations.
Although prior studies have evaluated both direct control and a harness with policy, they have not comprehensively profiled these agent configurations against post-trained VLA and WAM policies across diverse manipulation demands. Specifically, two central questions remain to be addressed. First, under direct control, on which tasks does the agent outperform post-trained VLAs and WAMs, where does it fall short, and what limits its performance? Second, in a harness-with-policy setting, how does invoking a post-trained policy complement the agent’s direct control, which limitations of direct control can it alleviate, and what new failure modes arise when the agent invokes a policy for execution and subsequently resumes decision-making?
To further explore these questions, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra as the core of an agent on EBench
(
Gao et al., 2026
)
. This diagnostic manipulation benchmark categorizes tasks by mobility, manipulation precision, and task horizon and evaluates robustness along the generalization dimensions of unseen objects, unseen backgrounds, paraphrased instructions, and their mixture. For a fair comparison, the agent operates under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, receiving only RGB camera images and proprioceptive robot states without depth, camera calibration, or simulator ground truth. For each task, the agent receives a task description annotated by GPT-6-Astra from a single training episode as single-shot in-context learning (ICL). Across all 510 test episodes, we evaluate both direct control and a harness with policy invoking either the VLA

Under direct control, the GPT-6-Astra-based agent achieves a 46.7% overall success rate and a 0.654 stage-completion score, outperforming post-trained policies such as Qwen-RobotManip and

Among the compared post-trained policies, the agent ranks first on short-horizon tasks with a 73.2% success rate, shows the smallest success-rate variation across the four generalization dimensions, and completes a novel composite instruction zero-shot on which both compared post-trained policies fail. Conversely, its success rate drops to 27.3% on long-horizon tasks, 20.0% on tabletop manipulation, and 11.3% on high-precision contact-rich tasks. Trajectory analysis shows that while the agent performs well at visual grounding and in-episode error recovery, its physical execution is limited by long action chunks between observations and by contact geometry that it must infer explicitly from RGB views.
Invoking a post-trained policy through the agent harness increases the overall success rate to 53.0% with

. The harness with policy retains the agent’s high success rate on short-horizon tasks and improves performance on long-horizon and bimanual tasks where the post-trained policy is competent. At the same time, case analysis identifies two limitations of the current harness with policy. First, neither component resolves high-precision contact-rich manipulation. Second, agent and policy coordinate loosely in three respects: the agent invokes the policy for most execution steps even on tasks where that policy alone rarely succeeds, the policy follows the fixed task instruction instead of the agent’s subgoal, and the agent often leaves a held grasp unmaintained when it resumes control after a policy invocation, which makes object drops more frequent.
The main contributions of this report are as follows:
•
Paired evaluation across agent configurations and post-trained policies.
Under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, we evaluate an GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control and in a harness with policy across all 510 EBench test episodes. We compare both agent configurations against standalone post-trained VLA and WAM policies across all task groups and generalization dimensions.
•
Characterization of agent capabilities under direct control.
We locate where the GPT-6-Astra-based agent leads or trails eight post-trained policies while using only a single annotated task demonstration and no parameter updates, trace its unsuccessful episodes to their failure mechanisms, and examine its in-episode adaptation, the safety of its execution, and its zero-shot composition of skills on a novel instruction. Together, these analyses show where the agent and the policies complement each other.
•
Analysis of harness with policy and implications for agent harness design.
We evaluate the harness with either policy against each of its components on every task, trace the episodes that newly fail under the harness and those that fail with both policies to their decisive incidents, and analyze the agent’s policy invocation and the resulting token cost. These analyses locate the remaining gap to the better component in policy invocation, subgoal passing, and grasp maintenance when the agent resumes control, which informs the design of future agent harnesses.

4.1

The Capability Boundary
Taken together, the results of this section place the capability boundary of the direct-control agent at the transition from task-level reasoning to physical execution, and the way in which the agent acts explains why the boundary lies there. On the reasoning side, the semantic and spatial priors of multimodal pretraining supply the task-level knowledge, so that one annotated demonstration per task suffices to direct them. On the execution side, the agent acts through EEF waypoint chunks and observes the scene only after each chunk, so it lacks the continuous physical feedback that precise contact, coordinated two-arm motion, and long horizons require. The post-trained policies learn their control from demonstration trajectories and act on fresh observations throughout execution, so they receive this feedback by design.
The two sides are complementary: the direct-control agent is stronger in
visual grounding, robustness across generalization dimensions, in-episode adaptation, and zero-shot skill composition
, and the post-trained policies in
closed-loop physical execution
. Section
6
therefore examines whether this boundary and its token cost shift in a harness with policy, where the MLLM core retains task-level reasoning and invokes a post-trained policy for closed-loop execution.
6

Conclusions and Future Directions
This report profiles GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness. The agent observes the scene under the same visual and proprioceptive protocol as post-trained policies and acts first under direct control and then in a harness with a post-trained VLA or WAM. Under direct control, the capability boundary of the agent lies between flexible task interpretation and reliable physical execution. Without robot-specific post-training of the MLLM, the direct-control agent draws on multimodal pretraining and one annotated demonstration for each task to compete with post-trained policies overall, with particular strengths in visual grounding, robustness to generalization shifts, adaptation to failures during an episode, and zero-shot composition of skills. Physical execution, by contrast, exposes a tension in how the agent controls the robot. The agent chooses its corrections between waypoint chunks, whereas grasps, contacts, and the alignment of parts evolve within each chunk, so precise contact, bimanual coordination, and long horizons limit its success. Because each correction also resends the accumulated context, the unsuccessful and long-horizon episodes that this tension produces account for most of the agent’s token cost. The same unconstrained execution also drops held objects outside the agent’s deliberate grasp tests and at times produces abrupt wrist rotations that risk damaging physical hardware.
Invoking a post-trained policy moves part of this boundary. With InternW0-
Δ
\Delta
, the harness with policy reaches the highest SR and score in Table
1
, and with either policy the agent needs far fewer tokens per success on long-horizon tasks, where direct control is costliest. However, two shortfalls of the combination indicate where further progress is needed. First, precise contact limits the agent and each policy alike, so combining them leaves this ceiling in place. Second, the combination falls short of its better component on many tasks, because the coordination between agent and policy remains loose. The agent delegates without regard to the policy’s competence, the policy pursues the task instruction rather than the agent’s subgoal, and when control returns from the policy, the agent often leaves the holding arm unmaintained, allowing grasped objects to slip. These limitations motivate us to explore several directions.
Designing subtask interfaces and training policies as learnable tools.
In the evaluated harness, the agent passes the policy only a step count, so it decides when the policy acts but can neither assign a subgoal nor receive a report of its completion. A finer interface would not only expose learned skills as tools that a planner selects
(
RLinf, 2026
)
but also pass an explicit subgoal to the policy, verify the entry and exit conditions of each subtask
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, and return whether the subgoal was reached. Such an interface also requires a policy that can serve it. The evaluated policies are post-trained on complete EBench task trajectories under the task instruction, whereas the harness invokes them mid-episode from states that the agent has reached and for subgoals that the agent has chosen. The policy itself therefore has to be trained as a learnable tool of the harness. This training spans three levels and can build on the subtask instruction following of
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
Black et al., 2025a
)
and on the subtask descriptions and execution feedback that the authors of InternW0-
Δ
\Delta
list as future extensions of its interface
(
Miao et al., 2026
)
. First, the policy should follow the agent’s subgoals rather than only the task instruction. Second, it should be trained on the mid-episode states in which the agent transfers control, including disturbed and displaced ones. Third, it should end each segment on subgoal completion or failure, returning structured feedback to the agent and leaving any held object in a stable grasp. The agent, in turn, can be trained to delegate a subtask according to the policy’s competence on it and to use the proprioceptive state returned at every control transfer to keep a held object grasped.
Grounding exploratory experience into reusable memory and tools.
Within an episode, the agent diagnoses slips and displaced objects and revises its strategy, yet every new episode starts again from the same static prompt. Recent work turns such experience into reusable assets. Language-model programs compose perception and control APIs into robot behavior
(
Liang et al., 2023
)
, and recent harnesses synthesize task programs around post-trained policies
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
, expose embodiment-specific primitives
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
, or extend their control interfaces during deployment
(
Li et al., 2026c
)
. To admit only experience that generalizes, recent work also validates candidate skills on held-out episodes
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
and isolates the evaluation from the agent that revises its own prompt and tools
(
Elmaaroufi et al., 2026
)
. For embodied agents, two questions follow: which recoveries generalize beyond a single trial, and whether experience accumulated with one MLLM serves other MLLMs as well. The stated reasons of the agent offer a natural starting point, as each names a diagnosed failure together with the revised action that follows it. Validated pairs of failure and revision can be retained across episodes as memory or compiled into tools that wrap closed-loop control.
Transferring the agent’s exploratory and corrective strategies to smaller policies.
The recorded rollouts contain corrective strategies such as withdrawing for a wider view after a slip and lowering a sweep that missed the beans. The agent produces these strategies at the latency and token cost of a frontier MLLM. Distilling them into smaller models that run at deployment speed would pair failure states with the agent’s revised strategies and their outcomes, including corrections that did not succeed. Such distillation would thereby extend behavior cloning from trajectories toward the intentions behind them. Policies already improve from their own experience and from corrective interventions
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
)
, and an LLM agent can run the cycle of training and evaluating a VLA without a human in the loop
(
Yu, 2026
)
. Because agent rollouts carry the reason for every correction, they extend such training data to corrections that the agent discovers on its own.
Coupling geometric perception with active safety constraints in execution.
Precise contact and safe execution both depend on geometry that the agent infers from RGB views without depth. On insertion, threading, and seating, the agent has to judge the height of a surface, the clearance of a part, and the onset of contact from images, and its commands reach the robot without checks against the table, the workspace bounds, or the speed of the motion. The harness can therefore pair perception tools with a safety layer. Perception tools such as depth estimation, open-vocabulary detection and segmentation, and visual checks of the terminal state can estimate these quantities from the same camera views. The safety layer can check each command against workspace, reachability, and velocity limits and interrupt chunk execution on slip or collision. On real hardware, a queryable model of the robot’s body already lets an agent convert functional targets into control targets
(
Lou et al., 2026
)
, and such a model can supply the kinematic limits that this safety layer enforces. Reporting safety events beside SR and score would let benchmarks measure this progress.
Limitations.
This report mainly studies the capability profile of one frontier MLLM, GPT-6-Astra, as the core of an agent on one simulated benchmark with synchronous execution, both under direct control and in a harness with two post-trained policies. Natural extensions include measuring the agent’s execution time, asynchronous execution in which the scene keeps evolving while the model deliberates, self-improvement of the agent with or without training the post-trained policy, a full evaluation of other frontier MLLMs as agent cores under the same protocol, and deployment on a physical robot. article.headline: 前沿MLLM当机器人智能体：直接控制与调用策略的边
article.lede: 在EBench的510个测试回合上，GPT-6-Astra分别以直接控制和调用后训练策略两种方式控制机器人。
article.problem: 前沿多模态大模型不经机器人专门后训练就能输出末端执行器指令，但它与后训练的VLA、WAM策略在不同操作需求下谁强谁弱、边界在哪，此前没有被系统刻画。另一方面，让智能体通过harness调用一个后训练策略执行动作，能否补上直接控制的短板、又会引入哪些新的失效模式，同样缺少配对证据。
article.method: 作者在诊断性操作基准EBench上把GPT-6-Astra作为智能体核心，采用与后训练策略完全相同的RGB图像加本体感觉观测协议，不使用深度、相机标定或仿真真值，每个任务仅提供一段标注演示作为单次上下文学习。评测两种配置：直接控制下由模型直接生成路径点命令；harness-with-policy下它还可以调用后训练VLA（π0.5）或WAM（InternW0-Δ）执行动作。全部510个测试回合分别与排行榜上的后训练策略对比，并对配对回合做执行轨迹与失败事件分析。
article.results: 直接控制下整体成功率为46.7%、阶段完成分0.654，超过在6600条域内演示上训练的Qwen-RobotManip与π0.5等后训练策略；短时程任务成功率73.2%排名第一，在四个泛化维度上的成功率波动最小，并能零样本完成两条对比策略都失败的新组合指令。但长时程任务成功率降至27.3%，桌面操作20.0%，高精度接触密集任务仅11.3%。通过harness调用策略后，整体成功率升至53.0%（π0.5）和56.0%（InternW0-Δ），每次成功所耗token减少一半以上，其中InternW0-Δ配置超过表1中所有对比的后训练策略。
article.why_it_matters: 结果把前沿MLLM智能体的能力边界定位在“任务级推理”与“物理执行”之间：语义与空间先验足以支撑任务理解、泛化与回合内纠错，但执行侧仍要靠后训练策略的闭环反馈，两者是互补而非替代关系。论文进一步把剩余差距归因于策略调用的子目标接口、按能力委派和恢复控制后的抓取保持，为后续harness设计给出了具体抓手。
article.limitations: 评测只覆盖一个前沿MLLM（GPT-6-Astra）、一个同步执行的仿真基准和两个后训练策略，未测真实机器人、执行时延与异步执行，也未系统比较其他模型作为智能体核心。即便在harness配置下，高精度接触密集任务仍无进展，且由于智能体对多数步骤不加区分地委派、策略只执行固定指令而不理会子目标、智能体恢复控制后未维持抓取，多个任务的表现低于单组件各自的上界。
article.figure_caption_zh: 同一测试场景下GPT-6-Astra智能体在直接控制与以π0.5为工具的harness两种配置中的关键帧，标注了视频时间、每帧的执行者与回合结果，包括(a)(b)玻璃入展示盒与(c)(d)茶杯、茶碟与茶壶两组任务。

email_papers.title: Does VGGT Know What It Does Not Know?
email_papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT regress cameras and geometry in a single forward pass, but they report no uncertainty for the camera poses they predict: an incorrect relative pose looks no different from a correct one. We ask whether the frozen model nonetheless knows when its pose is wrong. On HardMatch, a benchmark of 1,000 deliberately difficult image pairs on which VGGT fails on 35% of pairs, a linear probe on VGGT's frozen features predicts pose failure on held-out categories with ROC-AUC 93.5%, compared with 79.7% for VGGT's own point-map confidence and 77.7% for a classifier trained on all of VGGT's outputs. The probe catches failures VGGT is confident about, lets a downstream system abstain on the pairs it distrusts, and transfers without retraining to rotation failures on PhotoTourism and ScanNet-1500, beyond what co-visibility explains. This knowledge is absent from the per-image encoder: it is computed partway through the layers that fuse the two views, and the same holds for a second model, $π^3$. In essence, we find that VGGT knows more about its own failures than it reports.

Does VGGT Know What It Does Not Know?
Adityan Thirumani Srinivasan
Affiliation:
University of Wisconsin–Madison
David Nordström

Abstract
Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT regress cameras and geometry in a single forward pass, but they report no uncertainty for the camera poses they predict: an incorrect relative pose looks no different from a correct one.
We ask whether the frozen model nonetheless
knows
when its pose is wrong.
On HardMatch, a benchmark of 1,000 deliberately difficult image pairs on which VGGT fails on 35% of pairs, a linear probe on VGGT’s frozen features predicts pose failure on held-out categories with ROC-AUC 93.5%, compared with 79.7% for VGGT’s own point-map confidence and 77.7% for a classifier trained on all of VGGT’s outputs.
The probe catches failures VGGT is confident about, lets a downstream system abstain on the pairs it distrusts, and transfers without retraining to rotation failures on PhotoTourism and ScanNet-1500, beyond what co-visibility explains.
This knowledge is absent from the per-image encoder: it is computed partway through the layers that fuse the two views, and the same holds for a second model,
π
3
\pi^{3}
.
In essence, we find that VGGT knows more about its own failures than it reports.

It outputs a per-pixel confidence for depth and point maps, but no uncertainty for the camera poses it regresses. Downstream systems, such as SLAM, mapping, novel-view synthesis, therefore cannot distinguish a reliable relative pose from a badly wrong one.
Two observations make this gap worth studying.

article.headline: VGGT冻结特征比自身置信度更早知道失败
article.lede: 线性探针在冻结的VGGT特征上预测位姿失败，ROC-AUC达93.5%，远高于模型自带点图置信度的79.7%。
article.problem: 前馈三维重建模型（如VGGT）一次前向就回归出相机与几何，却对预测的相机位姿不提供任何不确定性，错误的相对位姿与正确的看上去没有区别。而这类模型确实会失败：在HardMatch基准上，VGGT有35%的图像对几何明显错误。论文追问的是，冻结的模型内部是否「知道」自己的位姿错了。
article.method: 作者在VGGT冻结特征上训练线性探针（PCA降到128维后接L2正则逻辑回归），采用按HardMatch类别分组的10折交叉验证，保证测试类别从未在训练中出现，并与点图置信度、深度置信度以及「在VGGT全部输出上训练的分类器」对比。为了定位信号来源，他们逐块探测编码器与聚合器的每一层，并在第二个模型π³上重复同样流程。最后把在HardMatch上训练好的探针不做任何重训，直接迁移到PhotoTourism与ScanNet-1500。
article.results: 过滤后HardMatch共903对、97个类别，VGGT在50 px阈值下失败率34.9%（10/20/100 px下分别为63.7%、51.5%、25.1%）。探针在未见类别上的ROC-AUC为93.5%［91.7, 95.2］，而VGGT的点图置信度为79.7%［76.6, 82.4］，在其全部输出上训练的分类器也只有77.7%；以0.5为阈值，探针判对87.5%的样本，以78.9%的精确率抓到87.6%的失败。在VGGT最有信心的那一半样本中仍有12.2%失败，此时探针AUC为90.0%，置信度仅69.9%；按置信度四分位分层后，层内置信度接近随机（47%–64%），探针仍有82%–92%。信号在聚合器中部突然出现：编码器各块不超过65.2%，块11之后为69%，块12后升到81%，块15后达93%。π³上同样成立，最好探针91.7%对比其自身置信度62.2%（其最有信心一半上仅52.8%）。零样本迁移到PhotoTourism的旋转失败，10°阈值下AUC 94.6%、15°下97.5%，高于真值co-visibility的87.0%/89.8%。选择性问题：保留探针最信任的50%样本，失败率降到3.8%（按置信度排序为12.4%），风险-覆盖率曲线下面积为0.096，接近完美排序0.070，约填补了置信度与oracle之间70%的差距。
article.why_it_matters: 这意味着在SLAM、建图、新视角合成等下游系统中，只需在模型本来就算出的特征上加一层线性分类器，就能在不可信位姿上主动弃权，而不必依赖模型输出的置信度。它也说明语言模型中被广泛研究的「内部知道自己错了」现象，同样存在于三维基础模型中。
article.limitations: 硬伤有三处：探针本身是有失败标签监督训练的，而VGGT的置信度是免费的，作者的应对是同一协议下训练输出分类器并做跨数据集测试；HardMatch没有真值位姿，失败由每对约11个标注点对应的极射误差定义，混入了旋转、平移与内参误差。研究只覆盖VGGT与π³两个模型、且以两视图为主，多视图下PhotoTourism失败率降到0.3%、探针不再明显优于置信度，用探针筛边也没有改善旋转平均。更要紧的是,单一探针无法覆盖ScanNet上主导的短基线平移失败（AUC仅44%–48%，置信度为61%–64%），而ScanNet自训练的探针能达到90.5%–91.0%，说明模型内部的失败感知不是单一标量。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图1：同一座大门的航拍与地面视角——VGGT对该图像对的置信度高于74%的HardMatch样本，但其预测相机推出的极线偏离标注点141 px，而冻结特征上的线性探针成功标出了这次失败。

email_papers.title: Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces
email_papers.abstract: Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Harnesses are often revised and judged by how an already trained model performs under them, which assumes that what the model learned under one harness carries over to the next. We ask what a policy learns from its harness and what survives when the harness changes. Under KL-regularized control, we show that the log odds of an optimal policy recover how strongly its harness favors each action over the others, so a trained policy carries the preferences of its harness. Deployed return then equals the ceiling of the harness, the best return it offers, minus the mismatch of the policy, the return lost to its own suboptimal decisions. Training changes only the mismatch, while changing the harness moves both terms. Comparing harnesses with a fixed model therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well that model uses it. In MiniWoB++, post-training makes a model's preferences specific to its training harness. Reversing the order of the observation fields leaves every optimal decision unchanged yet lowers a trained model's success from 85.0% to 19.2%. Conversely, every new harness that a fixed-model comparison rejects but that raises the ceiling outperforms the original agent after further training under it, and ceiling and mismatch measured beforehand predict these gains. For coding-agent harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite, ceiling minus mismatch estimated with a stronger model as a stand-in for the optimum reproduces the accuracy ranking, while either term alone does not. Code is available at https://github.com/2020-qqtcg/HRP.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Harnesses are often revised and judged by how an already trained model performs under them, which assumes that what the model learned under one harness carries over to the next. We ask what a policy learns from its harness and what survives when the harness changes. Under KL-regularized control, we show that the log odds of an optimal policy recover how strongly its harness favors each action over the others, so a trained policy carries the preferences of its harness. Deployed return then equals the ceiling of the harness, the best return it offers, minus the mismatch of the policy, the return lost to its own suboptimal decisions. Training changes only the mismatch, while changing the harness moves both terms. Comparing harnesses with a fixed model therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well that model uses it. In MiniWoB++, post-training makes a model’s preferences specific to its training harness. Reversing the order of the observation fields leaves every optimal decision unchanged yet lowers a trained model’s success from 85.0% to 19.2%. Conversely, every new harness that a fixed-model comparison rejects but that raises the ceiling outperforms the original agent after further training under it, and ceiling and mismatch measured beforehand predict these gains. For coding-agent harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite, ceiling minus mismatch estimated with a stronger model as a stand-in for the optimum reproduces the accuracy ranking, while either term alone does not.

Introduction
Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Interface design and prompt formatting change agent performance
(
Yang et al., 2024
;
Sclar et al., 2024
)
. Automated harness design revises prompts, tools, and workflows and scores each candidate by how a fixed model performs under it
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025b
;
Fernando et al., 2023
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. Such a score assumes that what the model learned under earlier harnesses carries over to each candidate, yet the same interface change can raise one model’s accuracy and lower that of a fine-tuned model
(
Mu et al., 2025
)
. At the same time, training can move behavior that a prompt or a harness supplies into the weights
(
Snell et al., 2022
;
Ye et al., 2026
)
, and recent methods adapt harnesses and weights together
(
Hebbar et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
. These practices raise the question we study:
What does a policy learn from its harness, and what survives when the harness changes?
Two experiments make the question concrete. In the first, we take a web agent post-trained under one harness and reverse the order of the fields in its observation, a JSON object with fields such as the task instruction, the page state, and the available actions. The fields keep their contents. We also hold fixed the actions, their execution, the rewards, and the reference policy that regularizes training, so every optimal decision stays the same. The model still changes its most probable action at about half of the states, and its task success falls from 85.0% to 19.2%. Keeping the decisions a model should make does not keep the decisions it makes.
Figure 1:
Adaptation reverses a frozen comparison. The left group evaluates the model trained under Harness 0, the source checkpoint, under both harnesses with its weights frozen. The right group evaluates the models after equal further training under each harness. The dotted line marks the source checkpoint’s success under Harness 0, and colors mark the evaluation harness.
In the second, a new harness adds batched clicks, which execute two clicks in one decision. The new actions raise the best achievable return, yet the trained model’s success drops when we move it to the new harness without changing its weights. A frozen comparison, which evaluates candidate harnesses with the same trained weights, would therefore reject the new harness. We then train the model further for the same budget under each harness, starting from the same trained weights, which we call the source checkpoint. We call further training under the new harness adaptation, and further training under the original harness continuation. The adapted model succeeds more often than both the source checkpoint and the continued one. The harness that first hurt the model gives the best agent. Figure
1
shows the task success at each step, with the new harness as Harness 1.
We explain both results in the control problem that a harness induces over semantic actions, the operations an agent executes together with their arguments. Under KL-regularized control, the optimal policy is a softmax over action scores. Each score adds an action’s long-term value to its log probability under the reference policy, so an optimal policy’s log odds between two actions are proportional to the difference of their scores. A policy trained to optimality under a harness therefore carries the relative action scores that the harness induces, even though it contains none of the harness’s code, tools, or execution machinery. In this sense, a policy is secretly a harness. In our controlled study, real post-training moves a model’s action scores toward the optimum of its training harness, and each harness leaves its own preferences in the model.
Figure 2:
A harness revision and a weight update act on different terms. Summit heights are the ceilings, the robot’s altitude is its return, and the gap between them is the mismatch. Moving the trained model to the new harness with frozen weights (① to ②) raises the ceiling but lowers the return. Updating the weights under the new harness (② to ③) lowers only the mismatch. The adapted model beats the source checkpoint under the original harness once its mismatch
M
′
M^{\prime}
falls below
T
T
, the new ceiling minus the source checkpoint’s return under the original harness.
Action scores also show why a trained policy can fail after it is moved to a new harness. The scores a policy carries are the ones it expresses through its training interface, which we call its readout through that interface, and the same weights can express different scores through another interface. A policy is thus secretly its training harness, as read through that harness. A new harness can therefore change which actions are optimal, by moving the optimal scores, and separately change which actions the model picks, by moving the readout. Reversing the observation fields leaves the optimal scores in place and moves only the readout.
Scores fix decisions but not how much return a harness offers, since raising every reward by the same constant changes no decision. To convert score changes into return, we therefore add this value back by applying the regularized performance-gap identity
(
Geist et al., 2019
;
O’Donoghue, 2022
)
to the harness-induced problem. Deployed return equals the harness’s ceiling
C
C
, the best return any policy can reach under it, minus the policy’s mismatch
M
M
, the return the policy loses by departing from the optimal policy. The mismatch is the KL divergence from the optimal policy, accumulated along the policy’s own trajectories. The ceiling does not depend on the model’s weights, so training under a fixed harness changes only
M
M
, while a harness change can move both terms. A frozen comparison of harnesses therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well the current checkpoint uses it. In the batched-click example, the new harness raises the ceiling slightly but raises the frozen model’s mismatch about ten times as much, so return falls. Adaptation then lowers the mismatch, and once the mismatch falls below a threshold we derive, the adapted model beats the original model under the original harness. Figure
2
illustrates both steps. Our contributions are as follows.

Measuring Mismatch in Deployment
The results so far use full action distributions and a solved optimum. A deployed agent exposes only sampled actions and may have no known optimum, so we estimate mismatch from action samples, first against a known optimal policy and then against a teacher model in its place.
6.1

Discussion and Conclusion
A policy trained under a harness learns the harness’s relative action scores and expresses them through its interface. Post-training makes these preferences harness-specific, and a new interface can change the model’s choices even when every optimal decision stays the same. Because deployed return is the ceiling minus the mismatch, a harness that offers more can hurt a trained model and become the best choice after adaptation. Mismatch estimated from sampled actions predicts these changes when the optimum is known, and for coding agents, teacher-based estimates of ceiling minus mismatch order harnesses by accuracy. Harness evaluations should therefore report the ceiling next to the frozen return, evaluate several checkpoints under each harness rather than a single one, and check how presentation changes move the model’s choices. Harness distillation and joint adaptation of harnesses and weights
(
Ye et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
can use sampled-action measurements to track the ceiling and the mismatch separately. Appendix
A
discusses related work.

Experimental Details
We describe the experiments in the order of the main text: the MiniWoB++ setup and post-training study, the readout study, the H0-to-H1 adaptation study, the adaptation across harness swaps, the calibration of finite measurements, the independent prediction study, the coding-agent harness study, and the exact comparison of harness scores with task success.
F.1
MiniWoB++ Setup and Post-Training
The controlled study pairs language-model post-training with a finite control model of each harness. This gives every checkpoint a fixed optimal policy to compare against, while retaining task instructions, parameterized actions, and controller feedback in the model’s input.
We compare six harnesses, H0–H5, using H0 as the direct baseline.
Tasks and observations.
We use three tasks from MiniWoB++
(
Liu et al., 2018
)
. In
click-checkboxes
, the agent toggles checkboxes to match the requested labels and submits the selection. In
click-checkboxes-soft
, the requested words and checkbox labels are matched by synonym meaning. In
ascending-numbers
, the agent clicks five tiles in numerical order, with the remaining numbers hidden after the first click. We retain the initially visible layout in the public observation, together with spatial tile IDs, the remaining tiles, and the number of completed clicks. Checkbox observations contain the instruction, each label and its checked status. All actor observations also expose the remaining decision budget and the harness’s controller state.
The reward is one for exact task completion and zero otherwise, including partial completion. All explicit action and tool costs are zero. Each episode allows at most ten actor decisions, with discount
γ
=
0.95
\gamma=0.95
per decision. We compile the physical transitions, remaining budget, and controller memory into a finite acyclic graph. For every retained task, we verify a successful run in the native browser and separately compare the compiled transitions and termination rules with the page behavior. Training and exhaustive policy evaluation use these compiled graphs.

article.headline: 策略其实是框架：换接口为何让智能体崩溃
article.lede: 论文把智能体回报拆成框架上限与策略失配：换接口抬高上限却放大失配，重新训练后又反超。
article.problem: 语言模型智能体在后训练和部署时都依赖一套 harness（提示、工具与控制逻辑），而自动化的 harness 设计通常用固定权重的模型给候选接口打分，默认模型在旧接口学到的东西能迁移到新接口。但同一处接口改动可能让一个模型变好、让微调后的模型变差，因此需要回答：策略究竟从 harness 里学到了什么，换掉 harness 之后什么会留下来。
article.method: 作者在 KL 正则化控制下证明，最优策略的 log odds 正比于动作分数之差，即策略携带了训练 harness 对各动作的相对偏好；再用正规化性能差恒等式把部署回报写成「上限 C 减失配 M」，训练只改变 M，换 harness 则同时移动两项。实验在 MiniWoB++ 的三个任务、六套 harness（H0–H5）上做受控对照：翻转观测字段顺序、加入批量点击动作，并比较冻结权重与等量继续训练后的表现。在 Terminal-Bench Lite 上，则以更强模型代替最优策略来估计 C 与 M。
article.results: 翻转观测字段顺序不改变任何最优决策，但训练模型的成功率从 85.0% 降到 19.2%；批量点击的新 harness 抬高了上限，却把冻结模型的失配放大约十倍，回报因此下降。在同一份源 checkpoint 上等量继续训练后，被冻结比较否决但抬高上限的九个换 harness 情形全部反超原智能体，且事前测得的 ceiling 与 mismatch 能预测增益（预测式为 T−r2）。Terminal-Bench Lite 上，用更强模型估计的「上限减失配」复现了编码智能体的准确率排序，而单看上限或单看失配都做不到。受控任务每回合最多十次决策，γ=0.95；C 与 M 的具体数值论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明用单一份冻结权重给 harness 打分，会把「接口提供多少」和「当前模型用得多好」混在一起，可能系统性否决那些先伤模型、适配后却最优的接口。作者据此建议 harness 评测同时报告 ceiling 与冻结回报，并在多个 checkpoint 上评估。
article.limitations: 受控部分只覆盖 MiniWoB++ 的三个任务，ceiling 与 mismatch 依赖把 harness 编译成有限控制图并已知最优解；真实部署只能靠采样与教师模型近似，Terminal-Bench Lite 上的排序复现属于代理指标，并非真值验证。增益预测需要事先估计 T 与 r2，这套分解在更大模型、更长任务上是否成立，论文未给出具体数字。

email_papers.title: MLE-World: Predicting Machine Learning Experiment Outcomes with a Learned World Model
email_papers.abstract: AI research agents can propose, execute, and improve programs that solve machine learning tasks. However, executing each candidate program requires training and evaluating ML models, limiting how many candidates an agent can explore at each step. We introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program's terminal output (error traces, training logs, and validation scores) from its code and data description without executing it, together with a confidence score estimating the prediction's correctness. Because a prediction costs one inference call rather than a training run, MLE-World makes test time scaling (TTS) affordable for these agents. We build five TTS policies, guided by MLE-World, that compare several candidates per step by their predicted outputs: Sequential revision, Best-of-N, Pairwise judging, Fusion, and a UCB style rule that also adds an exploration bonus from this confidence score. Since predictions can be wrong, we run a candidate for real only when its confidence score is low. On 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks, MLE-World matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held out programs, versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models. MLE-World guided TTS achieves up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance than the agent without a world model, with less real execution. Project webpage: https://mle-world.github.io/.

Abstract
AI research agents can propose, execute, and improve programs that solve machine learning tasks. However,
executing each candidate program requires training and evaluating ML models, limiting how many candidates an agent can explore at each step. We introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program’s

together with a confidence score estimating the prediction’s correctness. Because a prediction costs one inference call rather than a training run, MLE-World

Limitations and conclusion
Limitations.
Our main evaluation is in distribution: new programs on 17 tasks seen in finetuning
(Appendix
E
). On three tasks excluded from finetuning, the 4B MLE-World, without
reasoning, still predicts terminal output more accurately than much larger prompted models (53.3%
versus 42.1% for DeepSeek with reasoning and 21.1% for Coder; Appendix
R
). This opens
a generalizable world model as future work, for example by adding reasoning or scaling up the model.
Training uses about 500,000 prior executions, including earlier trajectories from a 9B agent but no
reported runs, favoring settings with accumulated logs. Zero shot baselines and Base AIDE lack this task knowledge;
nonparametric corpus baselines trail MLE-World (Table
1
), while Base AIDE with corpus access
remains untested. Real execution determines final scores; prediction errors can misdirect search. Timeouts are
the least accurately predicted outcome, and a missed timeout still costs a full run; improving runtime prediction is future work.
Conclusion.
A 4B model finetuned on logged executions predicts the outcomes of new programs more accurately
than much larger prompted models, at 13–1,061
×
\times
less GPU inference time. This makes test
time scaling affordable for MLE agents: all five world model guided policies have higher observed mean
percentiles than the agent without a world model. Gating reduces real execution time by 30–40% while broadly maintaining performance.

Ethics statement
This work raises no ethical concerns. Its experiments use only public Kaggle competition data
distributed with MLE-bench and involve no human subjects or personal data.

LLM usage
LLMs are part of the method: Qwen3.5 models generate agent programs and Qwen3-Coder-Next
judges outputs. An LLM coding agent (GPT-5.6 Sol) developed the judge prompt
under the protocol of Appendix
I
. The authors also used LLM assistants to write
experiment and analysis code and to edit the text, and remain responsible for all content.

article.headline: 4B 世界模型预测 ML 实验，替代真实执行
article.lede: 微调 Qwen3.5-4B 预测程序终端输出与置信度，让 ML 智能体的测试时扩展变得可负担。
article.problem: AI 研究智能体能反复提出并改进机器学习程序，但每个候选都要真实训练和评估，执行时间限制了每步可探索的候选数量。因此，让反馈变便宜、只对少数候选真实执行，成为高效搜索的核心问题。
article.method: 作者从 Qwen3.5-4B 微调出世界模型 MLE-World，只输入当前程序代码与数据描述，预测其终端输出（报错轨迹、训练日志、验证分数），并给出一个估计预测正确性的置信度；代价是一次推理调用而非一次训练。以它为基础构建五种测试时扩展策略：顺序修订、Best-of-N、两两比较、融合，以及用置信度作探索奖励的 UCB；只有当置信度低时才真实运行候选，即门控。
article.results: 在 17 个 MLE-bench Lite 任务上，MLE-World 对 1,700 个留出程序的终端输出预测与真实执行一致率为 77.9%，规模更大的提示模型为 41.1%。由它引导的测试时扩展策略比没有世界模型的智能体最多高出 22.1% 的观测平均性能，同时真实执行更少；报告中 GPU 推理时间少 13–1,061 倍。门控使真实执行时间减少 30–40%：置信度门控每 trial 用 4.49 小时，随机门控用 5.54 小时，少 19%，而平均百分位差为 −0.15±2.32（标准误），即未确立质量差异。
article.why_it_matters: 把昂贵的执行反馈换成一次便宜的前向预测，ML 智能体就能在相同时间预算内比较多得多的候选，为研究型智能体的测试时扩展提供了可落地路径。
article.limitations: 主实验是分布内评估（微调时见过的 17 个任务）；在 3 个未参与微调的任务上，4B 模型的预测准确率为 53.3%，虽高于带推理的 DeepSeek（42.1%）与 Coder（21.1%），但泛化仍是未来工作。超时是最难预测的结果，漏判一次超时仍要付一次完整运行代价，预测错误也可能把搜索引向错误方向。

Each policy uses four candidates and returns one program.

email_papers.title: EmbodiedLab: Benchmarking Embodied Agents That Act to Know
email_papers.abstract: Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings. For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know. Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries. We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know. Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly. Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras. Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers' coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab.

Abstract
Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings.
For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know.
Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries.
We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know.
Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly.
Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras.
Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable.
We evaluate six frontier models in their developers’ coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents.
With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning.
The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at
https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab
.

Overview of EmbodiedLab.
Thirty quantitative experiments in five disciplines ask the agent to measure, predict or configure a system drawn anew per instance, by changing its state and reading the feedback on the instruments. Agents are ranked by their success rate at the lowest interface level, T0, and also evaluated at T1; the diagnostic level T2 and four capability dimensions serve the analysis.
1
Introduction
What distinguishes embodied intelligence from traditional robotics is who decides how to interact with the world
[
1
,
2
]
.
A traditional robot carries out a procedure engineered in advance for its task; an embodied agent is given a goal and must decide for itself what to interact with, how and when, in the environment it finds
[
3
,
4
]
.
Many real-world goals, such as finding out whether a wire is live, why a pump fails to start, or how to set a power supply so that it holds its voltage under load, cannot be reached by acting toward a known target.
The agent must first change the physical state of the system through interaction, observe the feedback, and explore until it either reaches the goal itself or learns what the goal requires; what it comes to know decides how it proceeds.
We call this
acting to know
: action whose purpose is to uncover information, with changing the physical state as its means
[
5
,
6
]
.
Embodied agents that couple frontier foundation models with tools and skills have begun to address tasks of this form
[
7
,
8
,
9
]
, solving long-horizon dexterous tasks without task-specific training
[
10
]
and adapting robots to the protocols of real biology laboratories
[
11
]

Quantitative science experiments are a controlled entry point to this setting.
An experiment poses an objective about a physical system rather than a procedure: determine one of its properties, predict its response, or configure an apparatus to meet a specification.
To meet it, the agent must set up and operate the apparatus, take readings under conditions of its own choosing and analyze them, and, for a prediction or a configuration, act again on what it has learned (
Fig.
2
).
The physical laws involved are familiar, yet the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result must be established on the system at hand; because it is a physical quantity or state, it can be hidden from the agent and scored exactly.
The difficulty arises from the physics and the experimental method, as in a teaching laboratory.
To this end, we introduce EmbodiedLab, a simulated laboratory of 30 quantitative experiments in mechanics, electricity, optics, thermal physics and chemistry on 14 apparatus platforms, operated by a robot arm with a two-finger gripper and observed through three cameras (
EmbodiedLab: Benchmarking Embodied
Agents That Act to Know
).
Its task, environment and metric each follow from acting to know (
Table
1
).
The
task
states the objective, the apparatus and the rules, and prescribes no method.
The
environment
is open as a real laboratory is: the bench offers more instruments, tools and materials than any one method needs, every operation is physical, readings appear on scales, pointers and displays that the agent reads through its cameras or in the records of data-logging instruments, and the agent acts through a code interface on which it builds its own tools for perception, control and analysis.
The
metric
checks what the agent came to know: a run succeeds only if its result lies within a tolerance set by the instruments, rests on readings recorded in the same episode, and leaves the bench in the state the task requires.
The last condition belongs to acting to know: the agent must undo every change it made except those the objective requires, and so keep track of them over the whole episode.
EmbodiedLab exposes its interface at three nested levels that take over more and more of the acting while leaving the experiment to the agent, so the change in success across levels shows how much of an agent’s failure lies in acting: T0 gives camera images, robot state and joint control, T1 adds privileged perception and motion planning, and T2 adds manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents’ successful runs (
Section
3.2
).
We evaluate six frontier models from five developers, each in the coding agent released by its developer at its middle reasoning setting, at T0 and T1, and the three whose runs contributed no skills also at T2 (
Section
4
).
Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra reach success rates of 43.3% and 40.0% at T0, the other agents at most 28.3%; for the strongest agents the stages with the lowest pass rates are knowing the result and restoring the bench, while the other agents lose most of their runs before their readings suffice.
Perception and motion planning change the success rate by at most 10 points, and manipulation skills raise it by 10 to 27 points, yet no agent that receives them reaches the strongest agent at T1.
Our contributions are summarized as follows.
•
A task formulation for acting to know.
We formulate embodied tasks in which the agent must change the physical state of a system to find out what its goal requires, instantiate them as quantitative experiments whose objective is a property, a prediction or a configuration, and describe how such tasks are constructed and validated.
•
A validated benchmark.
EmbodiedLab comprises 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms in an open laboratory environment, scored on the result, the evidence recorded in the episode and the required bench state. Every experiment is verified to be solvable and has its tolerance set by its instruments. We release the benchmark with its evaluation code.
•
Evaluation across levels of support.
We evaluate six frontier models in their developers’ coding agents at three nested levels, and measure where their runs stop and what each level changes. The strongest agent reaches a success rate of 43.3% at T0; added perception and planning help little, and manipulation skills help the weaker agents most.

An open laboratory
The 30 experiments run on 14 apparatus platforms (

Each is a parameterized scene in Isaac Sim

Every T0 policy is also a T1 and a T2 policy, so comparing the levels shows what each level changes.
T0 and T1 are the evaluation levels.
T2 is a diagnostic level: its skills come from successful runs on the same experiments, so a T2 run partly reuses known solutions; we use it only to measure how much of the failure lies in acting, and it is not part of the released protocol.
At every level the agent reads, records and analyzes for itself.

4.5
How agents fail
We attribute a failed run to its first decisive error: the earliest error the agent does not correct and after which success is no longer possible (
Appendix
F
).
The causes follow the stages of acting to know: acting on the apparatus (motion, contact), observing it (locating parts, reading instruments), knowing (procedure, analysis, deciding when to stop) and restoring the bench;
Fig.
10
a in the appendix gives the share of each cause among an agent’s failed runs with an attributed cause.
Acting is the largest group for every agent, and acting, observing and restoring together account for 75% to 100% of every agent’s failed runs, knowing for at most 25%.
For the DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM agents acting accounts for 64% to 69% of the failed runs, and contact alone for 45% to 62%: grasps that slip, parts that tip over, keys that are missed.
For the three strongest agents acting falls to 35% to 42%, and the failures spread over the later stages: knowing accounts for 15% to 25% and an untidy bench after an accurate result for 25% to 33%.
Observing errors are rarer but final, as reading instruments is still hard for vision-language models
[
55
]
: one misread digit decides the run, and they account for 23% of the failed runs of Claude Opus 5.5, its second largest cause.
GPT-6 Astra stops too early in 19% of its failed runs, for example by submitting fringe positions while the screen shows a single spot.
5
Conclusion
We introduced EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which an embodied agent must act to know, changing a physical system and reading instruments through cameras.
Acting to know is far from solved: at T0 the strongest agent reaches a success rate of 43.3%, and three agents at most 10%.
What an agent can know is bounded by how reliably it interacts: for strong and weak agents alike, most failed runs break in the physical loop through which the result is found out, as acting on the apparatus, observing it and restoring it account for 75% to 100% of them, and at most 25% fail in reasoning from readings already in hand.
The decisive errors are small, a grasp that slips, a digit misread, a part not put back, and lie in what the agent’s code does to the apparatus, not in the code itself.
The levels narrow it down: perception and motion planning change the success rate by at most 10 points, while manipulation skills raise the weaker agents by 10 to 27 points, yet with them these agents reach at most 14.3% in long-horizon work.
Acting to know therefore hinges on interacting with the physical world reliably enough, over a whole experiment, that what the agent does and sees can serve as evidence.
By scoring what an agent finds out with the evidence behind it and the bench it leaves, EmbodiedLab makes this measurable, and we release it to track progress toward embodied agents that act to know.

article.headline: 机器人要「动手才知道」，最强也难过半
article.lede: EmbodiedLab 用 30 个仿真物理实验考智能体：自己搭装置、读仪表、得结论，再按答案、证据和台面状态打分。
article.problem: 现有操作类基准把目标状态直接告诉机器人，只考察「动手改变」；科学发现类基准虽要求智能体找出隐藏规律，但动作是文本指令或数值查询，结果以文本或精确数值返回，中间没有真实的物理操作。真实任务里两者是耦合的：怎么动手决定能看到什么，看到什么又决定下一步怎么动手，而这一环此前没有被单独评测。
article.method: 作者把「act to know」形式化为定量实验任务：每个实例的隐藏参数重新采样，智能体拿到目标、公开参数和规则，但不给方法，必须在 Isaac Sim 的开放实验室里用 Franka 机械臂操作电路板、光具座等装置，通过三路相机读数。基准覆盖力学、电学、光学、热学和化学五个学科的 30 个实验、14 个装置平台，接口分为 T0（原始相机图像与关节控制）、T1（加分割、真值深度和避障规划）、T2（加由最强智能体成功轨迹蒸馏的操作技能）三层；评分同时检查结果是否在仪器容差内、引用读数是否来自本回合记录、台面是否复位。
article.results: T0 上 Claude Opus 5.5 成功率 43.3%、GPT-6 Astra 40.0%、GPT-6.1 Sol 28.3%，DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 与 Kimi K3 各 10.0%，GLM-5.3-Flash 为 0%，后三者没有一个解出进阶实验。30 个实验中 27 个至少被一个智能体解出，黑盒电阻、透镜焦距和双透镜中继无人解出。从 T0 到 T1，感知与运动规划只带来 1.7 到 10.0 个百分点的提升；T2 操作技能带来 10.0 到 26.7 个百分点的提升，但拿到技能的智能体在长程任务上最多只有 14.3%。失败归因显示，动手操作、读数观察与复位合计占各智能体失败运行的 75% 到 100%，仅有不超过 25% 败在推理环节；最强三个智能体的瓶颈在「结果在容差内」（阶段通过率 0.73 到 0.82）和「复位台面」（0.55 到 0.79）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「动手是为了知道」从操作基准和科学发现基准的缝隙里单独拿出来，并用同一物理回路打分，说明当前前沿模型的主要瓶颈不是推理而是可靠地与仪器打交道。对做具身智能体评测的人来说，这提供了一个可精确判分、参数不可预先查到的封闭测试床。
article.limitations: T2 层使用的技能是从最强智能体在同一批实验上的成功轨迹蒸馏出来的，部分复用了已知解，作者自己也只把它当作诊断层而非发布协议的一部分；所有实验都是教科书实验或直接延伸，且完全在 Isaac Sim 中完成，与真实湿实验室的摩擦、噪声和长尾故障仍有距离。此外每个实验的重复运行次数论文未给出具体数字，六个模型也只在各自厂商的默认 harness 与中等推理档位下评测。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图：所谓「动手才知道」——操作基准止于把场景改成给定目标状态，科学基准则不经物理动作直接获知；EmbodiedLab 让智能体在同一回路中改变装置状态、读取反馈再据此行动，提交时对所得结论、记录的证据和台面状态一并打分。

figure.caption: {Acting to know.} (a)~Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change the scene into a named target state; science benchmarks find things out without physical action. (b)~Given a goal, a agent changes the state of the apparatus through interaction, observes the feedback and acts again on what it learned, in the same loop across disciplines; at submission, what it found out, the evidence it recorded and the bench state are scored.

email_papers.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
email_papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) Timely tool invocation remains unreliable: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) Query-free reminders remain poorly covered: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.

Introduction
Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) such as GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-Omni, and Qwen3-Omni bring joint audiovisual understanding into conversational systems
(
Hurst et al., 2024
;
Xu et al., 2025a
;
Xu et al., 2025b
)
. Emerging streaming systems extend this ability to deciding when to speak, remain silent, or invoke tools
(
Chen et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2026b
;
ByteDance Seed, 2026
)
. For an assistant observing a changing environment, these decisions must serve a user’s ongoing needs: retrieve information when a requested event occurs, relay a relevant sound to a user with hearing impairment, or provide continue guidance as an activity unfolds (see Figure
1
). Useful assistance therefore requires connecting perceptual evidence to
what intervention is needed, when it is useful, and whether further responses remain necessary
.
Figure 1:
Overview of Omni-InteractScope.
Top:
Representative interactions connect user requests or general assistance needs with events in audiovisual streams and the content and timing of the required responses. The examples span event-timed tool invocation, a gesture reminder conditioned on an image and text request, and hearing
assistance under a general instruction without an event-specific query.
Bottom:
Distributions of task types, scene categories, and stream durations across the benchmark’s 1,479 interactions. Clips reused across multiple interactions are counted once for each interaction in which they appear.
Evaluation has progressed from video comprehension toward interactive assistance. Early works, such as Video-MME and LongVideoBench, assess understanding of supplied videos
(
Fu et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2024
)
, while StreamingBench and OVO-Bench restrict observations to available stream prefixes and test responses to unfolding events
(
Lin et al., 2026
;
Niu et al., 2025
)
. Recent benchmarks further evaluate multimodal turn-taking, audio-dependent proactivity, and event-triggered response windows
(
Wang et al., 2025b
;
Zhao et al., 2026
;

An assistant’s obligation extends beyond the content of its next answer. A specified event can require a tool call at a useful moment, a general assistance need can require intervention without an event-specific question, and a standing request can require further responses after an initial answer. Evaluating these requirements together calls for explicit links between user context, response content, valid timing, and successive targets. It also calls for distinguishing scene evidence from request priors and target coverage from the opportunities allowed to respond. This combination makes it possible to examine both whether an intervention obligation is fulfilled and which evaluation conditions shape the result.
We introduce
Omni-InteractScope
, a benchmark organized around the relationship between stream evidence, user needs, and required interventions. It contains 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets. The assistance panel draws on 207 self-recorded first-person videos. The benchmark links four dimensions: input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs. Eight task groups span tool invocation, notifications, warnings, cumulative-state tracking, temporal conditions, nonverbal cues, continuous responses, and impairment assistance. Each target specifies response content and a valid time or interval. Interactions with multiple targets record the responses required after an initial answer. This organization supports evaluating both individual interventions and coverage of continuing obligations within a shared resource.
Within this broad coverage, we focus on two complementary demands of proactive interaction. Tool invocation requires selecting the appropriate tool and acting when a user-specified event occurs. Query-free assistance requires recognizing when a general user need warrants a reminder without an event-specific query. Paired controls examine the roles of scene evidence and response policy, while successive targets assess whether the assistant delivers the further responses required as an interaction unfolds.
Evaluation across 12 models reveals substantial limitations in both timely intervention and sustained assistance. Every evaluated model produces an on-time first response for at most 40% of tool-invocation targets, and joint accuracy reaches at most 32.0%. Timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders never exceeds 23.0%. Although guidance-step recall reaches 51.7%, nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and no model covers more than three.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We introduce Omni-InteractScope, a comprehensive benchmark for timely and sustained omnimodal intervention. It comprises 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions across eight task groups, with 1,790 targets specifying what to produce and when, including successive responses under continuing user needs.
•
We provide focused evaluation of event-timed action and query-free initiative through 200 tool-invocation targets and 122 query-free reminders. Our diagnostics distinguish tool choice from timing and test whether invocation scores depend on scene evidence. Paired controls further examine how explicit event cues, response scheduling, history, and response frequency affect coverage on the same
reminder targets.
•
We perform a comprehensive evaluation of 12 multimodal models, providing empirical insights into timing, query-free assistance, and sequence coverage, exposing gaps between tool selection and timely action, question answering, and query-free reminders, and step coverage and complete guidance.

Omni-InteractScope
Omni-InteractScope comprises 1,479 interactions across eight task groups, organized around the interventions an assistant should deliver as a stream unfolds. Figure
1
summarizes the design, and Figure
2
illustrates each task group in details.
Figure 2:
Representative interactions across the eight task groups of Omni-InteractScope.
Each panel links a user request (Q), timestamped stream observations, and reference responses (A) to illustrate what intervention is required and when.
