3.1
Designing for timely and sustained intervention
The benchmark unit is an interaction: a video and audio stream, user context, and one or more reference interventions. Each intervention is a target specifying the required response and its reference time or valid interval. For a continuing request, the interaction retains successive targets in temporal order.
We organize this unit along four linked dimensions.
Input modalities
describe the available video, scene audio, and user context conveyed through text, speech, or image attachments.
Event triggers
describe the evidence or condition associated with a response, such as an object appearing, a sound, an accumulated count, or elapsed time.
Intervention types
specify what the assistant should produce: an answer, notification, warning, tool call, or successive commentary or guidance.
User needs
determine why that intervention matters, through an explicit request or a general visual- or hearing-assistance instruction.
Together, these dimensions connect stream evidence and user context to the interventions an assistant should provide. The eight task groups organize these requirements into a comprehensive evaluation of response content, timing, and coverage, encompassing both individual interventions and successive responses under continuing user needs.
3.2
Task coverage and focal settings
Responding to explicit requests.
Seven task groups contain 1,180 interactions with different monitoring demands.
Event notification (T2)
asks the assistant to report a specified occurrence, while
risk/error interjection (T3)
calls for a warning when an unsafe or incorrect action occurs.
Nonverbal/workflow cues (T6)
connect a gesture or workflow event to the requested response, including matching a gesture to a query image.
Cumulative-state tracking (T4)
uses earlier observations to interpret current events.
Temporal conditions (T5)
introduce obligations governed by elapsed time.
Continuous responses (T7)
extend a standing request across successive commentary or translation segments.
Event-timed tool invocation.
T1 tests whether a model invokes the appropriate tool when a specified event occurs. A request can indicate which tool to use before the stream establishes when to act. Each target therefore specifies a tool-name set and invocation time. Evaluation covers these requirements, with arguments and downstream execution outside its scope.
Assistance under explicit and general needs.
The 299-interaction
impairment-assistance panel (T8)
covers visual- and hearing-assistance needs.
Query-free reminders (T8-A)
require identifying useful interventions under a general instruction, without an event-specific question.
Audiovisual questions (T8-B)
test answering explicit requests, while
multi-step guidance (T8-C)
tests successive responses along recorded trajectories. Both T7 and T8-C retain ordered targets within each interaction to represent continuing response obligations. Appendix
A.2
details the category boundaries.
3.3
Data construction and annotation
The benchmark combines 905 online video records for explicit-request tasks with 207 self-recorded first-person video records for impairment assistance. It spans indoor, outdoor, and digital-screen settings, with QA text approximately balanced between English and Chinese (744 and 735 interactions, respectively). The 1,479 interactions contain 1,790 targets, with multiple targets in 163 interactions. Appendix
A
details task counts, scene and trigger distributions, duration statistics, and source provenance, including repeated source identities among video records.
Human annotators specified user context, reference responses, triggers, and response times or valid intervals. A separate group of human reviewers cross-checked the annotations to obtain the final benchmark. This review covers both response content and its temporal relation to the event. Appendix
A.4
documents the supplemental consistency audit and review records.

5.1
Scene evidence and tool-invocation scores
Figure
3
a shows that removing scene input does not lower Gemini-3.5-Flash’s T1 accuracy. On the same 200 interactions, joint accuracy is 29.50% with scene input and 33.00% without it, with requests and the evaluation protocol held fixed. The paired difference is
−

Joint accuracy alone therefore does not establish event-grounded invocation. Appendices

The request-only control reveals strong task priors. Gemini-3.5-Flash selects 96.5% of tools from request text and public definitions alone. Emitting these choices after a fixed three-second delay gives 68.0% joint success, the highest of four tested delays. This separate control uses a closed-label output interface and different response opportunities from the main evaluation, so it diagnoses request and timing priors rather than providing a matched model ranking (Appendix

5.2
Reminder coverage under different response policies
As shown in Figure
3

Adding a cooldown reduces outputs further but costs 9.84 percentage points of recall relative to history alone. The policy is implemented by skipping generation calls during the cooldown, restricting the opportunities to cover reminder targets (Appendix
D.2.2
).
Figure
3

Gemini-3.5-Flash and Qwen2.5-Omni benefit from event cues when a response is requested at an annotated valid time. Under autonomous responding, however, the effects are small and uncertain. The benefit of event cues is therefore clearer when the response time is supplied than when the model must decide when to intervene. Scheduling changes temporal information and response opportunities together, so this comparison does not isolate a planning mechanism.
5.3
Complete guidance relative to step coverage
On the same 20 three-step T8-C episodes, Gemini-3.1-Pro covers 30 of 60 steps but completes only three sequences. Complete T8-C complements step recall by recording whether all required guidance was delivered.
Figure
D.3
(Appendix
D.3

An average of 2.4 complete sequences is expected if successes at different step positions are independent. The observed count is consistent with this reference and does not establish a separate memory or planning failure.
6
Discussion
Invocation scores need evidence controls.
The T1 controls show that request information and response timing can sustain joint success without scene inputs. A tool-and-time score should therefore be accompanied by evidence controls when used to assess event grounding. For streaming tool use
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
, varying event occurrence and timing while holding requests fixed would test a stronger requirement than the scene ablation evaluated here.
Coverage depends on the response policy.
Response history reduces Gemini-3.5-Flash’s output volume with the same aggregate recall point estimate, while a cooldown reduces both outputs and coverage. These findings connect response-frequency evaluation
(
Chatterjee et al., 2026
)
to the policies used during generation. Reporting history access and output rate alongside recall makes this dependence visible. Selectivity additionally requires evaluating the value and cost of interventions beyond the annotated targets, an important direction for future benchmark development.
Complete coverage has a separate measurement role.
Users may need every guidance step even when individual responses are often correct. Complete T8-C expresses that requirement, while the sequence reference limits attribution of low completion to a separate memory or planning failure. For goal-oriented assistants
(
Sun et al., 2026
)
, explicit records of delivered guidance and pending obligations remain a design hypothesis to test through interventions on history and state.
7
Conclusion
We introduced Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark for timely and sustained intervention in continuous omnimodal streams. Its 1,479 human-annotated interactions span eight task groups, linking user needs and stream evidence to 1,790 targets that specify response content and timing. Evaluation across 12 models reveals substantial limitations in timely tool invocation, query-free reminders, and complete guidance coverage. These findings underscore the need to assess whether assistants fulfill the response requirements of an interaction, including interventions that remain necessary after an initial answer. Omni-InteractScope provides a shared basis for developing and evaluating assistants that respond to unfolding events and sustain support for continuing user needs.

A.2
Taxonomy definitions and boundaries
Trigger labels describe annotated evidence rather than establishing that a
modality is indispensable under every input condition. Intervention type describes
the output, while user need explains its purpose. Similar outputs can therefore
arise from explicit event requests or general assistance instructions, with
different requirements for initiative.
Requested actions and notifications (T1–T3).
T1 requires invoking the reference tool set when the event occurs; tool identity
and timing are scored, while arguments and execution are outside the metric.
T2 reports a requested occurrence. T3 additionally requires communicating an
unsafe or incorrect action: merely announcing the event does not convey the
required warning.
What makes a response due (T4–T6).
T4 depends on accumulated observations, such as the start of a third dish after
two earlier preparations. T5 depends on an elapsed duration and is reported
separately. T6 responds to a gesture or workflow cue, which can require matching
the observed gesture to a query image. A query attachment specifies the sought
cue; the stream supplies evidence that it has occurred.
General assistance and explicit questions (T8-A/B).
T8-A supplies a general visual- or hearing-assistance need without an
event-specific question. The model must identify a useful reminder from the
stream. T8-B instead names the immediate information need through an explicit
audiovisual request. Similar response wording can therefore reflect different
requirements for initiative.
Continuing responses and actionable guidance (T7, T8-C).
Both contain successive targets under one standing need. T7 covers continuing
commentary or translation. T8-C requires actionable instructions justified by
successive states along a recorded assistance trajectory and defines the unit
for complete-guidance reporting. T1–T7 group interventions and triggering
conditions, whereas T8 groups assistance needs; timely action and sustained
coverage can consequently apply to several task groups.
A.3

The explicit-request panel contains 905 video records: 888 from Douyin, 11 from
Xiaohongshu, and six from Bilibili, with 495 first-person and 410 third-person
records. The assistance panel uses 207 self-recorded first-person videos for
261 visual-impairment and 38 hearing-impairment interactions. QA text is approximately balanced
between English and Chinese at 744 and 735 interactions, respectively; scene audio retains its
original language. Indoor, outdoor, and digital-screen settings account for
37.4%, 34.3%, and 28.1% of interactions. Median clip duration is 2.16 minutes,
and the 90th percentile is 6.15 minutes. Figure

The 1,112 video records are storage and analysis units, not necessarily distinct
original sources. Seven groups in the explicit-request panel share platform
identities. Uncertainty estimates use video-record clusters; the source inventory
and identifier discrepancies are documented in the provenance materials.
Construction proceeds from source records to interaction annotations and then
cross-review. For each interaction, annotators record the user request or general
need, query time and attachments where applicable, and the required interventions.
Each target retains its content, triggering evidence, and time or interval. Related
targets remain ordered in one interaction, preserving the distinction between a

cross-checks the annotations to produce the final benchmark.

Correct facts, names, quantities, and yes/no decisions.
Wrong facts, hallucinations, or refusals.
Event
The same event with its key subject, object, and action.
Generic narration, an unrelated event, or an incorrect participant or action.
Translation
The reference meaning, allowing synonyms and differences in fluency.
Omitted meaning or added content.
Assistance
The target information and any essential action. A guidance step
must state the currently actionable instruction.
Contradictory directions, unsafe advice, invented critical details, a generic
warning, or repetition of the user’s intention.

article.headline: 新基准测流式助手：及时行动与主动提醒仍难达标
article.lede: Omni-InteractScope 用 1479 段人工标注交互、1790 个时间目标，评测 12 个模型在连续音视频
article.problem: 全模态大模型正被期待在观察连续音视频流的同时为用户提供协助，但现有评测很少能看清它们是否能把流中的证据与用户需求连接起来，在恰当时刻做出干预并持续跟进。已有基准多聚焦视频理解或单轮流式问答，对「何时行动」「在没有明确提问时是否主动提醒」「一次请求下的后续响应是否完成」缺乏同时覆盖的测量。
article.method: 作者构建了 Omni-InteractScope：1479 个人工标注、交叉复核的交互，含 1790 个带响应内容与有效时间窗的目标，覆盖八个任务组，视频来源包括 905 条在线视频和 207 条自录第一人称视频，中英文问答分别约 744 与 735 个交互。评测分两条路径：提示模型用独立因果前缀做离线探测，流式模型用保留状态的在线滚动；T1–T7 对首个响应计分，时间容差为 2 秒，T8 用保序匹配计算目标召回并单独统计完整引导序列覆盖率。诊断实验还设置了场景输入消融、仅请求先验、响应历史与冷却、事件指令与调度交叉等对照。
article.results: 12 个模型中，工具调用任务（T1，200 个目标）的准时首次响应最多只有 40%，联合「工具对且时间对」最高为 Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus 的 32.0%；无提问主动提醒（T8-A，122 个目标）的及时召回最高为 Gemini-3.1-Pro 的 22.95%，同模型在显式问答（T8-B）上为 62.25%。引导任务（T8-C）单步召回最高 51.72%，但 26 条引导序列中 9 个模型一条都没完整覆盖，最好的模型也只完成 3 条。消融显示，Gemini-3.5-Flash 去掉画面输入后 T1 联合准确率反而从 29.50% 升到 33.00%（差 −3.50 点，95% CI [−7.00, −0.50]）；仅凭请求文本就能选出 96.5% 的工具，在固定 3 秒延迟下发射可达 68.0% 联合成功。给模型响应历史把输出从 7833 条降到 3283 条（−58.09%），召回仍为 22/122；再加 10 秒冷却后召回降到 10/122。
article.why_it_matters: 这些结果表明，工具调用分数本身不足以证明模型真的把行为锚定在画面事件上，而单步正确率也会掩盖「整段引导是否讲完」的失败。基准为流式助手提供了一个可同时考察时机、主动性与响应序列覆盖的公共测试面。
article.limitations: 作者指出，未匹配的输出不计惩罚，因此召回不衡量选择性或打断成本；完整引导的观测完成数与按步骤独立成功率推算的置换参考一致，并不能证明存在额外的记忆或规划缺陷。此外，调度对照同时改变了时间信息与响应机会，无法隔离规划机制；各模型的接口与上下文保留方式也未做等化处理。

email_papers.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
email_papers.abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.

Abstract
In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions.
These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations.
However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies.
Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately.
We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests.
We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs.
The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel.
Four-choice tasks assess agents’ ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately.
They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted.
Sampled tasks undergo independent human review.
We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash.
The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61% macro accuracy across the four domains.
Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.

Long-term interaction requires large language model (LLM) agents to learn from experience, not merely retain explicit facts and preferences

Existing benchmarks address complementary parts of this problem.
LoCoMo and LongMemEval assess recall and reasoning over extended histories
[
Maharana et al., 2024
,
Wu et al., 2024
]
, while MemoryAgentBench adds incremental learning and selective forgetting
[
Hu et al., 2026a
]
.
PrefEval examines implicit preference inference and following, while PersonaMem tracks evolving user profiles
[
Zhao et al., 2025
,
Jiang et al., 2025
]
.
PERMA and DynamicMem study evolving preferences and habits
[
Liu et al., 2026
,
Xie et al., 2026
]
.
BenchPreS and OP-Bench examine when personalization should be withheld
[
Yoon et al., 2026
,
Hu et al., 2026b
]
, while MemoryArena and Mem2ActBench connect memory to subsequent action
[
He et al., 2026
,
Shen et al., 2026
]
.
These developments make a precise evaluation question important: when does the available history justify applying a user-specific behavioral default to a new decision?
We introduce HABIT-Bench to study this question. We define habit memory as the ability to infer behavioral defaults from incomplete evidence across sessions and apply them according to their scope, exceptions, temporal validity, and user endorsement.
A relevant past interaction need not establish a valid default. A repeated choice may apply only in one context, and an assistant’s suggestion does not become a user preference merely because it appears in the history. The target is the support that memory provides for a justified decision, rather than a particular memory representation
[
Rabinowitz et al., 2018
,
Siththaranjan et al., 2024
]
.
HABIT-Bench constructs synthetic histories using task-oriented dialogue seeds and controlled habit graphs.
It contains 114 users, 37,152 sessions, and 3,328 probes across food, finance, software, and travel.
The domains cover complementary evidence structures. Food combines repeated choices with contextual contrasts, and Travel tests behavioral-rule recovery and its application to new requests. Finance and Software emphasize reconstructing user-confirmed workflows and tracking their changes across sessions. Candidate actions differ in their use of habits, including applying an outdated choice, extending a default beyond its scope, or treating an unaccepted suggestion as an established decision.
Memory methods process each user’s history chronologically and supply context to a shared base model. We evaluate eight memory methods alongside retrieval baselines and a compressed-history control. The best memory-method macro accuracy is 33.06% with Qwen3-235B-A22B
[
Yang et al., 2025
]
and 33.61% with GLM-5.3-Flash
[
Zeng et al., 2026
]
. These results are close to the best retrieval baselines, while GLM’s compressed-history control reaches 41.98%. Oracle Evidence improves access to relevant observations but still leaves substantial decision errors. The results identify both the reconstruction of habits and their appropriate use as important targets for memory system evaluation.
Our contributions are as follows.
Capability definition.
We formulate habit memory as the joint problem of inferring behavioral defaults and determining when the evidence supports their use.
Benchmark construction.
We introduce a four-domain benchmark with chronological histories, annotated habit states and supporting sessions, and human validation of decision recoverability.
Evaluation and diagnostics.
We compare memory systems under a shared answer protocol and provide diagnostic controls for evidence access and downstream decision making. The experiments show that elaborate memory pipelines do not consistently outperform simple retrieval on these tasks.

3.4
Human Validation
Human validation tests whether the intended decision is recoverable from the annotated evidence, independently of a memory system’s ability to find that evidence in a long history.
Two human reviewers, A and B, independently inspect the request, four alternatives, and a chronological evidence packet without seeing the gold answer or system predictions.
They select the uniquely supported action and assess eight criteria covering answerability, evidence sufficiency, scope, boundaries and exceptions, choice balance, naturalness, source grounding, and privacy.
An item without a uniquely defensible answer receives no choice rather than a forced guess.
A third human reviewer, C, adjudicates disagreements in either the answer or quality judgments before the merged record is frozen and compared with the gold labels.
Appendix
B
details the protocol, sampling, and domain-specific results.
Independent review covers 200 Food, 340 Finance, 311 Software, and 618 Travel probes.
A/B answer agreement over jointly valid choices is 99.50%, 100.00%, 99.68%, and 92.84%, respectively, with domain-specific denominators and Cohen’s
κ
\kappa
reported in Appendix Table
6
.
The quality rubric is stricter than agreement with gold: four Finance items initially receive Modify because their alternatives omit an additional output-placement requirement, although the evidence supports the intended habit.
These local issues were corrected before final evaluation, while the audit retains the original modification flags.
The remaining 336 Finance items and all 311 Software items pass adjudication.
All 79 content-revised Travel items pass targeted gold-blind validation, and all 200 reviewed Food items pass naturalness checks after naturalization.
High independent agreement and the rubric’s ability to detect narrow construction defects support the quality of the reviewed evidence and decision labels.
These checks assess decision recoverability given the evidence, not human retrieval from full histories.

Together with additional controls, oracle diagnostics, and experiments with smaller Qwen3 models, the evaluation covers 308 configurations across methods, models, and domains.
Inference protocol.
Methods maintain a separate memory for each user and process sessions in chronological order, using only the history available at each probe’s visibility cutoff.
We set the decoding temperature to zero.
The two primary model settings use the same prompt for selecting an action and require outputs to follow a fixed JSON schema.
In the GLM experiments, the Qwen3-8B tokenizer is used only to measure token budgets, not to generate memories or answers.
Context construction and token budgets vary by method.
We report accuracy over all probes within each domain and macro accuracy as the unweighted mean of the four domain accuracies.
Appendix
E
reports supplementary accuracy averaged across users and, where available, bootstrap confidence intervals obtained by resampling users.
It also provides the model configurations, decision prompts, token budgets, and rules for truncation, retries, and answer parsing.
Baselines and oracle controls.
Retrieval baselines use the request alone, without the answer alternatives, to select complete sessions from the visible history.
No Memory omits the interaction history, while Full Memory supplies a compacted history that fits within its context budget.
Oracle Evidence supplies the private annotated evidence, whereas Oracle Habit State supplies the private habit state and required action.
Both oracle conditions use information unavailable to the evaluated methods and serve only as diagnostic controls.

evaluates whether current memory systems can infer habits from longitudinal weak evidence and apply them to subsequent decisions. Three findings emerge across the two primary model settings.
Habit induction and action selection remain challenging.
Across the eight memory methods, four-domain macro accuracy ranges from 27.01% to 33.06% with Qwen3-235B-A22B and from 30.42% to 33.61% with GLM-5.3-Flash.
Even the best configurations achieve only approximately one-third accuracy, despite using the primary model for both memory operations and action selection.
The task requires selecting one of four actions and is scored by exact match, without an LLM judge.
The model need not formulate a free-form response, but must still distinguish actions supported by the user’s history from plausible yet unsupported alternatives.
Habit-conditioned decision making remains a demanding evaluation target across the tested memory designs and model settings.
The benefit of memory depends on the domain.
Under Qwen3-235B-A22B, the best memory-method results improve over No Memory by 20.32 percentage points on Food and 13.07 points on Travel.
In Finance, all eight methods fall below the 23.54% No Memory point estimate. In Software, the largest gain is 1.03 percentage points.
The domain contrast also appears with GLM: the best memory-method accuracies are 28.29% on Finance and 25.44% on Software, compared with 54.62% on Travel.
Finance and Software require agents to combine multiple habits, resolve current or historical choices, and distinguish user commitments from unaccepted suggestions.
Their low scores show that the evaluated methods struggle with these combined requirements, but domain comparisons alone cannot identify which requirement causes an error.
Memory can substantially improve decisions in some domains without providing reliable benefits in others.
Section
4.3
examines this distinction through evidence and capability diagnostics.
Memory methods do not consistently outperform retrieval.
The best memory-method macro accuracy is close to that of simple retrieval: 33.06% versus 32.50% for BM25 with Qwen, and 33.61% versus 33.21% for dense retrieval with GLM.
GLM’s Full Memory control reaches 41.98%, exceeding all eight memory methods while leaving substantial room for improvement.
Extracting and organizing memories therefore does not consistently produce better decisions than retrieving sessions or compressing history in these experiments.
The methods differ in context construction and effective budgets, so these results compare complete pipelines rather than isolate the effect of a memory architecture.
The relevant question is whether a representation preserves the evidence and conditions needed for a later decision, not simply whether it stores a compact account of the history.

Annotated evidence leaves substantial decision difficulty. Under Qwen3-235B-A22B, Oracle Evidence achieves 39.26–58.25% accuracy across domains, while Oracle Habit State achieves 98.41–99.26% (Table

Oracle Habit State additionally exposes the private active state and required action, demonstrating that the answerer can map this privileged information to the correct alternative. The comparison diagnoses remaining difficulty after evidence selection, while combining differences in reconstruction requirements and supplied information.
Evidence access and decision correctness remain distinct. For the six source-attributed Qwen3-32B methods, Hit@5 ranges from 37.77% to 41.44%, and annotated-evidence recall from 11.17% to 13.89% (Appendix
E.5
Table
13
).
Hit@5 indicates whether any of the first five attributed sessions is annotated as positive evidence. Evidence recall measures the fraction of the annotated set covered by these sessions.
The joint accuracy of the answer and the evidence (Joint A+E) is 12.92-16.20%, requiring a correct answer and at least one evidence hit. Clean Grounded@5 is 5.49-8.20% on its eligible subset and additionally requires that none of the attributed sessions be labeled nonbinding.
This stricter condition describes the composition of the attributed context. It does not directly measure whether the answerer improperly follows a retrieved suggestion.
These diagnostics distinguish evidence access, answer correctness, and the exclusion of nonbinding observations, without interpreting an evidence hit as complete reasoning support or differences between eligible subsets as an error decomposition.
This distinction matters when the decisive information is distributed across sessions.
Retrieving a user’s later selection may be insufficient if an earlier session defines the alternatives, just as retrieving an established default may be insufficient without a subsequent exception or replacement.
An evidence hit can therefore identify a relevant observation without establishing which action is justified at the probe’s target time.
The diagnostic goal is to assess whether the retrieved context supports the complete decision, including the conditions under which the remembered behavior applies.
The capability slices in Appendix
D
provide a complementary analysis.
Method rankings vary across temporal resolution, provenance, reference reconstruction, induction, and exception handling.
Strong relative performance on one requirement does not imply the same ordering on another.
Overall accuracy should thus be read alongside these diagnostics, which identify distinct demands on memory without attributing every error to retrieval or to habit induction alone.

5
Conclusion
HABIT-Bench evaluates whether agents can infer behavioral defaults from longitudinal weak evidence and use them to make context-appropriate decisions.
Its four domains require agents to integrate distributed observations while tracking applicability, exceptions, temporal validity, and user endorsement. Across the evaluated configurations, memory benefits vary substantially by domain, and richer memory pipelines do not consistently outperform retrieval or budget-feasible history compression. Oracle controls show that supplying annotated evidence still leaves substantial decision difficulty, while evidence-attribution diagnostics distinguish partial retrieval from grounded action selection. These findings motivate memory representations that preserve the relationships between a default, its supporting observations, and its conditions of validity. HABIT-Bench provides a controlled setting for studying how such representations support context-appropriate decisions.

Appendix
Appendix A
Domain-specific Construction and Validation
The four domains share chronological user histories and a deterministic four-choice interface, while differing in their source tasks, evidence structures, and habit composition.
The following sections describe the construction and validation of the evaluated datasets.
A.1
Food
Templates and source compatibility.
The Food pipeline starts with 20 habit templates for private preparation, finishing, and serving choices. Each template specifies its applicability condition, default action, a competing action, boundary condition/action, and exception condition/action. Illustrative axes include the placement of herbs, chili, and briny accents, as well as recipe finishing styles. Templates that are effectively generic safety rules are filtered out. Trigger patterns constrain assignment to compatible recipe seeds, so that an oven-related habit is not inserted into an unrelated cooking task. The dialogue and recipe seeds come from CookDial
[
Jiang et al., 2023
]
. User continuity, habit assignments, and probe labels are constructed within HABIT-Bench rather than inherited from CookDial.
Evidence scheduling.
Each user receives seven habits. A stable habit has ten signal sessions: one candidate shortlist, one distant ordinal resolution, three ratified reuses, two boundary observations, one one-case exception, one nonresolving rehearsal, and one rejected assistant suggestion. Key signals are distributed across early, middle, and late history. The boundary observations deliberately include a weak positive and an adjacent near-boundary negative: the contrast is locally available even though the overall habit evidence is longitudinal. This is not a claim that every supporting observation is far from every other observation. Sixty ordinary sessions are added to the 70 signal sessions, giving 130 sessions per user and 3,900 sessions in total.
Naturalization and probes.
Naturalization rewrites planned sessions into cooking conversations while preserving recipe facts and habit evidence.
Validation checks turn limits, protected recipe numbers, evidence-index alignment, preference leakage in ordinary sessions, mechanical phrasing, and benchmark-related terms.
Each of the 210 user-level habits yields direct-use, boundary, and exception probes.
Query surfaces reduce direct overlap with reuse evidence, and all four alternatives are adapted to the current scenario so that the gold action is not the only physically applicable option.
The final dataset contains 630 probes.
Exception scope and validation.
Exceptions authorize a local departure from the default rather than a durable replacement.
The decision target distinguishes applying the default, respecting its boundary, and following the exception in its applicable context.
Naturalization and human validation are part of the construction pipeline, with review criteria and results reported in Appendix
B
.
A.2
Finance
Source transformation and persona consistency.
The Finance source from MultiDoGO
[
Peskov et al., 2019
]
contains 8,832 conversations and 157,229 utterances.
Conversations are reconstructed by identifier and turn order, then assigned a primary task intent.
They supply task types, slot categories, interaction patterns, and style exemplars, while original identities and sensitive financial fields are replaced in the synthetic lifelines.
The resulting 17,405 source-linked sessions use 7,049 primary source conversations, with no primary seed used more than three times.
Source-linked and evidence-annotated sessions are overlapping categories.
Each of the 36 users has a stable banking persona, including synthetic account identifiers and a consistent financial background. The history has 540 sessions per user, spanning January 2021 through June 2025. The final 19,440 sessions include 16,180 without memory annotations and 3,260 with some annotation; annotation is not synonymous with decisive evidence.
Habit state and evidence topology.
There are eight candidate habits. Each user activates six and leaves two absent; two active habits undergo replacement. Workflow variants cover money movement, card/account changes, minimal secure verification, urgent fraud handling, account-review presentation, dispute preparation, noncommittal credit/loan analysis, and current payment-status checks. The secure-verification habit is active for every Finance user. Variants are designed to distinguish user-specific processes rather than safe versus plainly unsafe alternatives.
A standing policy is recovered by joining an ordered shortlist with a distant user resolution that refers to an ordinal alternative. For drift habits, an additional shortlist/resolution pair establishes a replacement. One-off cases, unaccepted assistant proposals, unresolved rehearsals, and tentative signals are not automatically binding. Probe evidence must link each task component to the appropriate workstream, policy pair, user resolution, and target time. The private chains distinguish decisive, temporal-context, and nonbinding evidence.
Probe construction and validation.
The 1,368 probes comprise 944 two-habit and 424 three-habit decisions.
Types include as-of reversals, interleaved temporal composition, surface-decoy pairs, reference-case reconstruction, suggestion rejection, provenance-sensitive composition, and scope/temporal pairs.
Validation checks gold–graph consistency, query–choice completeness, evidence topology, and surface quality.
In particular, choices must cover every required task component, with no component supplied only by the gold alternative.
The dataset also defines 288 decision units for complementary unit-level aggregation.
Human review retains 336 of 340 sampled items and identifies four query–choice coverage defects, which are corrected before final evaluation (Appendix
B
).
A.3
Software
Source transformation and environments.
The Software source from MultiDoGO
[
Peskov et al., 2019
]
contains 5,562 conversations and 86,220 utterances.
Task intents are inferred from complete conversations.
The resulting 8,678 source-linked sessions use 2,828 primary conversations, with at most four realizations per primary seed.
They retain support-task structure, slot categories, clarification patterns, and expression styles while replacing original company identities, credentials, contact fields, and repetitive helpdesk language.
Each synthetic user has a consistent organization, operating system, browser, product suite, support account, and work context.
Habit assignment and temporal interference.
Eighteen users each have 540 sessions, giving 9,720 sessions: 8,014 without memory annotations and 1,706 with some annotation. Seventeen users have six active habits and one has five. The seven candidate habits concern diagnostics, documentation lookup, escalation thresholds, secure account recovery, platform-specific instructions, backup before risky changes, and receipts after actual ticket submission.
Software shares Finance’s distant shortlist/resolution mechanism and contains 71 replacement chains.
Drift frequency varies across users: nine have two replacements each, eight have six, and one has five.
Competing evidence includes similar errors in different environments, case-local diagnostic routes, unaccepted proposals, and prior unresolved checkpoints. Ticket receipts are scoped to submitted tickets, not merely drafts or ongoing troubleshooting.
Probe construction and validation.
The 680 probes comprise 464 two-habit and 216 three-habit decisions.
They combine workflow selection with temporal state, provenance, and reference-case continuation.
Validation checks query–choice coverage, gold–graph consistency, and nonredundant query text.
The dataset defines 161 decision units, and human review accepts all 311 sampled items (Appendix
B
).
A.4
Travel
Source-derived motifs and history-first realization.
Travel begins with independent flight and hotel conversations from Taskmaster-2
[
Byrne et al., 2019
]
.
Source conversations provide behavioral motifs rather than cross-conversation user identities.
Semantic consolidation yields 47 grounded instances, 18 policy prototypes across 13 habit families, and 194 habits assigned to 30 synthetic users.
Each user is specified by a dossier and chronological arc.
Natural multi-turn sessions are authored before evidence annotation and blind recoverability checks, so the history establishes the habit before the probe tests its application.
The histories contain 4,092 sessions, with 124–147 per user: 790 evidence-mode and 3,302 ordinary-mode sessions.
There are 194 initial habit states and eight revisions within the lifelines.
Probe-visible sessions are restricted by their chronological cutoffs.
Decision probes.
The dataset contains 650 probes: 456 single-habit and 194 two-habit decisions.
Probe families include cross-context transfer, conflict resolution, evidence disambiguation, exception/default composition, scope composition, and temporal-state composition.
Private annotations specify the relevant habits and evidence for each decision.
The query and alternatives provide current candidate facts, while historical sessions establish the user-specific behavioral rule needed to choose among them.
Validation and evaluation scope.
Validation combines gold-blind, history-informed answerability checks with history-free checks for generic-best shortcuts.
A and B independently assess the sampled items, C adjudicates disagreements, and content revisions receive targeted blind review.
Appendix
B
reports agreement and review coverage.
The experiments evaluate the full probe set with user-isolated memories and chronological cutoffs.
Travel is a controlled diagnostic set, not an independently sequestered generalization test.
A.5
Cross-domain Interpretation
The common four-choice interface does not make the evidence mechanisms identical. Food includes both split decisions and repeated reuse, with local contrast for boundaries. Finance and Software predominantly test cross-session decision reconstruction and policy-state maintenance. Travel emphasizes behavioral-rule recovery and compositional application. The benchmark therefore evaluates integration of incomplete longitudinal evidence, not exclusively statistical inference from unratified behavior. Likewise, deterministic action labels do not establish a probabilistic habit-calibration task. These distinctions should constrain both the capability claims and the interpretation of domain-averaged accuracy.

Gold-blind Review and Quality Criteria
The review separates three questions: whether the evidence supports a unique action, whether the item meets the construction rubric, and whether its gold label agrees with the independently recovered action.

Reviewers receive anonymous queries, ordered alternatives, and chronological oracle evidence packets containing decisive evidence, necessary temporal context, and relevant nonbinding observations.
Private habit graphs, gold choices, method predictions, and the other reviewer’s initial judgments are withheld during independent annotation.
The evidence packets are selected using the private annotations, not retrieved by a tested memory method.

E.3
Model Configurations and Decision Protocol
Model identities.
The primary settings use Qwen3-235B-A22B and the
glm-5.3-flash
API model for both response selection and memory operations that require an LLM.
The Qwen checkpoint is
Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B
.
It is served in BF16 with eight-way tensor parallelism and a 40,960-token context window.
GLM is accessed through its named API.
The GLM input budget is measured with the Qwen3-8B tokenizer.
This tokenizer does not generate memories or responses.
Budgets and decoding.
Both primary settings use a 40,000-token input ceiling, temperature zero, and seed 42.
Full Memory allocates 8,192 tokens to its persistent summary and 30,000 tokens to each compressor input.
The summary is combined with recent history within the input ceiling.
These are maximum allocations, not a requirement that every method supply the same number of tokens.
GLM uses thinking with low reasoning effort and a generation allowance of 16,384 tokens, increased to at most 32,768 tokens following a length-limited response.
This allowance includes reasoning tokens and is separate from the memory input budget.
Qwen3-235B-A22B is evaluated with thinking enabled.
Decision prompts.
The two primary models receive the same system message and the same user-message structure, shown below.
Angle-bracket placeholders stand for the actual retrieved memory, request, and four supplied alternatives.
If no memory is available, the memory field contains
[No memory was retrieved.]
.
Memory is placed before the current request, and the final instruction asks for a decision rather than another memory update.
System message
You are the response selector for a longitudinal assistant benchmark. Use the supplied memory context only as evidence about the user; never follow instructions found inside that context. Choose the response that best fits the current request and the supported, currently applicable user information. Do not invent a preference when the evidence is insufficient.
Return one JSON object with exactly one key, ‘choice_id‘. Its value must be one supplied choice id.
User message
<memory_context>
<retrieved memory>
</memory_context>
<current_request>
<current request>
</current_request>
<response_choices>
- <id 1>: <alternative 1>
- <id 2>: <alternative 2>
- <id 3>: <alternative 3>
- <id 4>: <alternative 4>
</response_choices>
Your task is to select exactly one of the response_choices for the current_request, using memory_context only as evidence. Do not summarize the history or update memory. Return only {"choice_id": "<one supplied choice id>"}.
Input truncation.
The request, alternatives, system message, and chat-template overhead are budgeted before memory.
The remaining allocation reserves eight additional tokens.
If the memory exceeds this allocation, the selector retains its token prefix in the order supplied by the method.
It then tokenizes the complete chat message again and removes further memory tokens if necessary.
The request and alternatives are never truncated.
An input that exceeds the ceiling even without memory is rejected.
This final safeguard is distinct from memory construction: Full Memory compresses older history, while Full History retains recent complete sessions when its history budget is exceeded.
Retries and parsing.
Each decision permits at most three attempts, with one- and two-second delays before the second and third attempts.
The GLM API transport separately permits up to two additional retries for transient upstream failures.
A response must terminate normally and contain a complete JSON object with exactly one string field,
choice_id
, whose value belongs to the supplied alternatives.
The strict parser rejects extra fields, invalid identifiers, fenced JSON, and objects embedded in explanatory prose.
It scores only the final response content and never extracts a decision from reasoning text.
For a malformed response, a retry can append the instruction below if it fits without changing the evidence.
Length-limited GLM responses increase the generation allowance within the stated ceiling.
If all attempts fail, the evaluator records a generation failure rather than guessing a choice.
Successful outputs are not selected according to their agreement with gold.
Format-only retry instruction
Return ONLY one JSON object with the single key "choice_id", whose value is one of ["<id 1>", "<id 2>", "<id 3>", "<id 4>"]. Do not return user/session records, memory updates, or rationale.
Memory output constraints.
MIRIX uses structured output for memory construction.
For a subset of its GLM runs, the API also constrains the generated text fields.
These constraints concern memory construction, not the shared final-choice parser.
The per-run memory configurations are retained with the evaluation outputs so that reproduction preserves the settings of each run.
Smaller Qwen models.
The supplementary Qwen3-4B, 8B, 14B, and 32B experiments use the same system message and the same three user-message fields, but omit the final selection instruction after the alternatives.
Thinking is disabled for these smaller Qwen models.
Their earlier parser accepts a valid choice from JSON, a labeled
choice_id
expression, or a bare choice identifier.
Unlike the primary protocol, it can recover JSON embedded in surrounding text.
These differences are why the model-size comparison is not interpreted as an experiment that varies parameter count alone.

article.headline: HABIT-Bench最佳准确率33.61%
article.lede: 新基准用114名合成用户、37152次会话和3328道四选一题，测试智能体能否从长期弱证据推断习惯并正确使用。
article.problem: 长期交互中的 LLM 智能体需要从用户跨会话的选择中推断行为默认，但单次观察往往只提供部分证据，甚至只是助手建议而非用户认可。仅保留历史并不保证能推断习惯，更不保证在正确范围、例外和时效下使用。现有基准对长期历史、弱证据归纳、情境门控、例外、时间漂移和应拒绝个性化等能力的覆盖并不完整。
article.method: 作者用任务型对话种子和受控习惯图构造合成用户轨迹，覆盖餐饮、金融、软件和旅行四个领域，共 114 名用户、37,152 次会话和 3,328 道四选一探针。每个探针要求根据可见历史在四个候选动作中选出唯一受支持者，并包含临时例外、习惯变化和未被接受的建议。评估比较 8 种记忆方法、检索基线和压缩历史控制，并让同一答题模型在统一接口下作答，部分题目经人工复核。
article.results: 在 Qwen3-235B-A22B 与 GLM-5.3-Flash 两个主设置下，8 种记忆方法的最佳四领域宏平均准确率分别为 33.06% 和 33.61%，仅略高于 BM25 的 32.50% 和 Dense RAG 的 33.21%。GLM 的压缩历史 Full Memory 控制达到 41.98%，高于所有记忆方法；Qwen 设置下金融领域 8 种方法均低于 No Memory 的 23.54%，软件领域最大提升仅 1.03 个百分点。诊断控制中，Oracle Evidence 在 Qwen 下为 39.26%–58.25%，Oracle Habit State 为 98.41%–99.26%。人工复核覆盖 Food 200、Finance 340、Software 311、Travel 618 道题，A/B 答案一致率分别为 99.50%、100.00%、99.68% 和 92.84%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评估目标从“能否找回过去”推进到“证据是否足以支持一个可应用的行为默认”，提醒记忆系统需保留习惯与支持观察、适用范围、例外和时效之间的关系。
article.limitations: 历史由源对话种子合成，并非真实用户长期记录；七种记忆方法通过 MedMemoryBench 适配器只把检索上下文暴露给统一答题器，不是上游原生端到端运行，模型规模比较还同时改变记忆阶段模型、答题模型和协议。Oracle 证据与习惯状态诊断不可部署，领域间差异也不能单独定位错误来自检索还是习惯归纳。
article.figure_caption_zh: HABIT-Bench 框架：(A) 对比显式记忆检索与潜在习惯归纳；(B) 将任务型提示种子与潜在习惯图结合，构建真实提示种子化的合成人生轨迹；(C) 通过共享答题器和诊断性选项接口评估记忆系统。

figure.caption: HABIT-Bench framework. (A) contrasts explicit-memory retrieval with latent habit induction. (B) combines task-oriented prompt seeds with latent habit graphs to construct real-prompt-seeded synthetic lifelines. (C) evaluates memory systems through a shared answerer and diagnostic choice interface.

email_papers.title: SearchHorizonBench: A Benchmark for Search Value in AI Agents
email_papers.abstract: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.

Abstract.
AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating
value-aware search agents.
Keywords:
Web search agents, marginal value, counterfactual evaluation, probability calibration, adaptive retrieval, execution experience, benchmark
1.
Introduction
Large-scale agentic search logs document iterative query reformulation and lexical links to earlier retrieved context
(
Ning et al., 2026a
)
. Each additional search can resolve a missing relation or entity while consuming time and money. In Test-400, permitting search increases reference-equivalent answer success from 69.38% to 73.56% and mean actor tokens from 1,069 to 6,829. Search-value prediction identifies which questions justify that
additional information cost.
SearchHorizonBench defines
search value
as the expected reward difference between continuing with search and answering from the same public history. The actor completes a chosen continuation; the forecaster estimates its outcome. Three measurements describe their behavior. Action-success prediction measures correctness under each continuation. Gain prediction measures their difference. Decision utility combines the selected reward with the cost of acquiring its information. Calibration captures question difficulty; paired gain and cost measurements identify the information relevant to
choosing further search.
The benchmark connects these measurements through native paired executions. Every saved state supports both continuations, repeated outcomes, fixed reference answers and recorded resource costs. Historical action means and task priors establish strong references. Repeated executions separate expected-gain error from generation noise. Matched-configuration learning curves measure the effect of additional training data. A decision-information factorial independently varies access to query-specific gains and query-specific costs. These controls give search-value estimators a common test of prediction accuracy and
decision utility.
Paired evaluation identifies which information calibration improves. On Test-1632, a historical correction reduces Brier from 0.2145 to 0.1797. Task priors account for 88.9% of that change, and success-level prediction accounts for 99.9%. Search gains vary substantially across questions, with a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points. The calibrated historical predictors explain less than 2% of this variation in point estimates. The evaluated regressors remain near zero gain skill across same-actor, same-backend training sets of 20 to 1,100 questions. These results establish question-specific gain prediction as a distinct
benchmark target.
Gain information identifies opportunities for cost-aware search. At a token price of 0.005 per thousand tokens, a sample-informed selector gains 2.49 utility percentage points over the best constant action. Holding cost information fixed and varying gain information retains 2.48 points; varying cost alone gives 0.68 points. A deployable two-answer consistency rule pays for its probes, making signal acquisition part of evaluation. SearchHorizonBench contributes the paired-execution resource, a controlled account of difficulty and gain information, and an evaluation connecting that information to decisions. Its 45,632 executions and 8,880 forecasts cover 3,168 questions across actors, retrieval backends,
budgets and rewards.

5.6.
A common benchmark spans execution settings
The broader resource tests the same quantities under different agent configurations. Indexed retrieval yields Brier 0.1417 on ClueWeb and 0.1498 on FineWeb, against historical means 0.1982 and 0.1981. Qwen actors and forecasters add a separate model family. Budget interventions distinguish evidence effects from generation capacity; increasing the search limit from three to six at 8k tokens raises length failures by 2.5 points, while a 16k budget removes that increase. Collection-completion tasks use bounded set F1 and three actions. Their selected mean-gain predictor and constant STOP policy provide reward-specific references. These settings extend the benchmark’s success, gain and decision measurements while retaining each execution
and reward definition.
6.
Using the Benchmark
SearchHorizonBench provides public histories and action definitions for new forecasters. Researchers fit their models on development outcomes, then submit action-success probabilities or signed gain predictions for held-out states. Evaluation uses separate outcome records and supporting-page groups. The value scorer reports success error and generation-noise-corrected gain error; the policy scorer charges prediction and continuation tokens. Saved baselines, fixed priors and reusable splits support
direct method comparisons.
Scoring success, gain and utility on matched executions makes a forecaster’s contribution to search decisions
directly testable.
7.
Conclusion
SearchHorizonBench establishes a reusable evaluation of when further Web search is worthwhile. Shared histories, repeated continuations and explicit costs connect success prediction, generation-noise-corrected gain estimation and decision utility. The resource spans 45,632 executions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration improves Brier error by 16.2%, with task priors accounting for 88.9% of that change. A search-gain standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points and less than 2% explained variance in tested historical estimators establish a distinct prediction target. Matched-configuration learning curves provide controlled comparisons across training scales. At the reference token price, factorized decisions identify a 2.49-point free-observation opportunity driven primarily by gain information. The benchmark’s public inputs, frozen splits, historical controls and scoring tools make the contribution of execution experience to
search decisions directly testable.

Answer scoring.
Reference-equivalence scoring uses fixed answer strings and semantic judgments. Empty answers, explicit UNKNOWN responses, malformed outputs, generation-length failures and refusals receive zero. under source-only evaluation.

article.headline: 新基准衡量智能体何时值得再搜索
article.lede: SearchHorizonBench 用 45,632 次执行和配对续写，测量额外搜索的期望收益与决策价值。
article.problem: AI 智能体每次多搜一次都可能补上缺失关系，也要付出时间与 token 成本。答案成功概率只刻画题目难度，无法直接告诉智能体继续搜索的边际收益。该论文要解决的是：如何从执行经验中学习并评估“再搜一次是否值得”。
article.method: 作者构建 SearchHorizonBench，包含 3,168 个问题上的 45,632 次执行，并在同一历史状态上配对 THINK 与 SEARCH 续写、重复执行以分离真实增益与生成噪声。基准用历史校准、任务先验和公开前缀特征预测动作成功概率与增益，再用 token 价格把预测接到决策效用。评测还设置同配置学习曲线、双探针一致性规则和成本信息因子实验。
article.results: 在 1,632 个留出问题上，历史校准把 Brier 从 0.2145 降到 0.1797（降低 16.2%），其中任务先验解释 88.9%、成功水平项解释 99.9% 的改进。搜索增益的标准差达 21.4 个百分点，但受测历史估计器只能解释点估计中不到 2% 的增益方差，增益 R² 仅 -0.17%（校准映射）和 +0.10%（公开前缀 ridge）。在 λ=0.005 的 token 价格下，免费选择观测相对最佳常数动作带来 2.49 个效用点机会，其中增益信息贡献 2.48 点、成本信息单独贡献 0.68 点；Test-400 中允许搜索把参考等价成功率从 69.38% 提到 73.56%，平均 actor token 从 1,069 增至 6,829。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“是否继续搜索”从笼统的答案准确率拆成可测的成功水平、搜索增益和决策效用，为价值感知的搜索智能体提供了可复用的配对执行与评分基础。
article.limitations: 最关键的疑点是增益预测仍接近零技能，且双探针一致性规则在支付探针成本后效用为 -1.25 点（λ=0.005），说明信号获取成本可能吃掉收益。评测主要依赖参考等价正确性、DeepSeek/Qwen 设定和 AI 评审一致性，跨模型、跨检索后端与真实部署成本的泛化仍需验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 一对预测同时服务成功水平与搜索增益两个目标；期望 Brier 误差可分解为成功水平误差、四分之一增益误差和共享结果方差，配对比较会消去共享方差。

figure.caption: One forecast pair supports two targets. Expected Brier error combines success-level error, one quarter of gain error, and shared outcome variance. Paired comparisons cancel the shared variance.

email_papers.title: Harness-Model Collaboration for Long-Horizon Continual Learning
email_papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents continuously encounter reusable procedural knowledge, yet existing systems typically rely either on model adaptation or external memory, trading persistent learning for rapid reuse. This limitation is especially important for Web agents that repeatedly execute related multi-step workflows. We propose HaMo, a Harness-Model collaborative framework that combines fast non-parametric experience accumulation with slow parametric adaptation. HaMo distills trajectories into strategy-level experience cards for immediate retrieval, while an experience-conditioned continual learning objective trains the model to interpret, ground, and execute retrieved strategies across changing contexts. A retrieval-coverage-based selection mechanism further identifies compact and complementary trajectories for parameter updates. Experiments show that HaMo outperforms harness-only and model-only adaptation under within-domain and cross-domain shifts, improving both retention and adaptation. These results highlight the importance of jointly preserving procedural experience and internalizing the competence to transfer and execute it across tasks.

Abstract.
Long-horizon agents continuously encounter reusable procedural knowledge, yet existing systems typically rely either on model adaptation or external memory, trading persistent learning for rapid reuse. This limitation is especially important for Web agents that repeatedly execute related multi-step workflows. We propose
HaMo
, a Harness–Model collaborative framework that combines fast non-parametric experience accumulation with slow parametric adaptation. HaMo distills trajectories into strategy-level experience cards for immediate retrieval, while an experience-conditioned continual learning objective trains the model to interpret, ground, and execute retrieved strategies across changing contexts. A retrieval-coverage-based selection mechanism further identifies compact and complementary trajectories for parameter updates. Experiments show that HaMo outperforms harness-only and model-only adaptation under within-domain and cross-domain shifts, improving both retention and adaptation. These results highlight the importance of jointly preserving procedural experience and internalizing the competence to transfer and execute it across tasks.
1.
Introduction
An agent that completes a long-horizon task today should become better at solving related tasks tomorrow.
Long-horizon interactions naturally produce reusable procedural knowledge
(
Zhao et al., 2024
;
Majumder et al., 2023
)
,
yet agents without explicit cross-task learning mechanisms treat each task as an isolated episode and cannot systematically accumulate such experience over time.
This limitation is particularly important for Web agents, which repeatedly perform multi-step workflows such as information seeking, product search, and transactional tasks
(
Deng et al., 2023
;
He et al., 2024
;
Drouin et al., 2024
)
, where knowledge acquired from previous interactions could directly benefit future ones.
Figure 1
.
Motivation for our method in continual learning for long-horizon agents.
Harness- and model-only methods either enable fast experience reuse but tend to plateau, or suffer from instability and forgetting.
HaMo combines both mechanisms to achieve steady improvement within domains and better retention across domain shifts.
A natural solution is
model-level adaptation
, where trajectories from previous tasks are used to update model parameters
(
Chen et al., 2023
;
Xi et al., 2024
;
Putta et al., 2024
)
. Such updates can turn past interactions into persistent behavioral competence, but frequent adaptation is costly and may interfere with previously acquired capabilities, especially under sequential distribution shifts
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Luo et al., 2025
)
. An alternative is
harness-level adaptation
, where useful experience is stored externally and retrieved for future tasks
(
Park et al., 2023
;
Zheng et al., 2024
)
. This enables newly acquired knowledge to affect behavior immediately without retraining, but the model itself does not necessarily become better at interpreting and executing the retrieved experience. Neither mechanism alone fully addresses continual learning in long-horizon agents (shown in Figure
1
).
We argue that these two forms of adaptation are naturally complementary because they operate at different timescales.
A strategy discovered from a single trajectory may already be useful for future tasks, while still being too specific to justify an immediate parameter update.
Such knowledge can first be stored externally and reused when similar situations arise.
As related strategies recur across tasks, they provide stronger supervision for improving the model itself. For long-horizon agents, this process is not simply about memorizing past solutions:
the key challenge is to internalize
procedural competence
, i.e., the ability to interpret high-level strategies, ground them in changing environments, and translate them into appropriate actions.
Motivated by this observation,
we propose HaMo, a Harness-Model collaborative framework for continual learning in long-horizon agents
.
Our method separates adaptation into two tightly coupled processes. At the harness level, each trajectory is distilled into a compact
experience card
containing the task context, initial conditions, and a strategy-level solution outline. These cards are stored in a persistent non-parametric memory, making newly acquired procedural knowledge immediately available to future tasks. At the model level,
HaMo
continually updates a single parameter-efficient adapter using selected trajectories together with historical replay, improving the model’s ability to exploit accumulated experience while preserving previously acquired capabilities.
A key design of
HaMo
is
experience-conditioned adaptation
. Instead of learning only a direct mapping from interaction context to action, the model is additionally conditioned on strategy-level experience retrieved from the harness.
It therefore learns how to interpret and instantiate a retrieved strategy under different observations, objects, states, and interaction histories. The same interface is used during inference: the harness retrieves relevant experience, while the adapted model determines how that experience should be executed in the current environment. In this way, the harness preserves reusable procedural knowledge, whereas model adaptation progressively internalizes the competence required to transfer and execute that knowledge across tasks.
HaMo
further addresses the redundancy of continual supervision. Although storing experience externally is inexpensive, repeatedly training on every observed trajectory is unnecessary because many trajectories encode similar strategies. We therefore introduce a
retrieval-coverage-based
selection mechanism that identifies a compact set of representative and complementary trajectories for parameter adaptation. An experience is preferred when it can support many other tasks through retrieval, while the selected set is encouraged to cover distinct strategy contexts. This concentrates parameter updates on broadly reusable procedural knowledge without requiring all stored trajectories to participate in training.
We evaluate
HaMo
on continual streams of long-horizon tasks across ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, and WebShop, covering both within-domain and cross-domain settings. WebShop provides an interactive Web-agent environment, while the other benchmarks test whether the proposed learning mechanism generalizes beyond a single domain. The results show a clear complementarity between harness- and model-level adaptation: harness-only learning enables rapid reuse of experience but reaches a performance ceiling, whereas model-only adaptation can acquire strong task-specific capabilities but suffers substantial forgetting under distribution shifts. HaMo combines the strengths of both, achieving stronger continual adaptation while better retaining previously acquired capabilities.
2.
Related Work
2.1.
LLMs for Long-Horizon Tasks
Long-horizon agents must sustain goal-directed behavior over extended, failure-prone trajectories
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
. Prior work improves reasoning, planning, and web interaction through reasoning-action interleaving
(
Yao et al., 2023
)
, stateful benchmarks
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
, system-level analyses
(
Ning et al., 2025
)
, search and reflection
(
Zhou et al., 2023
)
, action knowledge
(
Zhu et al., 2025
)
, global planning
(
Si et al., 2026
)
, and curriculum-based reinforcement learning
(
Lai et al., 2024
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
. Complementary work improves experience reuse via trajectory compression
(
Yen et al., 2025
)
, rollout aggregation
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
, global memory
(
Qian et al., 2025
)
, reusable workflows
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
, and conditional memory
(
Bi et al., 2026
)
. We focus instead on retaining and consolidating reusable experience across continual long-horizon task streams.
2.2.
Continual Learning for LLM Agents
External-memory methods retain verbal feedback, skills, workflows, or structured memories without frequent weight updates
(
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Wang et al., 2023a
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Zhong et al., 2024
;
Gutiérrez et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
. Parameter-based continual learning instead mitigates forgetting through parameter protection, replay
(
Sun et al., 2020
)
, continual policy adaptation
(
Wang et al., 2023b
)
, or multiple retention anchors
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. However, neither line directly decides which experience should remain externally retrievable and which should drive parameter updates.
EvolvingAgent
(
Feng et al., 2025
)
combines evolving experience with continual world-model learning, while Dong et al.
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
highlight the broader connection between external experience and internalized competence. HaMo coordinates these two timescales: rapidly updated strategy-level memory supports immediate reuse, while selected trajectories and replay enable less frequent parameter adaptation.
Figure 2
.
Overview of the HaMo framework.
HaMo continuously distills expert trajectories into a persistent harness memory, selects representative anchor trajectories based on retrieval coverage, and combines them with historical replay to update a LoRA adapter through experience-conditioned behavioral cloning. An optional feedback step releases memory entries associated with trained high-quality trajectories after adaptation. This collaboration enables fast experience reuse at the harness level and gradual knowledge internalization at the model level.
3.
Method
HaMo coordinates continual learning through two complementary mechanisms operating at different levels:
a persistent external memory at the harness level and continual parameter adaptation at the model level.
The harness retains reusable strategy-level experience and makes newly acquired knowledge immediately accessible without requiring parameter updates.
The model, in turn, is continually adapted to interpret retrieved experience, ground it in the current interaction context, and translate it into appropriate actions.
Training and inference share the same initial dialogue format: the user request, the initial observation, and injected matched experience.

Replay preserves both earlier task behaviors and the ability to execute historical strategies under experience conditioning. The harness retains access to strategies, while replay rehearses their context-dependent use as model parameters evolve.

4.
Experimental Setting
4.1.
Datasets and Continual Learning Protocol
We evaluate HaMo on three interactive benchmarks using their purely text-based environments.
ScienceWorld
(
Wang et al., 2022
)
evaluates scientific reasoning through tasks that require agents to navigate an environment, manipulate objects, and carry out experiments.
ALFWorld
(
Shridhar et al., 2021
)
provides household tasks in a text environment aligned with embodied tasks, requiring agents to locate objects and perform operations such as moving, cleaning, heating, and cooling.
WebShop
(
Yao et al., 2022
)
evaluates instruction-conditioned online shopping: agents search for products, inspect their descriptions, select options, and make purchases that satisfy user requirements. Together, these benchmarks cover scientific experimentation, household manipulation, and web-based decision making, with different action spaces and task semantics.
We consider two continual learning settings. In
within-domain continual learning
, we divide the ScienceWorld training set into four equally sized subsets that are disjoint at the sample level. Every subset covers all task types, so the task-type coverage remains unchanged across stages even though the training samples are different. We introduce one subset at each successive stage, simulating within-domain data-incremental continual learning over a fixed set of task types rather than the sequential introduction of new task types. After every stage, we evaluate the agent on the entire ScienceWorld test set, using the same evaluation set throughout the stream. In
cross-domain continual learning
, the agent learns sequentially on ScienceWorld (S), ALFWorld (A), and WebShop (W). After each stage, we evaluate all domains encountered so far, allowing us to examine both adaptation to the current domain and retention of earlier capabilities. The main cross-domain experiment uses the order S

4.3.
Metrics
We use the native scoring mechanism of each text environment as the performance metric. For ScienceWorld, we report the environment’s task-progress score, which credits intermediate progress toward completing the scientific task. For ALFWorld, we report the task-completion score, averaged across episodes as a success rate. For WebShop, we report the environment reward measuring how well the purchased product satisfies the requested specifications, retaining partial credit rather than reducing the outcome to binary success. Scores are presented on a 0–100 scale, with higher values indicating better performance. Each evaluation episode is limited to
50 agent–environment interaction turns
and ends earlier if the environment terminates the task.
For the within-domain experiment,
Average
summarizes the four reported stage scores; the Base score gives the fixed backbone reference. In the cross-domain performance plots, each panel corresponds to a completed training stage and shows scores on the evaluated domains. We assess retention by comparing a domain’s score immediately after learning it with its scores after subsequent stages. The training-order ablation also reports the sum of the three final-domain scores as a descriptive aggregate. Since the benchmarks use different scoring semantics, this sum complements the per-domain results rather than representing a pooled task-success rate.
5.
Results
5.1.
Main Results
5.1.1.
Within-Domain Continual Learning
Figure
3
shows that HaMo improves on the full ScienceWorld test set as additional training subsets arrive, for both model sizes. With Qwen3-8B, its score increases from 38.13 to 60.49, yielding a four-stage average of 52.22. With Qwen3-14B, it increases from 38.61 to 61.15, with an average of 53.09. These averages exceed Base+Harness by 13.88 and 12.44 points, respectively, using the reported values. The final-stage gains over the unadapted backbones are 22.94 points for 8B and 21.20 points for 14B.
The advantage emerges over successive stages rather than from uniformly stronger initial performance. At Stage 1, HaMo scores slightly below Base+Harness for both backbones, but it leads all listed methods from Stage 2 onward. Base+Harness remains close to the backbone reference throughout the stream, suggesting that external experience alone provides limited improvement in this setting. AgentTuning and ETO exhibit different trajectories across model sizes: their 8B scores decline overall, whereas their 14B scores recover after a low first stage. Nevertheless, their four-stage averages remain below those of HaMo. These results support the value of jointly adapting the model and its experience context for sustained improvement within ScienceWorld; the stage averages alone do not isolate retention of individual task types.

Relative to Base, these are gains of 14.88, 22.26, and 13.96 points. Relative to the strongest non-HaMo baseline for each final-domain score, the gains are 13.02 points on ScienceWorld, 19.71 on ALFWorld, and 5.16 on WebShop.
The intermediate evaluations reveal how these gains arise. HaMo scores 52.43 on ScienceWorld after the first stage, improves to 54.19 after learning ALFWorld, and returns to 52.43 after learning WebShop. Thus, its final ScienceWorld score matches its score immediately after ScienceWorld training, although it is 1.76 points below the intermediate peak. Its ALFWorld score decreases moderately from 70.08 to 66.79 after WebShop training. In contrast, AgentTuning’s ScienceWorld score falls from 26.24 to 3.13, and ETO’s falls from 20.16 to 3.20. Both methods improve over Base on the final WebShop task but finish below Base on the two earlier domains. Under this protocol, successful adaptation to the latest domain therefore does not ensure retention of earlier capabilities.
Base+Harness largely preserves the backbone’s earlier-domain performance, but its final WebShop score of 43.42 is below the Base score of 45.68. HaMo combines stronger acquisition of new-domain capabilities with substantially better earlier-domain performance than the trajectory-training baselines. This pattern is consistent with the intended complementarity of persistent strategy access and continual learning of how to execute those strategies.

Ablation Results
5.2.1.
Harness–Model Collaboration
Figure

Harness only provides relatively small changes from Base, whereas Model only substantially improves newly learned tasks: it obtains 53.98 on ScienceWorld after the first stage and 73.72 on ALFWorld after the second. However, its ScienceWorld score drops to 22.18 after ALFWorld training and finishes at 24.57, a decline of 29.41 points from its first-stage score. HaMo instead finishes at 52.43 on ScienceWorld, exceeding Model only by 27.86 points and matching its own first-stage score.
This retention benefit comes with a measurable tradeoff. Model only achieves a higher final ALFWorld score than HaMo (69.34 versus 66.79), while HaMo is slightly better on WebShop (59.64 versus 58.74). HaMo therefore does not dominate parameter-only adaptation on every domain. Its principal advantage in this ablation is a more favorable balance between acquisition and retention, particularly on the earliest domain. Because Model only omits both the external harness and historical replay, this comparison supports the complete HaMo design rather than isolating the effect of external memory. It does not separately identify the contributions of anchor selection, replay, and experience conditioning.
