article.headline: 新基准衡量智能体何时值得再搜索
article.lede: SearchHorizonBench 用 45,632 次执行和配对续写，测量额外搜索的期望收益与决策价值。
article.problem: AI 智能体每次多搜一次都可能补上缺失关系，也要付出时间与 token 成本。答案成功概率只刻画题目难度，无法直接告诉智能体继续搜索的边际收益。该论文要解决的是：如何从执行经验中学习并评估“再搜一次是否值得”。
article.method: 作者构建 SearchHorizonBench，包含 3,168 个问题上的 45,632 次执行，并在同一历史状态上配对 THINK 与 SEARCH 续写、重复执行以分离真实增益与生成噪声。基准用历史校准、任务先验和公开前缀特征预测动作成功概率与增益，再用 token 价格把预测接到决策效用。评测还设置同配置学习曲线、双探针一致性规则和成本信息因子实验。
article.results: 在 1,632 个留出问题上，历史校准把 Brier 从 0.2145 降到 0.1797（降低 16.2%），其中任务先验解释 88.9%、成功水平项解释 99.9% 的改进。搜索增益的标准差达 21.4 个百分点，但受测历史估计器只能解释点估计中不到 2% 的增益方差，增益 R² 仅 -0.17%（校准映射）和 +0.10%（公开前缀 ridge）。在 λ=0.005 的 token 价格下，免费选择观测相对最佳常数动作带来 2.49 个效用点机会，其中增益信息贡献 2.48 点、成本信息单独贡献 0.68 点；Test-400 中允许搜索把参考等价成功率从 69.38% 提到 73.56%，平均 actor token 从 1,069 增至 6,829。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“是否继续搜索”从笼统的答案准确率拆成可测的成功水平、搜索增益和决策效用，为价值感知的搜索智能体提供了可复用的配对执行与评分基础。
article.limitations: 最关键的疑点是增益预测仍接近零技能，且双探针一致性规则在支付探针成本后效用为 -1.25 点（λ=0.005），说明信号获取成本可能吃掉收益。评测主要依赖参考等价正确性、DeepSeek/Qwen 设定和 AI 评审一致性，跨模型、跨检索后端与真实部署成本的泛化仍需验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 一对预测同时服务成功水平与搜索增益两个目标；期望 Brier 误差可分解为成功水平误差、四分之一增益误差和共享结果方差，配对比较会消去共享方差。

figure.caption: One forecast pair supports two targets. Expected Brier error combines success-level error, one quarter of gain error, and shared outcome variance. Paired comparisons cancel the shared variance.

page_papers.title: Harness-Model Collaboration for Long-Horizon Continual Learning
page_papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents continuously encounter reusable procedural knowledge, yet existing systems typically rely either on model adaptation or external memory, trading persistent learning for rapid reuse. This limitation is especially important for Web agents that repeatedly execute related multi-step workflows. We propose HaMo, a Harness-Model collaborative framework that combines fast non-parametric experience accumulation with slow parametric adaptation. HaMo distills trajectories into strategy-level experience cards for immediate retrieval, while an experience-conditioned continual learning objective trains the model to interpret, ground, and execute retrieved strategies across changing contexts. A retrieval-coverage-based selection mechanism further identifies compact and complementary trajectories for parameter updates. Experiments show that HaMo outperforms harness-only and model-only adaptation under within-domain and cross-domain shifts, improving both retention and adaptation. These results highlight the importance of jointly preserving procedural experience and internalizing the competence to transfer and execute it across tasks.

Abstract.
Long-horizon agents continuously encounter reusable procedural knowledge, yet existing systems typically rely either on model adaptation or external memory, trading persistent learning for rapid reuse. This limitation is especially important for Web agents that repeatedly execute related multi-step workflows. We propose
HaMo
, a Harness–Model collaborative framework that combines fast non-parametric experience accumulation with slow parametric adaptation. HaMo distills trajectories into strategy-level experience cards for immediate retrieval, while an experience-conditioned continual learning objective trains the model to interpret, ground, and execute retrieved strategies across changing contexts. A retrieval-coverage-based selection mechanism further identifies compact and complementary trajectories for parameter updates. Experiments show that HaMo outperforms harness-only and model-only adaptation under within-domain and cross-domain shifts, improving both retention and adaptation. These results highlight the importance of jointly preserving procedural experience and internalizing the competence to transfer and execute it across tasks.
1.
Introduction
An agent that completes a long-horizon task today should become better at solving related tasks tomorrow.
Long-horizon interactions naturally produce reusable procedural knowledge
(
Zhao et al., 2024
;
Majumder et al., 2023
)
,
yet agents without explicit cross-task learning mechanisms treat each task as an isolated episode and cannot systematically accumulate such experience over time.
This limitation is particularly important for Web agents, which repeatedly perform multi-step workflows such as information seeking, product search, and transactional tasks
(
Deng et al., 2023
;
He et al., 2024
;
Drouin et al., 2024
)
, where knowledge acquired from previous interactions could directly benefit future ones.
Figure 1
.
Motivation for our method in continual learning for long-horizon agents.
Harness- and model-only methods either enable fast experience reuse but tend to plateau, or suffer from instability and forgetting.
HaMo combines both mechanisms to achieve steady improvement within domains and better retention across domain shifts.
A natural solution is
model-level adaptation
, where trajectories from previous tasks are used to update model parameters
(
Chen et al., 2023
;
Xi et al., 2024
;
Putta et al., 2024
)
. Such updates can turn past interactions into persistent behavioral competence, but frequent adaptation is costly and may interfere with previously acquired capabilities, especially under sequential distribution shifts
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Luo et al., 2025
)
. An alternative is
harness-level adaptation
, where useful experience is stored externally and retrieved for future tasks
(
Park et al., 2023
;
Zheng et al., 2024
)
. This enables newly acquired knowledge to affect behavior immediately without retraining, but the model itself does not necessarily become better at interpreting and executing the retrieved experience. Neither mechanism alone fully addresses continual learning in long-horizon agents (shown in Figure
1
).
We argue that these two forms of adaptation are naturally complementary because they operate at different timescales.
A strategy discovered from a single trajectory may already be useful for future tasks, while still being too specific to justify an immediate parameter update.
Such knowledge can first be stored externally and reused when similar situations arise.
As related strategies recur across tasks, they provide stronger supervision for improving the model itself. For long-horizon agents, this process is not simply about memorizing past solutions:
the key challenge is to internalize
procedural competence
, i.e., the ability to interpret high-level strategies, ground them in changing environments, and translate them into appropriate actions.
Motivated by this observation,
we propose HaMo, a Harness-Model collaborative framework for continual learning in long-horizon agents
.
Our method separates adaptation into two tightly coupled processes. At the harness level, each trajectory is distilled into a compact
experience card
containing the task context, initial conditions, and a strategy-level solution outline. These cards are stored in a persistent non-parametric memory, making newly acquired procedural knowledge immediately available to future tasks. At the model level,
HaMo
continually updates a single parameter-efficient adapter using selected trajectories together with historical replay, improving the model’s ability to exploit accumulated experience while preserving previously acquired capabilities.
A key design of
HaMo
is
experience-conditioned adaptation
. Instead of learning only a direct mapping from interaction context to action, the model is additionally conditioned on strategy-level experience retrieved from the harness.
It therefore learns how to interpret and instantiate a retrieved strategy under different observations, objects, states, and interaction histories. The same interface is used during inference: the harness retrieves relevant experience, while the adapted model determines how that experience should be executed in the current environment. In this way, the harness preserves reusable procedural knowledge, whereas model adaptation progressively internalizes the competence required to transfer and execute that knowledge across tasks.
HaMo
further addresses the redundancy of continual supervision. Although storing experience externally is inexpensive, repeatedly training on every observed trajectory is unnecessary because many trajectories encode similar strategies. We therefore introduce a
retrieval-coverage-based
selection mechanism that identifies a compact set of representative and complementary trajectories for parameter adaptation. An experience is preferred when it can support many other tasks through retrieval, while the selected set is encouraged to cover distinct strategy contexts. This concentrates parameter updates on broadly reusable procedural knowledge without requiring all stored trajectories to participate in training.
We evaluate
HaMo
on continual streams of long-horizon tasks across ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, and WebShop, covering both within-domain and cross-domain settings. WebShop provides an interactive Web-agent environment, while the other benchmarks test whether the proposed learning mechanism generalizes beyond a single domain. The results show a clear complementarity between harness- and model-level adaptation: harness-only learning enables rapid reuse of experience but reaches a performance ceiling, whereas model-only adaptation can acquire strong task-specific capabilities but suffers substantial forgetting under distribution shifts. HaMo combines the strengths of both, achieving stronger continual adaptation while better retaining previously acquired capabilities.
2.
Related Work
2.1.
LLMs for Long-Horizon Tasks
Long-horizon agents must sustain goal-directed behavior over extended, failure-prone trajectories
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
. Prior work improves reasoning, planning, and web interaction through reasoning-action interleaving
(
Yao et al., 2023
)
, stateful benchmarks
(
Zhou et al., 2024
)
, system-level analyses
(
Ning et al., 2025
)
, search and reflection
(
Zhou et al., 2023
)
, action knowledge
(
Zhu et al., 2025
)
, global planning
(
Si et al., 2026
)
, and curriculum-based reinforcement learning
(
Lai et al., 2024
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
. Complementary work improves experience reuse via trajectory compression
(
Yen et al., 2025
)
, rollout aggregation
(
Lee et al., 2026
)
, global memory
(
Qian et al., 2025
)
, reusable workflows
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
, and conditional memory
(
Bi et al., 2026
)
. We focus instead on retaining and consolidating reusable experience across continual long-horizon task streams.
2.2.
Continual Learning for LLM Agents
External-memory methods retain verbal feedback, skills, workflows, or structured memories without frequent weight updates
(
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Wang et al., 2023a
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Zhong et al., 2024
;
Gutiérrez et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
. Parameter-based continual learning instead mitigates forgetting through parameter protection, replay
(
Sun et al., 2020
)
, continual policy adaptation
(
Wang et al., 2023b
)
, or multiple retention anchors
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. However, neither line directly decides which experience should remain externally retrievable and which should drive parameter updates.
EvolvingAgent
(
Feng et al., 2025
)
combines evolving experience with continual world-model learning, while Dong et al.
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
highlight the broader connection between external experience and internalized competence. HaMo coordinates these two timescales: rapidly updated strategy-level memory supports immediate reuse, while selected trajectories and replay enable less frequent parameter adaptation.
Figure 2
.
Overview of the HaMo framework.
HaMo continuously distills expert trajectories into a persistent harness memory, selects representative anchor trajectories based on retrieval coverage, and combines them with historical replay to update a LoRA adapter through experience-conditioned behavioral cloning. An optional feedback step releases memory entries associated with trained high-quality trajectories after adaptation. This collaboration enables fast experience reuse at the harness level and gradual knowledge internalization at the model level.
3.
Method
HaMo coordinates continual learning through two complementary mechanisms operating at different levels:
a persistent external memory at the harness level and continual parameter adaptation at the model level.
The harness retains reusable strategy-level experience and makes newly acquired knowledge immediately accessible without requiring parameter updates.
The model, in turn, is continually adapted to interpret retrieved experience, ground it in the current interaction context, and translate it into appropriate actions.
Training and inference share the same initial dialogue format: the user request, the initial observation, and injected matched experience.

4.
Experimental Setting
4.1.
Datasets and Continual Learning Protocol
We evaluate HaMo on three interactive benchmarks using their purely text-based environments.
ScienceWorld
(
Wang et al., 2022
)
evaluates scientific reasoning through tasks that require agents to navigate an environment, manipulate objects, and carry out experiments.
ALFWorld
(
Shridhar et al., 2021
)
provides household tasks in a text environment aligned with embodied tasks, requiring agents to locate objects and perform operations such as moving, cleaning, heating, and cooling.
WebShop
(
Yao et al., 2022
)
evaluates instruction-conditioned online shopping: agents search for products, inspect their descriptions, select options, and make purchases that satisfy user requirements. Together, these benchmarks cover scientific experimentation, household manipulation, and web-based decision making, with different action spaces and task semantics.
We consider two continual learning settings. In
within-domain continual learning
, we divide the ScienceWorld training set into four equally sized subsets that are disjoint at the sample level. Every subset covers all task types, so the task-type coverage remains unchanged across stages even though the training samples are different. We introduce one subset at each successive stage, simulating within-domain data-incremental continual learning over a fixed set of task types rather than the sequential introduction of new task types. After every stage, we evaluate the agent on the entire ScienceWorld test set, using the same evaluation set throughout the stream. In
cross-domain continual learning

4.3.
Metrics
We use the native scoring mechanism of each text environment as the performance metric. For ScienceWorld, we report the environment’s task-progress score, which credits intermediate progress toward completing the scientific task. For ALFWorld, we report the task-completion score, averaged across episodes as a success rate. For WebShop, we report the environment reward measuring how well the purchased product satisfies the requested specifications, retaining partial credit rather than reducing the outcome to binary success. Scores are presented on a 0–100 scale, with higher values indicating better performance. Each evaluation episode is limited to
50 agent–environment interaction turns
and ends earlier if the environment terminates the task.
For the within-domain experiment,
Average
summarizes the four reported stage scores; the Base score gives the fixed backbone reference. In the cross-domain performance plots, each panel corresponds to a completed training stage and shows scores on the evaluated domains. We assess retention by comparing a domain’s score immediately after learning it with its scores after subsequent stages. The training-order ablation also reports the sum of the three final-domain scores as a descriptive aggregate. Since the benchmarks use different scoring semantics, this sum complements the per-domain results rather than representing a pooled task-success rate.
5.
Results
5.1.
Main Results
5.1.1.
Within-Domain Continual Learning
Figure
3
shows that HaMo improves on the full ScienceWorld test set as additional training subsets arrive, for both model sizes. With Qwen3-8B, its score increases from 38.13 to 60.49, yielding a four-stage average of 52.22. With Qwen3-14B, it increases from 38.61 to 61.15, with an average of 53.09. These averages exceed Base+Harness by 13.88 and 12.44 points, respectively, using the reported values. The final-stage gains over the unadapted backbones are 22.94 points for 8B and 21.20 points for 14B.
The advantage emerges over successive stages rather than from uniformly stronger initial performance. At Stage 1, HaMo scores slightly below Base+Harness for both backbones, but it leads all listed methods from Stage 2 onward. Base+Harness remains close to the backbone reference throughout the stream, suggesting that external experience alone provides limited improvement in this setting. AgentTuning and ETO exhibit different trajectories across model sizes: their 8B scores decline overall, whereas their 14B scores recover after a low first stage. Nevertheless, their four-stage averages remain below those of HaMo. These results support the value of jointly adapting the model and its experience context for sustained improvement within ScienceWorld; the stage averages alone do not isolate retention of individual task types.

The intermediate evaluations reveal how these gains arise. HaMo scores 52.43 on ScienceWorld after the first stage, improves to 54.19 after learning ALFWorld, and returns to 52.43 after learning WebShop. Thus, its final ScienceWorld score matches its score immediately after ScienceWorld training, although it is 1.76 points below the intermediate peak. Its ALFWorld score decreases moderately from 70.08 to 66.79 after WebShop training. In contrast, AgentTuning’s ScienceWorld score falls from 26.24 to 3.13, and ETO’s falls from 20.16 to 3.20. Both methods improve over Base on the final WebShop task but finish below Base on the two earlier domains. Under this protocol, successful adaptation to the latest domain therefore does not ensure retention of earlier capabilities.
Base+Harness largely preserves the backbone’s earlier-domain performance, but its final WebShop score of 43.42 is below the Base score of 45.68. HaMo combines stronger acquisition of new-domain capabilities with substantially better earlier-domain performance than the trajectory-training baselines. This pattern is consistent with the intended complementarity of persistent strategy access and continual learning of how to execute those strategies.

Ablation Results
5.2.1.
Harness–Model Collaboration
Figure

Harness only provides relatively small changes from Base, whereas Model only substantially improves newly learned tasks: it obtains 53.98 on ScienceWorld after the first stage and 73.72 on ALFWorld after the second. However, its ScienceWorld score drops to 22.18 after ALFWorld training and finishes at 24.57, a decline of 29.41 points from its first-stage score. HaMo instead finishes at 52.43 on ScienceWorld, exceeding Model only by 27.86 points and matching its own first-stage score.
This retention benefit comes with a measurable tradeoff. Model only achieves a higher final ALFWorld score than HaMo (69.34 versus 66.79), while HaMo is slightly better on WebShop (59.64 versus 58.74). HaMo therefore does not dominate parameter-only adaptation on every domain. Its principal advantage in this ablation is a more favorable balance between acquisition and retention, particularly on the earliest domain. Because Model only omits both the external harness and historical replay, this comparison supports the complete HaMo design rather than isolating the effect of external memory. It does not separately identify the contributions of anchor selection, replay, and experience conditioning.

The case illustrates attention to option availability and current constraints before purchase, without isolating the contributions of retrieved guidance and parameter adaptation.
6.
Conclusion
We presented HaMo, a harness–model collaborative framework for continual learning in long-horizon agents. HaMo combines persistent strategy-level memory with experience-conditioned parameter adaptation, enabling newly acquired procedural knowledge to be reused immediately while gradually improving the model’s ability to interpret and execute retrieved strategies. Experiments on ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, and WebShop show that HaMo achieves a better balance between adaptation and retention than harness-only or model-only approaches, with stronger robustness under both within-domain and cross-domain continual learning. These results highlight the value of coordinating external experience accumulation with internal model adaptation, and suggest a promising direction for building long-horizon agents that can continually learn from interaction while preserving previously acquired capabilities.
Limitations
HaMo can offset part of the forgetting induced by cross-domain training, but it does not fully prevent catastrophic forgetting. Subsequent adaptation may still reduce performance on previously learned domains, and the degree of retention depends on the domain sequence. The current results therefore support partial mitigation of forgetting rather than complete immunity to it.
Future Work
Adaptive experience use.
A useful extension is to learn when to retrieve a strategy, when to reject an unsuitable card, and when to refresh guidance during execution. Such decisions could combine retrieval confidence with observed task progress and explicit checks of strategy preconditions. This would allow the agent to respond to misleading experience rather than treating retrieval similarity as sufficient evidence of applicability.
Stronger evaluation and broader environments.
Controlled ablations of replay, anchor selection, experience conditioning, and decoding temperature would clarify their individual contributions and interactions. Repeated runs and longer task streams could assess variability and persistent forgetting, while end-to-end cost measurements would expose the tradeoff between performance and memory maintenance. Extending the framework to multimodal agents and changing web environments would further test whether experience-conditioned execution transfers beyond the present text-based benchmarks.

article.headline: HaMo：记忆与参数协同的持续学习
article.lede: HaMo把策略级经验卡与经验条件LoRA更新结合，在多个长程任务流中兼顾快速复用与能力保留。
article.problem: 长程智能体在执行多步工作流时会反复产生可复用的程序性知识，但现有系统通常只做模型参数适应或只依赖外部记忆，难以同时兼顾快速复用与持久学习。这一问题对重复执行相关多步流程的Web智能体尤其突出。
article.method: HaMo将专家轨迹蒸馏为包含任务上下文、初始条件和策略级解法的经验卡，存入持久的外部记忆以供即时检索。模型层面，它按检索覆盖度选出紧凑且互补的锚轨迹，与历史回放一起，通过经验条件行为克隆持续更新单个LoRA适配器，同时冻结骨干参数。训练和推理共享同一条件接口：记忆提供策略，模型学习在当前环境中解释并执行该策略。
article.results: 在ScienceWorld域内持续学习中，Qwen3-8B从38.13提升到60.49，四阶段平均52.22；Qwen3-14B从38.61提升到61.15，平均53.09，分别比Base+Harness高13.88和12.44分，最终阶段比未适应骨干高22.94和21.20分。跨域S→A→W最终阶段，HaMo在ScienceWorld、ALFWorld、WebShop分别得52.43、66.79、59.64，比Base高14.88、22.26、13.96分；相对各域最强非HaMo基线高13.02、19.71、5.16分。消融中Model only首阶段ScienceWorld为53.98，学完ALFWorld后降到22.18，最终24.57，较首阶段下降29.41分；HaMo最终52.43，比其高27.86分。
article.why_it_matters: 这提供了一条让长程交互智能体在不大幅重训的情况下快速复用经验、并逐步内化策略执行能力的工程路径，对Web智能体等多步工作流场景有直接意义。
article.limitations: 论文承认HaMo只能部分抵消跨域训练带来的遗忘，不能完全防止灾难性遗忘，保留程度还依赖领域顺序；组件消融也未单独区分锚选择、回放和经验条件各自的贡献。
article.figure_caption_zh: HaMo框架概览：持续将专家轨迹蒸馏为持久记忆，按检索覆盖度选择锚轨迹并与历史回放结合，以经验条件行为克隆更新LoRA适配器。

figure.caption: Overview of the HaMo framework. HaMo continuously distills expert trajectories into a persistent harness memory, selects representative anchor trajectories based on retrieval coverage, and combines them with historical replay to update a LoRA adapter through experience-conditioned behavioral cloning. An optional feedback step releases memory entries associated with trained high-quality trajectories after adaptation. This collaboration enables fast experience reuse at the harness level and gradual knowledge internalization at the model level.

page_papers.title: Timestral
page_papers.abstract: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.
page_papers.content:
Timestral
Abstract
We introduce
Timestral
, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters.
Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M  and Timestral-123M  take the top two places on every metric.
We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context.
This report describes the model design and its benchmark results.
Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face
1

1
https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/timestral
and inference code on GitHub
2

https://github.com/mistralai/timestral
.
Webpage:
https://mistral.ai/news/timestral
1
Introduction
Figure 1
:
Forecast error against parameter count on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench (lower is better; fev-bench skill scores are shown as one minus the skill score).
The dashed and solid curves show the Pareto fronts without and with Timestral, respectively.
All four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front across the six panels.
\Acp
tsfm enable forecasting across datasets and domains without retraining. By training on large collections of real and synthetic time series, these models provide a shared alternative to fitting a separate model for each forecasting problem
(
Ansari et al., 2024
;
Das et al., 2024
)
.
Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates
(
Khwaja et al., 2026
;
Ansari et al., 2025
;
Podest et al., 2026
;
Meyer et al., 2026
)
.
These developments place increasing importance on how models use the information available at each forecast origin and on the training distributions that support this use.
Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0
(
Ansari et al., 2025
;
Xia et al., 2026
)
sample a context length and a horizon length for each training example, so each forward pass covers a single combination of the two.
Causal decoder-only models instead forecast from every position of a sequence and thus cover many context lengths in one forward pass.
To also cover multiple horizon lengths, recent causal models are trained to forecast several patches ahead directly rather than autoregressively.
cpm
(
cpm
), used in TiRex, Toto-2.0, and TimesFM-3
(
Auer et al., 2025
;
Khwaja et al., 2026
;
Jain and Sen, 2026
)
, achieves this by masking spans of the input sequence.
The masked observations, however, are then also unavailable as context for later forecasts in the same training sequence, coupling the horizon distribution to full-patch context masking.
Known-future covariates pose a second challenge: their future values must be accessible to forecasts, while future target values must remain hidden.
We introduce
Timestral
, a family of four foundation models for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed time series forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters.
All four models share the same architecture and training recipe, offering a range of trade-offs between forecast accuracy and inference cost.
Timestral addresses the coupling of horizons and context masking through
dhf
(
dhf
), which separates causal context representations from learned prediction tokens, and the covariate challenge through a role-aware covariate framework that integrates known-future information while preserving target causality.
The models are pretrained on a synthetic corpus of univariate signals and structured multivariate dependencies, then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context.
Timestral-209M  sets a new state of the art in forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench.
As shown in
Figure
1
, all four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front for all benchmark metrics.
Timestral-123M  already outperforms every other model shown, including models with billions of parameters.
This report presents the released Timestral models, their benchmark results, and the main design choices behind them:
•
dhf
.
We introduce
dhf
, a forecasting formulation that separates missing observations from prediction tokens.
dhf
preserves observed values as context for later forecast origins within the same training sequence, allowing multiple forecast blocks to be supervised while controlling horizon sampling independently of artificial context masking.
•
Covariate conditioning within
dhf
.
We integrate past-only and known-future covariates through explicit series roles and asymmetric attention.
This enables prediction tokens to use known-future information at multiple forecast origins while preserving causality over target values.
•
A model family spanning accuracy and inference cost.
We release four model sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters.
The 209M model ranks first on all reported metrics among the models compared on GIFT-Eval
(
Aksu et al., 2024
)
, TIME
(
Qiao et al., 2026
)
, and fev-bench
(
Shchur et al., 2026
)
.
2
Background
We first describe
tsfm
within the framework of
pfn
, which interprets forecasting as amortised posterior inference (
Section
2.1
).
We then review how current
tsfm
model dependencies across variates and over time, and the drawbacks that motivate the design of Timestral (
Section
2.2
).
2.1
Time Series Foundation Models as Prior-Data Fitted Networks
Synthetic data has become a standard ingredient of
tsfm
training, and its share has generally grown.
TimesFM mixes 20% synthetic series built from ARMA processes, seasonal patterns, trends, and steps
(
Das et al., 2024
)
; Chronos samples 10% of its training series from KernelSynth, a Gaussian-process generator
(
Ansari et al., 2024
)
; and TiRex draws about a third of its training series from an extended KernelSynth generator
(
Auer et al., 2025
)
.
More recent models rely on synthetic data more heavily: 57.5% of Toto-2.0’s pretraining mix is generated with TempoPFN’s generators
(
Khwaja et al., 2026
)
, and Chronos-2 learns its multivariate and covariate capabilities from synthetic data only, with a variant trained without any real data performing only slightly worse than the full model
(
Ansari et al., 2025
)
.
At the other end, time series
pfn
such as ForecastPFN, Mamba4Cast, TimePFN, and TempoPFN are trained exclusively on synthetic data
(
Dooley et al., 2023
;
Bhethanabhotla et al., 2024
;
Taga et al., 2025
;
Moroshan et al., 2026
)
.
Timestral follows this direction: it is pretrained exclusively on synthetic data, and a significant part of our effort went into designing the generating processes.

3
Timestral
Timestral is a causal encoder-only model for multivariate forecasting that supports both past-only and known-future covariates (
Figure
4
).
As in bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0, forecasts are produced at dedicated prediction tokens rather than from context representations; unlike them, the context is encoded causally.
Two modelling choices define the dependency structure of Timestral, along time and across variates.
Along time,
dhf
(
Section
3.1
) decouples the context from the forecast horizon: prediction tokens attend to the context without affecting it.
Across variates (
Section
3.2
), targets exchange information with each other and receive information from covariates, but never pass information to them; only known-future covariates contribute values from later patches, including the forecast horizon.
Section
3.3
describes the patch embedding, normalisation, Transformer backbone, and quantile head.

This decoupling has the following advantages.
First, how often each forecast distance is trained can be tuned without side effects on the context.
Second, missing data can be simulated independently of the forecast distances: optional missing-data augmentation hides variable-length gaps at arbitrary time steps rather than whole patches, which is closer to realistic missing-data distributions, and the hidden values are still scored as targets.
Third, missing values, whether in the data or introduced by augmentation, are flagged in their context tokens and thus represented differently from forecast positions, whereas
cpm
represents a patch masked for forecasting in the same way as a fully missing patch.
These advantages come at the cost of roughly doubling the number of tokens during training, since forecast blocks tile the full sequence so that every patch except the first serves as a forecast target.
At inference, a single forecast block follows the context, so forecasts up to the maximum block length of 32 patches (1,024 time steps) are produced in a single forward pass.
Longer horizons can be forecast block by block, conditioning each block on the predicted medians of the previous ones, as in Toto-2.0
(
Khwaja et al., 2026
)
.
3.2
Multivariate and Covariate Modelling
Each variate of a multivariate series is represented by its own sequence of tokens and has one of three roles: target variate, past-only covariate, or known-future covariate (
Figure
4
).
Every variate has context and prediction tokens, but only the outputs at prediction tokens of target variates are used as forecasts.
Roles are not embedded in the tokens and enter the model only through the attention masks and the choice of normalisation (
Section
3.3
).
Along time, target variates and past-only covariates are processed causally, as described in
Section
3.1
.
The context tokens of known-future covariates instead attend over the entire window, including the forecast horizon, where they hold the known future values.
Normalisation follows the same distinction (
Section
3.3
).
Similar to Chronos-2 and Toto-2.0
(
Ansari et al., 2025
;
Khwaja et al., 2026
)
, variate attention exchanges information between the variates of a series at the same patch position, among context tokens and among prediction tokens.
It uses no positional encoding, so the order of the variates does not affect the forecasts.
To prevent future information leakage, known-future covariates attend only to each other.
Otherwise, a known-future covariate could read the value of a target variate or past-only covariate at patch
i
i
and, through its temporal attention, carry it back to earlier patches, from which it would reach the forecast of patch
i
i
.
Past-only covariates do not attend to target variates either; this is a modelling choice that treats covariates as exogenous, so that their representations do not depend on target values.
Forecasts can thus use future values of known-future covariates, but never future values of target variates or past-only covariates.
During training, some variates in a random subset of multivariate series are assigned the role of past-only or known-future covariates, while the others remain target variates.
These covariates are inputs only and are not scored, so ordinary multivariate series become forecasting tasks with covariates.

We describe the data and training setup shared by the four Timestral models, then report their forecasting performance on public benchmarks.

Training data.
The synthetic corpus includes both univariate signals and multivariate examples, covering temporal dynamics and cross-series dependencies.

.

Conclusion
We introduced Timestral, a family of four foundation models with 5M to 209M parameters for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed forecasting.
dhf
separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that observed values serve both as forecast targets and as context for later forecasts, and longer forecast distances are trained without masking context.
Role-aware attention masks let prediction tokens use known-future covariates at every forecast origin, while forecasts never use future values of target variates or past-only covariates.
The models are pretrained exclusively on synthetic data and then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context.
Timestral-209M  ranks first among the models compared on every reported metric of GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench using a single checkpoint.
It leads by a wider margin on IND-Eval.
Timestral-123M  ranks second, ahead of every model outside the Timestral family, and all four sizes lie on the Pareto front of accuracy against size.
Accuracy still improves from 123M to 209M parameters, which motivates training larger models.
Beyond standalone forecasting, Timestral can be embedded in existing monitoring pipelines or combined with language models in agentic workflows.
A further direction is to use the context representations as embeddings for tasks such as classification and anomaly detection.

Benchmark.
We additionally evaluate Timestral on IND-Eval
(

It comprises 187 tasks covering applications in energy, manufacturing, and transport.
Compared with general-purpose forecasting benchmarks, it emphasises finer sampling resolutions and multivariate targets.
Evaluation.
All IND-Eval results reported here come from our own evaluation runs, using publicly released checkpoints and inference code from the model authors’ public repositories under the official benchmark protocol.

article.headline: Timestral 时序基础模型登顶三大基准
article.lede: Mistral 发布 5M 至 209M 四个时间序列基础模型，称在 GIFT-Eval、TIME、fev-bench
article.problem: 现有因果解码器时序模型常用整块掩码（CPM）训练多步预测：被掩掉的观测既是预测目标，又无法作为后续预测起点的上下文，预测步长分布与上下文完整性因此耦合。同时，已知未来协变量需要在保持目标变量因果性的前提下进入模型，双向编码器虽能处理，却要为每个预测起点重新编码上下文。
article.method: Timestral 采用因果编码器结构，提出解耦步长预测（DHF）：上下文 token 与预测 token 分成两条独立流，上下文只做因果注意力、从不读取预测 token，因此上下文表示只计算一次即可被所有预测块共享；训练时序列被切分为多个预测块，块长分布独立采样，无需为拉长步长而掩码上下文。变量按目标变量、仅历史协变量、已知未来协变量三种角色，通过非对称注意力掩码接入，已知未来协变量在整个窗口（含预测期）内可见，目标与仅历史协变量保持因果。模型先在纯合成语料上以 8,192 步上下文预训练，再用真实与合成混合数据在 32,768 步上下文上后训练。
article.results: 在 GIFT-Eval 上，Timestral-209M 的 MASE 为 0.6575、CRPS 为 0.4460；在 TIME 上为 0.6262 与 0.5223；fev-bench 的 MASE 与 SQL 技能分分别为 39.49% 和 50.39%，六项指标均列第一，123M 版本六项均列第二。28M 版本在六项指标上均优于约大 4 倍的 Chronos-2 与约大 90 倍的 Toto-2.0-2.5B；5M 版本在 fev-bench 上超过全部 Toto-2.0，包括参数多约 480 倍的 2.5B 版本。在 2,048 步上下文、96 步单变量预测的工作负载下，8 线程 CPU 单次预测耗时 17–113 ms，单核吞吐 3.5–106 条序列/秒，单张 H100 为 3,650–18,770 条序列/秒。
article.why_it_matters: 若结果可复现，意味着百余 M 规模的模型即可在通用与工业时序基准上压过数十亿参数模型，且推理不依赖 GPU，这会明显改变时序基础模型的部署成本结构。
article.limitations: 训练时预测块铺满整条序列，token 数量约翻倍，训练成本高于 CPM；超过 1,024 步（32 个 patch）的预测仍需按块自回归、以预测中位数作为条件，存在误差累积风险。IND-Eval 结果为作者自评而非官方榜单，基准对比快照截至 2026 年 10 月 15 日且部分对比模型存在缺失项。
article.figure_caption_zh: Timestral 结构示意：目标变量、仅历史协变量与已知未来协变量各自成流，上下文 token 与预测 token 相互分离，只有目标变量的预测 token 输出进入分位数头。

Input boxes show target values $ { }_t$ and covariate values $ { }_t$ in patches of $P$ consecutive time steps. Within the Transformer, context and prediction tokens form two separate streams ( {sec:timestral:dhf}): $ _i$, $ _i$, and $ _i$ denote the context tokens of patch $i$ of a target variate, a past-only covariate, and a known-future covariate, respectively, and $ _i$ denotes the prediction token at the temporal position of patch $i$. page_papers.title: Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
page_papers.abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM.
page_papers.content:
Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
Haipeng Liu
Yang Wang
†
†
thanks:
Yang Wang is the corresponding author
Meng Wang
Affiliation:

Affiliation:

Email:

yangwang@hfut.edu.cn
eric.mengwang@gmail.com
Abstract
Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. In particular, the low-frequency band primarily captures color information, mid-frequency band encodes global structure, while high-frequency band corresponds to local texture.
Besides, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band, resulting in the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, tends to reinforce each other at the early stage, hence the pitfall of overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
We further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from
https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM
.

:
Personalized images generated by our
Dual-FDM
. (a) The generated examples of
Dual-FDM
cust
for customized references (left) and style references (above); (b) The generated examples of
Dual-FDM
cost
for color references (left) and style references (above).
1
Introduction
Figure 2
:
(a) Comparison of the generated results, as well as the attention score map of text prompts and image references, between IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
and MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
for image customization. (b) Comparison of the generated results between InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
and StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
for style transfer. (c) Comparison of generated results guided by different frequency band of the image reference.
Personalized image generation focuses on synthesizing text-driven images conditioned on reference images, which enjoys remarkable progress, benefiting from the powerful denosing capabilities of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)
Ho et al. (2020)
;
Liu et al. (2024)
;
Liu et al. (2025a)
,
e.g.
, Stable Diffusion
Rombach et al. (2022)
;
Esser et al. (2024)
;
Podell et al. (2023)
;
Qian et al. (2022)
;
Qian et al. (2023)
;
Wang et al. (2024c)
. Typically, the personalized image generation involves two key subtasks,
i.e.
,
image customization
and
style transfer
. Given text prompts, image customization
Xiao et al. (2025)
;
Zeng et al. (2024)
;
Pang et al. (2024)
;
Gal et al. (2022)
;
Ruiz et al. (2023)
;
Kumari et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2025b)
;
Ma et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2022)
;
Cao et al. (2026)
;
Jiang et al. (2026)
aims to generate images by substituting the foreground semantics in the text prompts with the foreground extracted from the reference images, while preserving the background of the text prompts. In contrast, style transfer
Qin et al. (2025)
;
Rout et al. (2025)
;
Liu et al. (2023)
;
Sohn et al. (2023)
;
Zhu et al. (2025)
;
Qi et al. (2024)
;
Hertz et al. (2024)
;
Lei et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2024)
;
Xing et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2024b)
;
Wang et al. (2024a)
;
Jeong et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2022)
focuses on disentangling style (
background
) from reference images and aligning the foreground with the text prompt. However, prior arts have struggled to align the generated image with the text prompts within each individual subtask.
Figure 3
:
Illustration of our proposed
Dual-FDM
pipeline (a); For customization style transfer (b), we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Sec.
2.3
). For the color style transfer (c), we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Sec.
2.4
). Each of the two personalized image generation tasks are conducted in the early and late stage of the whole denoising process guided by text prompts as illustrated in Eq. (
1
).
For image customization, substantial efforts
Ye et al. (2023)
;
Aiello et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
aim to
emphasize dense image references of the foreground while overwhelming sparse text prompts of the background, especially for complex ones
,
e.g.
, a degraded “
flower wreath
” and the missing “
coffee
” in the IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
of Fig.
2
(a). Building on this, layout-based methods
Wang et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Zhang et al. (2024)
exploit spatial layouts to explicitly constrain reference concepts to the foreground, while assigning background regions to text prompts.
This preserves the foreground identity, but the explicit separation of foreground and background in the layout disrupts overall consistency, leading to the misalignment with (complex / long) text prompts.
As illustrated in the MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(a), the generated spatial arrangement of “
flower wreath
” and “
coffee
” diverges from the prompt and instead resembles
“A flower wreath around a dog near a coffee”
.
When coming to style transfer, during the early stage of the denoising process with high-level noise, the foreground is reconstructed from sparse text prompts,
the dense style information intended for the background often leaks into the foreground, resulting in misalignment with the text prompts
,
e.g.
, the incorrect number of “
woman
" in the InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
of Fig.
2
(b). To resolve such issue, StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
applies style via instance normalization
Huang and Belongie (2017)
in the cross-attention layers and leverages layout to preserve foreground in the self-attention layers. Nevertheless, self-attention score maps highlight only the most salient regions, implying that the extracted layout can align only with simple text prompts (
i.e.
, “
a dog
") rather than the multi-objects (“
two pillows and one lemon
" in the StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(b)) text prompts, thereby
preventing it from handling the complex text prompts
.
So far, neither image customization nor style transfer achieves satisfactory alignment between the generated image and the text prompt for diffusion models. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands. Intuitively, as shown in Fig.
2
(c), the low-frequency and mid-frequency bands capture color and global structure, while high-frequency band focuses on local texture, where different frequency bands are mainly denoised during
different
stages of the denoising process. As we observed, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band (See Sec.
A
of the Appendix), the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, suggesting reinforce each other at the early stages, resulting in an overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance.
To resolve the text misalignment for personalization generation, we propose to solve the problem upon dual references and develop a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Specifically:
•
We propose to map the foreground or background of image references into the frequency domain via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), where a mask is applied from left to right to progressively disentangle the low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands. Notably, for customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Fig.
1
(a)). The style reference with the mid-frequency band substituted is used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer. For the color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Fig.
1
(b)). The style reference with the substituted low-frequency band is further utilized as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer.
•
To pop up the foreground or background of the image reference, we utilize the key projection matrices in the decoupled cross-attention layer to represent the foreground, which are then reformulated through singular value decomposition (SVD) to derive the corresponding
background matrix
for the background.
•
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages, so as to achieve a well-balanced performance between text alignment and dual-image similarity.
Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation.
2
Methodology
Central to our proposed Dual-FDM cover the following aspects: 1) how to pop up the background of the image references (Sec.
2.2
); 2) how to disentangle the mid-frequency band in customization style transfer (Sec.
2.3
); 3) how to disentangle the low-frequency band in color style transfer (Sec.
2.4
); 4) how to adaptively modulate the timesteps within the denoising process between early and late stages (Sec.
2.5
). Before shedding light on Dual-FDM, we elaborate the preliminary regarding decoupled cross-attention mechanism, which plays a pivotal role of personalized image generation.

Conclusion
In this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle dual image references within frequency-aware diffusion models, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Extensive experiments validate
the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models.

Appendix A
Frequency Variation During the Denoising Process
As mentioned in Sec.
1
of the mainbody, We claim that
during the denoising process, images recover low-and-mid frequency bands first, followed by high-frequency details
. To validate the claims via frequency analysis, we experimentally measure the changes in both low- and high-frequency bands at different timesteps during the denoising process. The results are reported in Tab.
5
:
•
Low-frequency information.
We adopt
Mean Gray
,
Mean HSV-V
, and
Mean Luma
, which primarily capture global brightness and luminance structure. These metrics quantify the stability of the low-frequency bands throughout the denoising process.
•
High-frequency information.
We use
Average Gradient
,
Variance
, and
LBP Variance
, which are sensitive to edge sharpness, local contrast, and texture complexity. These metrics reflect the recovery of high-frequency details.
The low-frequency metrics remain nearly unchanged from the beginning (e.g.,
Mean Gray varies only slightly from 119.5 to 120.9
). In contrast, the high-frequency metrics increase steadily throughout the reverse process (e.g.,
Avg Gradient rises from 59.01 to 233.88
), confirming that high-frequency details are refined gradually during denoising. This is consistent with
Sec.
1
of the mainbody
.

Appendix C
The algorithm of customization style transfer and color style transfer
Due to the page limitation, we summarize the process of customization style transfer in Algorithm
1
and color style transfer in Algorithm
2
.
To tackle the text-alignment issue in personalized image generation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages.

Appendix D
More details about the implementation details
As mentioned in Sec.3.1 of the mainbody, due to page limitation, we further provide more details about the implementation details as follows:
Datasets.
We evaluate
Dual-FDM
on combined datasets covering image customization, style transfer, and text-to-image (T2I) generation:
•
Image Customization
: 1)
DreamBench
Ruiz et al. (2023)
+
TI benchmark
Gal et al. (2022)
: a well-known single-object personalized image generation dataset comprising 38 subjects, covering unique objects and pets such as backpacks, stuffed animals, dogs, cats, sunglasses, and cartoons, with each subject associated with 25 prompts; 2)
DreamBench++
Peng et al. (2025)
: the latest human-aligned personalized image generation benchmark, comprising 65 object classes, 20 human classes, and 45 animal classes. For each image, 9 text prompts are generated by GPT-4o to span a range of difficulty levels.
•
Style Transfer
: 1)
IS-Plus benchmark
Wang et al. (2024b)
: a style evaluation benchmark containing 104 images across diverse styles; 2)
StyleBench
Gao et al. (2024)
: a style evaluation benchmark covering 73 distinct styles, ranging from paintings, flat illustrations, and 3D rendering to sculptures with varying materials. For each style, 5–7 distinct images with variations are collected. In total, StyleBench contains 490 images across diverse styles.
•
T2I generation
:
T2I-CompBench++
Huang et al. (2025a)
: an enhanced benchmark for compositional text-to-image generation. T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions. These are further divided into eight sub-categories.
Based on the above, we construct several combined datasets for different joint tasks: 1) for customization style transfer (small-scale), we concatenate
DreamBench
and
TI benchmark
as the customization references, and use
IS-Plus benchmark
as the style references; 2) for customization style transfer (large-scale), we take
DreamBench++
as the customization references and
StyleBench
as the style references; 3) for color style transfer, we combine
InstantStyle-Plus
and
StyleBench
as the color and style references, while text prompts are provided by
T2I-CompBench++
for stylized image generation.
Metrics.
We consider 9 evaluation metrics from three aspects to evaluate our
Dual-FDM
:
•
Text and Image Reference Alignment
: we follow previous methods and adopt two representative models,
CLIP
2
2
2
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.
and
DINO
Caron et al. (2021)
, for evaluation. Specifically,
CLIP-T
measures the similarity between generated images and the given text prompts;
CLIP-TC
and
CLIP-TS
evaluate the similarity between generated images and customized (or style) reference images while jointly considering the text prompts; finally,
CLIP-CS
assesses the similarity between generated images and dual-reference images.
•
Image Generation Quality
: we employ Image Reward (
IR
)
Xu et al. (2023)
to model human preferences for image quality and
HPS V2
Wu et al. (2023)
that combines perceptual studies with deep learning for comprehensive visual and semantic assessment. Both metrics measure the semantics consistency of the high-quality image generation aligned with human standards;
•
Time Complexity
: We employ the inference time (
Times
) and Video Random Access Memory (
VRAM
) consumption to evaluate the computational efficiency and memory footprint of different methods during image generation.
Model Configuration.
Our main experiments are conducted on the pre-trained IP-Adapter-Plus
Ye et al. (2023)
with SDXL
Podell et al. (2023)
model as the text-to-image diffusion model, configured with 30 sampling steps and and a fixed random seed of 42, to ensure high-quality outputs. We use the recommended hyper-parameters for each method across all images to ensure fair comparison. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

Our

NeurIPS Paper Checklist
1.
Claims
Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: We confirm the main claims reflect the paper’s contributions and scope.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

[No]
or
[N/A]
answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.
•
The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.
2.
Limitations
Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?
Answer:
[Yes]
Justification: The paper have conducted a discussion of limiations in the Appendix.
Guidelines:
•
The answer
[N/A]
means that the paper has no limitation while the answer
[No]
means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.
•
The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.
•
The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.
•
The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.
•
The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.
•
The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.
•
If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.
•
While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

D
of the Appendix and carefully described the experimental metrics in the experimental chapter. The information we provide is sufficient and detailed for replication purposes.

The answer

means that the paper does not include experiments.

If the paper includes experiments, a
[No]
answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example
(a)

article.headline: 按频段拆解双参考图，扩散模型兼顾定制与风格
article.lede: 合肥工业大学团队提出 Dual-FDM：用 DCT 掩码把两张参考图拆到不同频段再重组，缓解个性化生成中文本提示被压制的
article.problem: 个性化图像生成通常只给一张参考图，无论是图像定制还是风格迁移，都容易出现生成结果与文本提示错位：定制时背景文本被参考图压过，风格迁移时稠密的风格信息泄漏到前景。作者认为根源在于单张参考图中低频（颜色）、中频（全局结构）、高频（局部纹理）相互纠缠，而早期高噪声阶段以低中频为主导、彼此强化，从而压制了文本引导。
article.method: 方法在解耦交叉注意力层内，先对键投影矩阵做 SVD，并把奇异值取倒数（1/σ）构造背景矩阵，以抑制前景、增强背景。随后用 DCT 将参考图变换到频域，以掩码分离低、中、高频：定制风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cust）用定制参考图前景的中频替换风格参考图背景的中频；颜色风格迁移（Dual-FDM_cost）用颜色参考图前景与背景的低频替换风格参考图背景的低频。替换后的频段作为 key 和 value 重建去噪图像的 query，并用替换频段的信息熵比值自适应划分早期与晚期去噪时间步。
article.results: 在定制风格迁移上，Dual-FDM_cust 在 DreamBench/TI 与 DreamBench++ 等组合数据上取得 CLIP-T 0.3194、CLIP-TC 0.5031、CLIP-CS 0.6687、IR 5.3487、HPS 2.6007，均优于 IP-Adapter、MS-Diffusion 等基线；相对最强的 MS-Diffusion+CSGO 组合，论文报告的最大领先幅度为 CLIP-T 2.27%、CLIP-TC 7.5%、CLIP-CS 4.17%、DINO-CS 27.28%、HPS 2.24%。颜色风格迁移在 T2I-CompBench++ 上，Color 子类的 CLIP-TS 为 0.5015（StyleAligned 为 0.4832）、CLIP-S 0.7178、DINO-S 0.4970。效率上单次推理 10.26 秒、显存 12.48 GB，低于 MS-Diffusion 的 14.68 秒与 16.85 GB。消融显示去掉背景矩阵或让早晚阶段共用同一中频掩码都会掉点。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「文本对齐差」这一常见失败模式归因到频率纠缠，并给出了完全免训练、可插在 IP-Adapter+SDXL 上的注意力层改造，对同时需要保持身份与风格的控制类应用有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 作者自己承认，当风格参考图包含极稀疏的线条类图案时，中频定制线索会削弱高频风格细节，导致风格信息不完整；方法也只在 SDXL/IP-Adapter 体系与 30 步设置下验证。此外论文未报告误差棒与显著性检验（检查表中该项填 N/A），跨模型、跨步数的稳健性仍待确认。

page_papers.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
page_papers.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

Abstract
Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question.
In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate?
To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics.
The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws.
Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records.
These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention.
Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%.
The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) aid scientific discovery through hypothesis generation, experiment design, and evidence analysis.
Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question.
To pursue such inquiry autonomously, LLMs must decide what to investigate and test their explanations through experiments.
This ability could help scientists investigate unexpected phenomena and pursue questions they might otherwise overlook.
LongChang’s name reflects independent inquiry, inspired by the philosopher Wang Yangming’s introspection in a cave at Longchang, where he reconsidered how to seek knowledge and reached an insight that helped shape his own School of Mind
(
Yangming, 2026
)
.
Figure 1:
LongChang’s glass room. Explorers manipulate objects and build tools. Other LLMs evolve scenes using exploration records without human intervention.
Physical law discovery involves inferring an environment’s laws from observations and experiments.
PhysGym
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
, NewtonBench
(

)
, and DiscoverPhysics
(
Wiemann et al., 2026
)
assign law-discovery tasks.
Tab.

compares their exploration guidance and experiments with those of LongChang.
Without a research task or hints about altered physical laws, an LLM must notice phenomena worth investigating, choose a research question, and devise experiments to distinguish competing explanations.
Can LLMs turn unexpected observations into research questions, conduct experiments, and discover altered physical laws autonomously?
We introduce LongChang, an automated framework that generates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics.
This counterfactual setting tests whether LLMs independently notice departures from ordinary physics and investigate them without research tasks or hints about the altered physical laws.
For example, slower falls for heavier objects could lead an explorer to ask how mass affects falling and design controlled comparisons to test this link.
These laws are hidden from explorers but available for evaluating their reported explanations.
LongChang’s base set in Tab.
1
comprises a normal control and 14 scenes with one altered physical law each.
In the virtual “glass room” in Fig.
1
, explorers manipulate objects and build tools that interact with the scene objects within a shared MuJoCo rigid-body simulation
(
Todorov et al., 2012
)
.
Separate LLM agents review tool designs and evaluate reports against the altered physical laws and exploration records, requiring both correctness and experimental support for discovery.
Unresolved questions and corrected errors in these records guide LLM scene designers to generate, refine, and compose scenes for further exploration, continuing the entire discovery cycle without human intervention.
Among 12 evaluated LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7% under free exploration, while the other 11 score 0%.
Exploration records show some LLMs leave observed anomalies uninvestigated, while others experiment but only partially identify the altered physical laws, leaving their conditions or applicability unresolved.
We contribute the LongChang framework for the complete discovery cycle and an empirical study of autonomous physical inquiry.
We use model comparisons, controlled interventions, and exploration records to examine how LLMs form research questions and test explanations using experiments.

2
Related Work
2.1
Autonomous Scientific Discovery
PhysGym
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
and NewtonBench
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
ask LLMs to recover hidden equations through numerical queries, while DiscoverPhysics
(
Wiemann et al., 2026
)
studies law discovery in particle simulations.
These benchmarks specify discovery goals before experimentation, as summarized in Tab.
2
.
Other protocols require explicit initial hypotheses and a minimum number of experiments
(
Nägele and Marquardt, 2025
)
or supply the anomaly to explain
(
Geng et al., 2026
)
.
Open-ended systems let LLMs select questions within an assigned research role, using supplied datasets
(
Agarwal et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Yao et al., 2025
)
or an optical research setting
(
Zeng et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026
)
.
LongChang tests whether LLMs notice unusual effects of altered physical laws, initiate investigations, and establish these laws experimentally, without a preassigned research task or hints about these laws.
Left Alone
(
Szeider, 2025
)
studies self-directed behavior without an assigned task or a simulated physical world.
Explore-then-Act in Look Before You Leap
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
studies task-free exploration, including in ScienceWorld, with modeling instructions and a warning that expectations may fail.
It evaluates exploration and downstream task performance, rather than experimentally supported discovery of altered physical laws by the explorer.
Both WorldTest
(
Warrier et al., 2025
)
and OneLife
(
Khan et al., 2026
)
examine predictive world models and explicitly ask explorers to learn environment rules.
LongChang instead asks whether unexpected physical observations prompt LLMs to pose their own questions and establish altered physical laws through experiments, without research tasks or advance hints.
Tab.
2
therefore focuses on frameworks for physical law discovery.
Figure 2:
LongChang’s automated cycle of scene construction, free exploration, assessment, and scene evolution.
2.2
Tool Use and Design
DiscoveryWorld supplies instruments and abstracted object interactions in a grid world
(
Jansen et al., 2024
)
, while ChemWorld exposes chemical procedures through programmable modules
(
Qiu et al., 2026
)
.
Tool-design systems optimize tool geometry and use for a specified manipulation task
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
or propose detector layouts under given performance goals and resource constraints
(
Zoccheddu et al., 2026
)
.
LongChang ties tool construction to the explorer’s own investigation: LLMs decide whether a tool is needed, what to build, and how to use it to test a hypothesis.
The explorer’s constructed tools interact physically with the other objects in the same simulated world.
2.3
Environment Generation and Evolution
Environment-generation methods create tasks and rewards for agent training and adapt environments based on performance or trajectory feedback
(
Faldor et al., 2025
;
Kang et al., 2026
)
.
Programmable chemical worlds support controlled changes to private laws while preserving public experimental conditions
(
Qiu et al., 2026
)
.
Trajectory-based benchmark construction uses tool-use records to create new tasks with solutions checked by re-execution
(
Guo et al., 2025
)
.
In LongChang, LLM scene designers use unresolved questions and corrected errors in exploration records to generate, refine, and compose scenes.
Explorer LLMs choose observations to investigate, while separate LLM agents review tools and assess reports, continuing this discovery process without human intervention.
3
LongChang
Fig.
2
presents LongChang’s automated cycle of physical law discovery: environment construction (Sec.
3.1
), autonomous exploration (Sec.
3.2
), and discovery evaluation (Sec.
3.3
).
The evaluated LLMs serve as explorers, while separate LLM agents design and review scenes, review apparatus, and evaluate reports.
LLMs carry out the entire loop without human intervention, using exploration records to guide the subsequent evolution of scenes.
3.1
Environment Construction
Figure 3:
An example of an altered physical law. When the two balls are close, an upward force makes them rise together. Labels 1–5 identify successive snapshots.
Figure 4:
An example of an LLM-built tool. The pendulum uses its hinge angle to test whether local gravity is tilted. The instrument reads
