Physical Environment.
An LLM designer specifies each scene’s objects and geometry, physical program, and any altered physical laws.
The framework compiles these definitions into MuJoCo simulations
(
Todorov et al., 2012
)
containing manipulable balls and boxes, with colored floor tiles in some scenes.
Each base scene with altered physics modifies one physical law, producing effects that depend on object properties, spatial relations, contact events, or past actions.
Fig.
4
illustrates an altered physical law: when the balls are close, both rise under an upward force without an upward launch.
The designer records each altered physical law’s target objects, conditions, and observable effects for evaluation, withholding this information from the explorer.
LongChang’s base set in Tab.
1
comprises a normal control and 14 scenes with one altered physical law each.
The normal control assesses whether LLMs ground their conclusions in evidence when no physical law has been altered.
App.
A.1
details ordinary physics and each altered physical law’s scope, conditions, and parameters.
Scene Evolution.
To extend this set, an LLM designer proposes scene changes aimed at more challenging discovery tasks.
The designer receives source scenes and any available summaries of earlier explorations.
These summaries identify tested conditions, unresolved questions, and explanations supported or corrected by later observations.
The designer uses three operations: generation creates new laws and scenes from source mechanisms, refinement modifies an existing scene, and composition combines source laws in a shared environment.
Changes guided by these summaries must cite supporting exploration evidence.
Automated tests check simulated behavior against the altered physical laws, including interactions with constructed apparatus.
An LLM reviewer checks the program and test results against these laws.
Failed compilation, tests, or review trigger automatic revision requests to the designer.
Only accepted scenes are used in subsequent free-exploration assessments.
3.2
Autonomous Exploration
The explorer chooses which observations to investigate, formulates its own research questions, and tests explanations through physical interventions.
The initial prompt asks for free exploration without a research task or hints about the altered physics.
Structured observations give object positions, motion, and instrument readings, with distances in bricks and elapsed time in counts.
The explorer can push or throw objects, grasp and move them, release them, wait, and mark reference locations.
App.
A.2
documents the complete action interface.
When an investigation needs additional control or measurement, the explorer can design apparatus such as the pendulum in Fig.
4
.
It specifies the device’s geometry and mechanical connections, including joints and springs.
An LLM reviewer checks the compiled design for physical validity and returns feedback on rejections.
The explorer can revise a rejected design and submit it again, with successful designs installed into the current scene.
Once installed, the explorer can place objects on the apparatus or adjust its joints and receive updated motion readings with the next observation.
At each turn, the explorer records its observations and action rationale, then acts and receives updated observations.
The cycle continues until it stops or reaches the turn limit, retaining notes, actions, observations, and feedback from all attempts.
The final report summarizes the observations and explanations from this record.
Each conclusion must cite supporting turns and use only interpretations already recorded in the notes, preserving the uncertainty stated there.
The explorer may also report that it found no anomaly during exploration.
3.3
Discovery Evaluation
An LLM judge evaluates reports against altered physical laws and full exploration records, requiring law correctness (C) and evidence support (S) for discovery.
Law correctness requires identifying each altered physical law, its target objects, conditions, triggers, and constants identifiable in the reported units.
Proposed mechanisms may differ if they yield the same observable predictions under allowed interventions.
Evidence support requires recorded experiments to justify all claims and reasoning at the stated level of certainty.
Correct guesses may pass only C. Supported ordinary observations or partial findings may meet S alone.
3.4
Experimental Setup
Main evaluation.
All LLMs explore the same 15 scenes from fixed initial states for up to 100 turns.
LLMs.
We evaluate the 12 LLMs in Tab.
3
.
GPT-6.1-Sol judges the correctness and experimental support of their reports.
GPT-6-Astra reviews apparatus and generates and reviews new scenes.
App.
A.3
lists the prompts used across the pipeline.
Metrics.
For scenes with altered physics, C and S show the percentages of runs passing the relevant check.
Discovery rate (D) is the percentage passing both checks.
Rejection count (R) is the number of rejected normal-control reports, including those with false claims of anomalies or unsupported laws.
Exploration statistics.
Across all scenes, exploration length (L) is the mean number of turns used, and early stopping (ES) is the percentage of runs ending before the turn limit.
Action failure (AF) is the percentage of turns with failed actions.
Construction success (CS) counts explorations with at least one successful build, and construction failure (CF) gives the percentage of failed build attempts.
These statistics distinguish budget use, access to working apparatus, and action execution reliability.

4
Results and Analysis
Tab.
3
shows that GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7% under free exploration, while the other 11 LLMs score 0%.
Its evidence support rate reaches 97.6%, but law correctness is only 19.0%: supported observations and partial findings often leave the altered physical laws unresolved.
For example, a Scene 02 report supports attraction between the tested red balls without establishing its distance dependence or applicability to other red spheres.
Claude-Opus-5 shows the opposite pattern, identifying the altered physical laws in 16.7% of runs while no report passes the evidence support check.
These results separate correct identification of a law from experimentally supported discovery.
Exploration statistics reveal obstacles during investigation.
Gemini-3.7-Flash stops early in every run, averaging only 10.9 turns and leaving little opportunity for follow-up experiments.
The GLM models use about 90 turns and build working apparatus in every run, yet make no discoveries.
They also fail in more than 60% of build attempts, with failed actions accounting for 16.8–20.2% of turns.
Successful construction can thus coexist with repeated unsuccessful attempts.
Grok-4.7 stops early least often but makes no discoveries, so persistence and working devices alone do not ensure discovery.
4.1
Forming Research Questions
We study whether explorers turn unexpected observations into research questions and pursue them experimentally.
Fig.
5
compares two Scene 15 explorations with the same initial state and prompt.
When the red ball starts moving while the blue ball is held, GPT-6-Astra postpones its planned collision test to investigate.
It measures the restart delay and tests whether pushing blue also resets it, discovering that pushes or throws pause red’s northward force for ten counts.
Gemini-3.7-Flash observes a similar restart but continues its planned tests, leaving the unexpected motion unexamined.
We test guidance by giving GPT-6-Astra a law-discovery task, noting that physical laws may be altered, and supplying a scene-specific clue, with other settings fixed.
In Tab.
4
, discovery rises from 16.7% to 28.6%, while evidence support remains unchanged.
Guidance improves law identification when experimental support is already high.
Mean exploration length falls from 39.3 to 30.9 turns, yielding more discoveries with fewer interactions.

4.2
Validating Scientific Claims
Distinguishing competing explanations requires experiments for which they predict different outcomes.
Fig.
6
illustrates this process in Scene 12.
Two successive red–blue collisions change and restore the balls’ colors, consistent with both color exchange and independent red–blue flipping.
GPT-6-Astra tests two red balls, for which exchange predicts that both remain red and flipping predicts that both turn blue.
Both balls remain red, supporting exchange and ruling out independent flipping.
The normal control tests whether LLMs overinterpret observations under ordinary physics.
Across LLMs, 36.1% of reports are rejected for false claims of altered physical laws or unsupported explanations of ordinary physics.
For example, DeepSeek-Flash attributes a ball’s longer travel on the decorative gray tile to lower friction after comparing equal pushes.
The ball is already moving before each push, so different starting speeds could explain the difference in distance.
A fair comparison would start the ball from rest before each push.
4.3
Using Experimental Resources
We examine whether larger budgets or apparatus access helps LLMs resolve unanswered questions.
We compare budgets of 100 and 500 turns under free exploration without context compaction, with other settings matched.
Increasing the limit to 500 turns does not improve discovery: GPT-6-Astra uses about 40 turns under either limit and stops early, sometimes leaving questions unresolved.
Extra turns provide little value if explorers stop early.
The apparatus comparison uses a 100-turn limit.
Disabling construction removes its actions and instructions but retains basic object manipulation.
With construction enabled, discovery rises from 4.8% to 16.7% and law correctness from 4.8% to 19.0% in Tab.
4
, although action failures also increase.
The explorer chooses whether to build a tool, so these results concern access to construction rather than the contribution of tool use in each run.
Fig.
7
illustrates the construction and redesign of a weighing platform in Scene 15.
GPT-6-Astra builds a flat pan to compare the balls’ loads, but the red ball drifts off after release.
It adds retaining walls and increases the pan’s vertical travel, obtaining stable readings after releasing each ball.
5
Scene Evolution
Exploration records can also inform what LLMs investigate in subsequent scenes.
We study whether corrected errors from successful explorations can guide generation, refinement, and composition of new discovery challenges.
Each operation modifies a mechanism involved in the same error to create a scene with altered physics for further exploration.
We review successful GPT-6-Astra explorations for explanations corrected after later observations.
In Scene 15, red stops after a push, prompting the inference that no persistent northward force exists.
When red restarts, the explorer revises this explanation to account for a temporary pause in the force.
The designer receives this error, its correction, and the source laws, and uses the same evidence for all three operations.
Tab.
5
shows how the three designs retain the pause while modifying these laws.
Generation.
The designer replaces the fixed northward force on red with mutual repulsion between red and blue, making the force depend on their relative positions.
Swapping their positions at matched times after a launch should reverse the forces, distinguishing repulsion from a fixed directional force.
Refinement.
The designer introduces a spatial condition blocking red’s northward force while blue is inside the gray square, so waiting longer than ten seconds may still not restore it.
After the pause expires, the planned test moves blue by hand into or out of the square without resetting the timer.
Composition.
The designer combines the paused northward force with Scene 14’s delayed motion copying: green takes red’s launch velocity twelve seconds later.
The planned comparison launches blue after red, postponing red’s force recovery while leaving green’s scheduled velocity copy unchanged.
The explorer must identify both altered physical laws and their distinct triggers and timing.

A nonzero push or throw pauses the red ball’s northward force for 10 s.
Corrected error.

How the scene evolves
Altered physical laws
Generation
Replace the northward force with mutual repulsion between the red and blue balls, retaining the 10 s pause.
The red and blue balls are subject to mutual horizontal repulsion.
Any nonzero push or throw pauses this mutual repulsion for 10 s.
Refinement
Block the red ball’s northward force while the blue ball is inside the gray square, even after the 10 s pause ends.
Blue inside the gray square blocks the red ball’s northward force.
Nonzero pushes or throws also pause the northward force for 10 s.
Composition
Add Scene 14’s rule: the green ball copies red’s launch velocity 12 s after a nonzero push or throw acts on red.
A nonzero push or throw on any object pauses red’s force for 10 s.
Each red launch makes green copy red’s launch velocity 12 s later.

6
Conclusion
LongChang examines whether LLMs can turn unexpected observations into research questions and discover altered physical laws through experiments.
The evaluated LLMs manipulate objects and build tools without research tasks or hints about these laws.
Only one of the twelve evaluated LLMs makes discoveries, revealing the difficulty of turning observations into complete, experimentally supported laws.
Unanswered questions and corrected errors in exploration records guide separate LLM agents to evolve scenes, continuing the discovery cycle without human intervention.
This framework supports research into LLMs that decide what to investigate and design experiments to resolve uncertainties about the physical laws of these worlds.
7
Limitations
This study examines whether LLMs initiate investigations and discover altered physical laws in simulated worlds.
Our results show that this task remains challenging for current LLMs.
The altered physical laws provide a clear basis for evaluating discoveries, while many scientific questions in the real world remain unresolved.
Extending the framework to these open questions requires further research on evaluating exploration and its findings in settings where the answers are not yet established.
8
Ethical Considerations
LongChang uses no human annotation or testing and evaluates LLMs without human intervention.
The evaluation therefore raises no ethical concerns related to participant privacy or informed consent.

article.headline: 12个LLM中仅1个发现被改写的物理定律
article.lede: LongChang让LLM在无任务提示的模拟世界中自由探索，12个模型里仅GPT-6-Astra发现率达16.7%，其余
article.problem: 科学发现常始于一个意外的观察，但现有物理定律发现基准（如PhysGym、NewtonBench、DiscoverPhysics）通常先给出研究任务或待解释的异常，再让模型做数值实验。论文要问的是：如果不告诉LLM要找什么，它能否自己注意到「重的物体反而落得更慢」这类反常现象，把它变成研究问题并通过实验确认背后的定律。
article.method: 作者构建LongChang框架：LLM设计师在MuJoCo中生成15个场景，其中1个为正常对照、14个各改写一条物理定律（如随质量变化的落体加速度、振荡重力、接触变色、第三次碰撞弹跳等），改写规则对探索者隐藏，仅用于评测。被评测的LLM充当探索者，可推、抛、抓取物体，也可自行设计并提交工具（MJCF装置），由另一个LLM代理审核工具设计、另一个裁判依据隐藏定律与完整探索记录判定报告是否正确且有实验支撑。探索记录中未解决的问题与被修正的错误再反馈给场景设计师，用于生成、精修和组合新场景，整个循环无需人工介入。
article.results: 在12个模型中，GPT-6-Astra的发现率（同时通过定律正确性与证据支撑两项检查）为16.7%，其余11个均为0%；它的证据支撑率高达97.6%，但定律正确率只有19.0%，说明多数报告只是给出了有支撑的部分观察。Claude-Opus-5呈相反模式：定律正确率16.7%，但证据支撑率为0%。探索行为差异明显：Gemini-3.7-Flash平均只用10.9个回合就提前结束，GLM系列约用90个回合且每次都能建成装置，但发现率仍为0%，其建造尝试失败率超过60%、动作失败占16.8%–20.2%的回合。正常对照中，36.1%的报告因虚构异常或无依据解释被驳回。消融显示：加入任务提示后GPT-6-Astra发现率从16.7%升到28.6%，平均回合数从39.3降到30.9；禁用装置构建后发现率从16.7%降到4.8%；把回合上限从100提高到500并未提升发现率（14.3%）。在源场景Scene 15与Scene 14上发现率分别为33.3%和66.7%，而由其演化出的三个新场景发现率全部为0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「自主提出问题」而非「解给定方程」作为评测对象，并用可自动演化的反事实物理世界把探索、工具设计与报告审核串成闭环，为研究LLM能否自主发起科学探究提供了一个可复现的压力测试。结果说明当前模型的瓶颈不在证据引用，而在把反常观察收敛为完整、带触发条件的定律。
article.limitations: 实验局限于答案已知的模拟世界，论文自承如何评价真实世界中尚无定论问题的探索过程仍需进一步研究；判定依赖LLM裁判（GPT-6.1-Sol），存在认可无支撑结论的风险。此外几乎所有模型得分为0%，这与评测对触发条件和适用范围的严格要求有关，尚不能区分是模型能力不足还是评测门槛过高，且结论来自固定的15个场景与单一初始状态。

page_papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
Chunyu Luo
Hongyu Zhao
Guangyi Ni
Yue Song
Lingkai Kong
The University of Hong Kong  Beihang University
Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen  Independent Researcher  Tsinghua University
Correspondence to:
lingkaikong@hku.hk
.
Abstract
Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion-
and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy based on
Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL.
To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density,
we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the
negative MaxEnt objective.
Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same
actor, using action regression for value improvement and
distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy.
The actor updates require neither direct samples from
the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density
or score estimation.
Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove
convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step
limit followed by the long-time limit.
On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
achieves the highest aggregate
normalized return among all evaluated methods,
while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based
baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL).
Diffusion- and flow-based policies can capture multimodal
distributions that are difficult to represent with a single
Gaussian
(
Dong et al., 2025
;
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
However, many of these approaches generate actions through
iterative sampling, requiring repeated network evaluations
during training and inference.
Recent MeanFlow-based methods reduce this cost through
few-step or one-step action generation
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting offers a different way to train one-step
generators
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
At each training iteration, it uses target data to
move generated samples toward the desired distribution,
then trains the generator to reproduce the moved
samples from the same inputs.
Through these repeated updates, the generator learns
to produce samples from the target distribution in
a single forward pass at inference.
This approach has shown better performance than
MeanFlow variants in one-step image generation on
ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
These results motivate exploring Drifting for online
RL, where its use remains less studied.
We consider the maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL objective,
which balances expected return with policy entropy
to encourage exploration
(
Haarnoja et al., 2018
)
.
The critic defines a Boltzmann target distribution
for policy improvement, but does not directly provide
samples from it
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
We therefore adopt an energy-based view of Drifting
(
Gretton et al., 2026
;
Han et al., 2026
)
,
using the negative MaxEnt policy-improvement objective
as the energy.
This energy guides updates to actions generated by
the current policy.
For the value term, critic gradients tell us how to
move actions toward higher values.
The entropy term is harder to use: an implicit actor
generates actions but does not provide a tractable
density for computing their distribution’s entropy.
We therefore need training targets that capture
the effect of entropy without explicitly computing it.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy in the
Drifting model family for online MaxEnt RL.
Our key idea is to derive two updates from this energy
and fit them sequentially to the same actor through
repeated Drift–Spread cycles.
In each cycle, Drift uses critic gradients to move
generated actions toward higher values.
The actor then learns to reproduce these updated
actions from the same inputs through regression.
Spread captures the entropy contribution through
diffusion of the action distribution.
We approximate this diffusion by adding appropriately
scaled independent noise to actions from the updated
actor, then train the actor to match the resulting
distribution.
This allows the actor to learn the effect of entropy
without explicitly computing it.
For a fixed critic, we prove
that the learned policy converges to the Boltzmann
target distribution in the small-step, long-time limit.
Our main contributions are:
(1) We introduce
DriftSpread
, a Drifting model for online
MaxEnt RL with expressive policies and one-step action
generation.
(2) We develop sequential Drift–Spread training through
critic-guided regression and entropy regularization to
address the challenge of entropy computation for implicit
policies.
(3) On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
outperforms 13 baselines
in aggregate normalized return, with lower training
costs than the diffusion, flow, and MeanFlow baselines
(Figure
1
).

Related Work
Generative policies for online RL.
Diffusion and flow models provide expressive action
distributions for online RL.
One line of work optimizes policies by backpropagating
critic gradients through diffusion or flow sampling
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Lyu et al., 2025
)
.
DIME also differentiates through diffusion sampling
while optimizing a variational lower bound on the
MaxEnt objective
(
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
Another line of work constructs training targets
for learning critic-defined Boltzmann distributions.
DQS uses weighted averages of critic gradients
to construct score targets
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
.
SDAC and MaxEntDP instead use critic values to weight
denoising supervision and noise estimates, respectively
(
Ma et al., 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
.
Reverse flow matching unifies these gradient-expectation
and noise-expectation formulations through posterior-mean
estimation
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches use iterative action sampling,
motivating few-step and one-step policies for online RL.
MeanFlow was introduced for one-step generative modeling
and learns average velocities
(
Geng et al., 2025
)
.
Recent online RL methods use this formulation
to learn policies with fewer generation steps.
FPMD trains rectified-flow and MeanFlow policies
through policy mirror descent, with both variants
supporting one-step inference
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
MFPO trains few-step MeanFlow policies using velocity
estimates for critic-defined Boltzmann targets
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
, while SOM constructs velocity
targets from critic-based score estimates to train
one-step MeanFlow policies
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting models and policy learning.
Drifting learns one-step generators by repeatedly
moving generated samples and training the generator
to reproduce their updated positions.
This approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance
in one-step image generation on ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
Subsequent work relates specific Drifting fields
to Wasserstein gradient flows
(
Gretton et al., 2026
)
and uses
optimal-transport couplings to construct sample
updates
(
He et al., 2026
)
.
W-Flow derives sample movements from an objective
over distributions and trains a one-step generator
on the resulting samples
(
Han et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting has also been applied to policy learning.
For offline RL, DriftQL combines critic-guided
policy improvement with a Drifting regularizer
based on the behavior distribution
(
Houssaini et al., 2026
)
.
For offline-to-online RL, Drifting Field Policy
derives a KL-regularized policy update through
Wasserstein gradient flow and constructs training
targets from actions ranked by the critic
(
Koo et al., 2026
)
.
Our work focuses on online MaxEnt RL from scratch.

6
Conclusion and Limitations
We introduced
DriftSpread
, a Drifting-based approach to
learning expressive one-step policies for online RL.
Building on an energy-based view of Drifting, we derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from
the MaxEnt objective.
The two updates are learned sequentially by the same
actor: Drift moves actions toward higher values,
while Spread matches a broader distribution constructed
from the updated actor.
This design incorporates the effect of entropy without
estimating policy densities or scores, while allowing
each action sample to be generated in one forward pass.
Under exact fitting, our analysis establishes convergence
to the fixed-critic Boltzmann target in the small-step,
long-time limit.
MuJoCo experiments show that
DriftSpread
combines strong
control performance with efficient training and inference,
supporting Drifting as a practical approach to
generative policy learning.
Our work leaves two directions for future research.
First, our evaluation is limited to simulation
environments.
Testing on real-world control tasks would help
assess robustness to observation noise and changes
in system dynamics.
Second, we use a fixed spreading-noise distribution
and scale during training.
Adapting the spreading strength as learning progresses
may better balance exploration and value improvement.

article.headline: 一步生成策略DriftSpread用于在线RL
article.lede: DriftSpread 用漂移—扩散两步训练一步生成策略；MuJoCo 五任务聚合回报最高，推理 0.15 ms/动作。
article.problem: 扩散与流策略能表达多模态动作分布，但在线 RL 中常需多步迭代采样，训练和推理成本高。最大熵目标还要求策略熵，而隐式生成策略没有可处理的密度或 score，直接计算熵项困难。
article.method: 作者从负最大熵目标出发，基于 Drifting 的能量视角推导出 critic 引导的 Drift 与熵诱导的 Spread，并在同一个 actor 上顺序执行。Drift 以 critic 梯度构造回归目标，把动作推向高价值区域；Spread 通过分布匹配学习加噪后的动作分布，从而在不显式估计密度或 score、也不采样 Boltzmann 目标的情况下引入熵效应。推理时 actor 只需一次前向即可生成动作。
article.results: 在 MuJoCo-v3 的 HalfCheetah、Hopper、Walker2d、Ant、Humanoid 五个任务上，每任务 1e6 次环境交互、5 个随机种子，DriftSpread 在 13 个基线中取得最高聚合归一化回报。推理平均 0.15 ms/动作，低于 DIME 的 1.24 ms 和两步 MeanFlow 策略 MFPO 的 0.36 ms；训练成本也低于扩散、流和 MeanFlow 基线，但 DFP 与 WPPG 的训练时间略低。二维高斯玩具实验中，顺序拟合的最终 KL 为 0.000422，而调参后的联合拟合为 0.512165；步长从 0.01 降到 0.000625 时，顺序拟合 KL 从 0.001788 降到 6.29e-6，联合拟合仍在约 0.51。理论分析在固定 critic、精确拟合和小步/长时极限下证明收敛到 Boltzmann 目标。
article.why_it_matters: 它为在线最大熵 RL 提供了一种无需迭代采样、无需显式熵或密度估计的一步生成策略，有潜力在保留多模态表达力的同时降低训练与推理开销。
article.limitations: 实验仅限 MuJoCo 仿真，尚未验证真实控制任务中的观测噪声和动力学变化；理论保证依赖固定 critic、精确拟合及小步/长时极限，且 spreading noise 的分布与尺度固定、频率尺度对学习有影响，实际有限样本下的收敛与调参仍需检验。

page_papers.title: MatAnyone-E: Sparse Memory Propagation for Efficient High-Resolution Video Matting
page_papers.abstract: High-resolution video matting requires preserving fine details, such as hair strands and soft transparency, while maintaining consistency across frames. Memory-based methods achieve strong matting quality by matching current-frame features with information stored from earlier frames, but this process becomes increasingly costly as resolution grows. We present MatAnyone-E, an efficient extension of MatAnyone 2 that focuses computation where it is most needed. Our approach first performs low-resolution propagation to identify uncertain regions that require closer inspection and the memory candidates most relevant to them. It then performs high-resolution matching only for these regions using the selected memory, while reusing low-resolution matching results elsewhere. This strategy reduces both the number of locations requiring detailed matching and the amount of memory searched, while preserving the information needed to produce a complete matte. We further reduce the cost of generating high-resolution mattes with a lightweight decoder designed around measured runtime bottlenecks and trained to reproduce the original decoder's representations. Experiments show that MatAnyone-E maintains matting quality comparable to MatAnyone 2 while achieving an estimated 7.4x inference speedup and reducing peak GPU memory usage to 7.6% of the usage of MatAnyone 2 at 4K. With compilation-enabled inference on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, it reaches 73.07 FPS at 1080p and 28.62 FPS at 4K.

article.headline: MatAnyone-E 稀疏传播加速4K抠像
article.lede: MatAnyone-E 用低分辨率传播筛选不确定区域，再做稀疏高分辨率匹配，声称在 4K 下将峰值显存降至 MatAny
article.problem: 高分辨率视频抠像需要保留发丝、软透明等细节，并保持跨帧一致。基于记忆的方法通过当前帧与历史帧特征匹配提升质量，但随着分辨率升高，匹配与记忆搜索成本快速增加。
article.method: MatAnyone-E 先进行低分辨率传播，估计不确定性以及 query 与 memory 的亲和度，据此选出需要细查的位置和相关记忆。高分辨率阶段只对选中的 query-memory 对做匹配，其余位置复用上采样的低分辨率读出。轻量解码器按阶段延迟剖析设计，下层使用深度可分离块、后层使用更窄的密集卷积，并通过 MatAnyone 2 解码器的特征蒸馏训练。
article.results: 论文报告，MatAnyone-E 在保持与 MatAnyone 2 相当的抠像质量的同时，取得估计 7.4× 的推理加速；在 4K 下峰值 GPU 显存降至 MatAnyone 2 的 7.6%。在单张 NVIDIA H200 上启用编译推理时，1080p 达 73.07 FPS，4K 达 28.62 FPS。
article.why_it_matters: 若该稀疏传播策略在更多场景成立，可降低记忆型视频抠像的显存门槛，让 4K 实时或近实时处理更可行。
article.limitations: 7.4× 是估计加速比，质量仅称与 MatAnyone 2 相当而非更优。评测只在单张 H200 上给出帧率，稀疏选择在极端运动、遮挡或细小结构上的失效风险尚未量化。

figure.caption: {Overview of MatAnyone-E.} (a) MatAnyone-E retains the main architecture of MatAnyone~2~ {matanyone2}, while replacing its memory propagation and decoder with Sparse Memory Propagation and a lightweight decoder. (b) Low-resolution (LR) propagation estimates uncertainty and query--memory affinities to select query locations and relevant memory for high-resolution (HR) matching. HR propagation then performs matching only on the selected query--memory pairs, while reusing the upsampled LR readout elsewhere. (c) The lightweight decoder adopts depthwise-separable blocks in its lower-resolution stages and narrower dense convolutions in its later decoder stages, guided by stage-wise latency profiling and trained with feature distillation from the MatAnyone~2 decoder.

page_papers.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
page_papers.abstract: Recent test-time training (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient test-time adaptation method for scientific discovery. We introduce Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by 82.8-84.6% in FLOPs and 47.7-58.4% in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.

Introduction
Scientific discovery often involves proposing hypotheses, evaluation, and using the resulting evidence to guide further investigation
[
13
,
19
]
. Advances in reasoning, coding, and agentic tool-use capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have enabled systems that automate part of this discovery process
[
22
,
14
]
. In the iterative discovery loop, a failed attempt can reveal an implementation constraint, while a successful modification can suggest an idea worth applying elsewhere. A key design question is how to learn from this accumulated experience to improve subsequent search efficiently.
Recent
test-time training
(TTT) frameworks, such as TTT-Discover
[
36
]
and ThetaEvolve
[
33
]
, provide a promising solution to this challenge by combining iterative search with test-time reinforcement learning (RL)
[
28
,
8
]
. Specifically, an LLM generates candidate solutions and receives evaluation feedback. These evaluated attempts provide training data for RL, which internalizes search experience in model weights to guide subsequent generation.
Their results demonstrate that TTT is a powerful
test-time adaptation
method on challenging scientific discovery tasks, enabling smaller open-weight models to outperform inference-only systems based on frontier models, such as AlphaEvolve
[
22
]
. However, TTT requires online model weight adaptation during the whole discovery process, which is usually computationally expensive and time-consuming (see Table
3
). It makes TTT hard to scale to larger models for more complex discovery tasks. This motivates us to explore:
under the same discovery framework, is there a more efficient test-time adaptation method that can achieve comparable or even better performance than test-time training?
We hypothesize that evolving external memory could be a efficient alternative to online weight updates for scientific discovery. Our core intuition is that current LLMs already have broad foundational knowledge, reasoning and coding capabilities to use experience accumulated during discovery. Continually distilling and organizing this experience in external memory may therefore be sufficient to improve subsequent discovery, without internalizing it through weight updates. Building on this intuition, we introduce Test-Time Memory Evolution (TTME), a plug-and-play
self-evolving memory
system for scientific discovery. We update the memory from evaluation feedback and provide relevant content in the context to guide the subsequent steps.
Specifically, we divide the search experience into two components: practical lessons for implementing candidate solutions and algorithmic ideas for improving task scores. Correspondingly, TTME maintains two complementary memory modules:
Guideline Memory
and
Strategy Memory
. Guideline Memory distills execution and evaluation feedback into shared operational guidelines for reliable implementation. Strategy Memory extracts effective algorithmic ideas from score-improving modifications and consolidates related experiences into reusable strategies. We select and adapt relevant strategies to guide subsequent exploration, combining ideas from different search attempts.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We investigate whether a test-time memory evolution can outperform test-time weight updates in scientific discovery, and introduce an plug-and-play self-evolving memory method that continually updates external memory from evaluated search experience to guide subsequent discovery with a fixed-weight model.
•
We evaluate TTME under two TTT frameworks across five mathematical construction tasks and three models spanning 8B and 120B parameters.
We preserve each framework’s experimental configuration, replacing only its TTT part with TTME. TTME outperforms the reported TTT results in all evaluated tasks.
Our analysis shows that TTME reduces running time by
47.7
−
58.4
%
47.7-58.4\%
and computational costs by
82.8
−
84.6
%
82.8-84.6\%
relative to TTT. These results demonstrate that TTME is a more efficient alternative to TTT for scientific discovery.
•
We analyze the search behavior of TTME and TTT during the discovery. Both methods improve the implementation validity rate relative to the underlying discovery framework without TTT or TTME, but TTME achieves better performance. Moreover, compared with TTT, TTME more frequently builds on score-improving combinations of previously explored ideas.

Non-parametric discovery methods use fixed-weight LLMs to generate executable candidates and guide subsequent search with evaluation feedback

Parametric Adaptation.
Parametric methods update the LLMs through RL on evaluated search attempts

4.4
Search Behavior Analysis
Candidate validity and discovery performance.
Successful discovery requires candidates that are both valid and capable of improving the task score. We consider a program valid if it compiles successfully and receives a score from the evaluator. Figure
4
compares mean validity over 50 steps and best-found scores under the TTT-Discover framework with Qwen3-8B. Both TTT and TTME improve the mean program validity rate over search without TTT. On AC1 and Erdős, TTT and TTME achieve similar validity rates, while TTME achieves better best-found scores. This suggests TTME generates more effective ideas for improving task scores.

Beyond validity, we examine how search combines and builds on previously explored ideas under the TTT-Discover framework with Qwen3-8B. We count a candidate as a combination if it retains an idea from its parent and adds an idea previously explored outside its ancestry. The added idea must be absent from the parent. We measure how often these combinations are selected as parents for further search.

5
Conclusion
We investigate whether evolving external memory can outperform test-time training for scientific discovery within the same discovery frameworks. We introduce TTME, which distills search experience into operational lessons and algorithmic strategies to guide a fixed-weight model. Across two frameworks, three models, and five mathematical tasks, TTME achieves better scores than TTT in every evaluated setting. Under TTT-Discover with Qwen3-8B, it reduces runtime excluding evaluation by 47.7–58.4% and FLOPs by 82.8–84.6%, including all memory-related calls. These results establish self-evolving memory as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to test-time weight updates for the discovery tasks we study.

Guideline Memory.
1.
Summarize recent outcomes.
The outcome summary covers recent attempts across parents, including
valid results, their scores, and execution or validity failures.
2.
Distill guidelines.
The same fixed-weight base model reads the outcome summary and current
guidelines, then proposes up to three lessons per update, at most
one for failure avoidance. Each lesson specifies a trigger, explains
the mechanism, and gives a concrete action. The parser extracts the
lesson text from the response.

Match and merge.
For each proposed lesson, we compute its Jaccard similarity to stored

unmatched lesson enters memory with count one and the current step.
4.
Remove stale entries and enforce capacity.
Guidelines expire when more than 20 search steps have passed since
their last reaffirmation. Among the remaining entries, we retain at
most 24, ranked by recurrence count with recency breaking ties.

Include guidelines in generation prompts.
Both Direct Generation and Strategy-Guided Generation receive the
retained guidelines as shared context. Each prompt displays up to
240 characters per guideline; memory stores the full lesson text.

For each family receiving new notes, the model combines those notes

We store the entry, its summary, and the supporting notes with source
references. Families without new notes retain their existing entries.

Write ONE method memory for this family, with these four parts:

MECHANISM - what the method actually does, in its own terms.
2.
OBSERVED EXECUTION MODES - every distinct way it has been applied. Two modes are distinct when they differ in WHERE they run (before the loop, inside it, replacing the update, after it), in their SCHEDULE, in how the WORKING SET is chosen, or in their UPDATE / STATE-RESET semantics. They are the SAME mode when they differ only in wording or in ordinary numeric settings such as a step size or an iteration count.
3.
WHEN EACH MODE SUITS A PROGRAM - the structural condition that makes a mode applicable to the program being improved.

article.headline: 外部记忆演化胜过测试时训练
article.lede: 冻结模型权重、只更新外部记忆，在五个数学构造任务上全面超过测试时训练，算力降八成以上。
article.problem: 测试时训练（TTT）让开源权重模型在科学发现任务上超过了基于前沿闭源模型的推理系统，但它需要在整个发现过程中在线更新模型权重，计算和时间开销都很大，难以扩展到更大模型和更复杂任务。作者因此提出：在同一个发现框架下，是否存在更高效的测试时自适应方式，性能与原方法持平甚至更好。
article.method: 作者提出测试时记忆演化（TTME），模型权重全程冻结，只把搜索经验蒸馏进外部记忆。记忆分两部分：Guideline Memory 把执行与评测反馈整理成可迁移的操作准则，Strategy Memory 从「子程序有效且分数高于父程序」的案例中抽取算法思想，归并成可复用的策略族。每 K=2 个搜索步更新一次记忆，生成新候选时由选择器为每个父程序挑选策略，再改写为针对该父程序的具体修改指令，与不带指令的直接生成各占一半候选预算。
article.results: 在 TTT-Discover 框架配 Qwen3-8B 时，TTME 的 AC1 为 1.504329（TTT 为 1.50525，越低越好）、AC2 为 0.949248（TTT 0.9472，越高越好）、Erdős 为 0.380927（TTT 0.380932）；配 gpt-oss-120b 时三项分别为 1.502745、0.960784、0.380862，同样全部优于 TTT。在 ThetaEvolve 框架配 Distill-Qwen3-8B 时，AC2 为 0.948148（TTT 0.9469）、AC3 为 1.464224（TTT 1.4930，越低越好）、Hadamard 为 0.579938（TTT 0.5764）。在 TTT-Discover/Qwen3-8B 上，TTME 相对 TTT 减少 47.7–58.4% 的运行时间和 82.8–84.6% 的 FLOPs，例如 AC1 从 11.76 小时降到 5.36 小时、从 29.47 EFLOPs 降到 4.53 EFLOPs。TTME 还在不超过 25 个搜索步内就超过了 TTT 的最终分数。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明要从搜索经验中获益，未必需要在线更新权重：省掉强化学习训练环节不仅大幅降低算力门槛，也让这类自动发现系统更可能扩展到更大的模型和更长期的搜索。
article.limitations: 评测只覆盖五个数学构造任务和三个模型，且 TTT 基线的数字直接取自原论文而非在同一环境下重跑，公平性仍有讨论空间。TTME 相对 TTT 的提升幅度本身很小（如 Erdős 仅从 0.380932 变为 0.380927），而把 TTME 与 TTT 叠加反而更差（AC2 0.944141、Erdős 0.380944），作者也未解释这一现象的机制。
article.figure_caption_zh: 权重自适应通过测试时强化学习更新模型参数（上），记忆自适应保持权重不变、只更新用于条件生成的外部记忆（下），两者共用同一发现框架。

figure.caption: Weight adaptation updates model parameters through test-time RL (top). Memory adaptation updates external memory that conditions generation while keeping model weights fixed (bottom). Both retain the same underlying discovery framework.

page_papers.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
page_papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert
contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only
their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that
channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads,
because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget
actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks.
Second, top-

At the calibrated budget, a selector’s top-

The top-

Introduction
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity by routing each token to only a few experts
(
Shazeer et al., 2017
;
Fedus et al., 2022
)
. At the small batch sizes of interactive decoding,
latency is dominated by reading routed-expert weights from GPU memory (DRAM) to on-chip SRAM.
Within each routed expert’s gated MLP, however, most intermediate channels contribute little to any
single token and can be skipped with minimal loss
(
Park et al., 2026
)
. A channel selector
exploits this by predicting which channels matter and reading only their weights.
Every channel selector couples two components: a channel
score
that estimates each channel’s
contribution to the output, and a
keep rule
that decides which channels to compute. To balance
quality and sparsity without retraining, most selectors use a
calibrated threshold
, setting a
fixed per-layer cutoff on offline calibration data so that the model reads a target budget on that
data
(
Lee et al., 2024
;
Liu et al., 2025a
;
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
. The alternative keep rule is
top-
k
k
, which keeps each token’s
k
k
highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data itself
(
Liu et al., 2025b
;
Chen et al., 2026b
)
. Prior studies disagree on which rule is preferable. Prox
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
argues that a threshold’s variable channel count adapts computation to each
token, and both Prox and the Sparsing Law
(
Luo et al., 2025
)
find their threshold versions ahead of
top-
k
k
on dense models. Conversely, other studies find top-
k
k
ahead
(
Liu et al., 2025b
)
, while calibration introduces sensitivity to the choice
of calibration data
(
Williams & Aletras, 2024
;
Ji et al., 2025
)
.
We show that channel selection for frozen MoE decoding needs no calibration data.
Selectors calibrate a threshold for two reasons, and it delivers neither.
First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads (Section
4.1
).
The number of channels above a fixed cutoff changes with the input, so selectors with calibrated thresholds read less than the budget they were calibrated for in all 72 benchmark runs we made, and calibrating on the models’ own reasoning does not fix this.
On Qwen3-Thinking, the count follows the answer written so far more than how much each token needs.
Second, calibration gives no consistent accuracy gain over top-
k
k
(Section
4.2
).
We run each selector twice on its own score, once with its calibrated threshold and once with top-
k
k
, at the budget the threshold was calibrated for.
The top-
k
k
version matches or beats the threshold version in 40 of 43 comparisons across four MoE models at 13% and 18% budgets.
Under heavy sparsity, Gemma 4 with calibrated thresholds falls into repetition loops during long reasoning, which the same selectors with top-
k
k
avoid (Figure
1
).
With top-
k
k
as the keep rule, performance depends on how well a selector ranks channels before reading them and handles skipped channels.
Our reader is built entirely from the model’s weights (Section
5
).
For each token, it screens all candidate channels with a rotated ternary sketch of the weights (about 7% of the BF16 checkpoint), computes the top-

Limitations and conclusion
Limitations.
Our kernels turn only part of the saved reads into speed (Section
6.2
), and they were tuned for one budget on one GPU type (Appendix
J
).
Selecting channels for a whole batch at once, so the gain lasts to larger batches, is future work.
The share of coordinates the partial screen reads was chosen on OLMoE and checked only on Gemma 4 (Table
17
).
Our reader changes only routed experts in decoding.
Its sketch and recovery map add about 7% and 0.5% of a BF16 checkpoint, a larger share of a quantized one (Table
3
).
We tested models of up to 35B parameters.
What our results suggest.
We suspect two patterns hold beyond our models.
First, short likelihood evaluations hide failures of long generation.
On likelihood tasks, the two versions of a selector differ little and in both directions.
On generation tasks at a 13% or 18% budget, no threshold version beats its top-

article.headline: MoE 通道选择无需校准数据
article.lede: 论文发现校准阈值并不能固定读取量，改用 top-k 在 43 项比较中有 40 项不输阈值版本。
article.problem: MoE 模型在小批量交互式解码时，瓶颈在于把被路由专家的权重从显存搬到片上 SRAM。已有通道选择器大多依赖离线校准数据设定固定阈值，以便只读取贡献大的通道，但校准本身会引入对校准数据选择的敏感性，而且此前研究对阈值与 top-k 两种保留规则孰优孰劣结论相反。
article.method: 作者把通道选择器拆成「通道打分」和「保留规则」两部分，固定同一个打分器，只替换保留规则，在四个 MoE 模型上分别跑校准阈值版本和 top-k 版本。在此基础上，他们提出一个完全由模型权重构建的读取器：先用权重的旋转三值草图（约为 BF16 检查点的 7%）粗筛候选通道，精确计算 top-k，再用下投影的低秩映射（约 0.5%）恢复被跳过的通道。
article.results: 校准阈值并不能固定读取量：在全部 72 次基准运行中，带校准阈值的选择器实际读取量都低于其预算，例如 Prox 按 18% 读取预算校准，实测平均只读取 12.9%；校准在模型自身推理数据上也无法修正这一点。在 13% 和 18% 两个预算下，同一打分的 top-k 版本在 43 项比较中有 40 项追平或超过阈值版本，其中生成任务的 23 项全部如此；阈值版本在 Gemma 4 上重稀疏条件下会陷入重复循环，而 top-k 版本避免了这一问题。草图与恢复映射在 Qwen3-Thinking 上读取得分为 17.8%。
article.why_it_matters: 如果结论成立，部署方就不必为每个 MoE 模型收集校准数据，也能避免阈值在长生成任务上触发重复循环这类失效模式，通道选择可以只依赖模型自身权重。
article.limitations: 作者指出，其实现在只把节省的一部分读取转化为实际加速，且仅针对单一 GPU 类型上的单一预算调优，整批一起选择通道仍是未来工作；部分筛选读取的坐标比例在 OLMoE 上选定、只在 Gemma 4 上验证，且测试模型最大到 35B 参数。草图与恢复映射约占 BF16 检查点的 7% 和 0.5%，在量化检查点上占比更大。

Middle: the three stages. Bottom: reads at 17.8\% on Qwen3-Thinking.

page_papers.title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models
page_papers.abstract: The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely. We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families. The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones. Just Action Model
(JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely.
We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families.
The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM.
Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones.

Introduction
Pretrained visual models provide a starting point for robot control. Standard vision-language-action models (VLAs) adapt vision-language representations to predict actions
(
Kim et al., 2025b
;
Black et al., 2025a
;
Black et al., 2025b
)
. World-action models (WAMs) start from image or video generators and learn actions together with future visual prediction
(
Ye et al., 2026b
;
Yuan et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026b
;
Bi et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
. These approaches differ, as depicted in Figure
1
, in both their pretrained knowledge and how they use the robot trajectories: most VLAs learn only the actions in a trajectory, whereas a WAM also learns to generate the observations that follow. Comparing their success rates alone does not identify which difference matters.
We separate three choices:
backbone initialization

the modules used at inference
. Recent attempts such as FastWAM
(
Yuan et al., 2026
)
and ImageWAM
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
remove test-time video or image generation and suggest that visual generative objectives at training time are the key to WAMs. We ask a more basic question:
does learning from recorded future observations require a visual generative objective at all? If not, can backbones without visual generative pretraining learn from future observations in the same way?
We show that predicting future representations can replace visual generative supervision in policy training.
We introduce
Just Action Model
(JAM), a common recipe for a pretrained visual backbone and an action expert. The policy is trained with an action loss and a foresight loss: a prediction head maps current-observation features to targets supplied by a frozen future anchor. Future observations provide targets for the foresight loss, never inputs to the action path. The anchor branch and prediction head are used only during training, and fixed targets can be cached. At deployment, the backbone encodes the current context and the action expert predicts the action chunk. JAM requires no image or video generation during policy fine-tuning or deployment. The backbone may still come from generative pretraining, and the action expert still uses flow matching.

We evaluate the recipe in two stages. First, we replace the generative objectives of FastWAM and ImageWAM while keeping each policy’s architecture, data, optimizer, training budget, and deployment path fixed. Predicting future representations preserves or improves success, and targets at future positions are more effective than those at the current position. Backbone and future anchor pretraining play different roles: a pretrained FastWAM backbone remains effective with a randomly initialized, frozen future anchor, and direct VAE features give its strongest result. JAM (Ovis-U1) performs best with targets from the pretrained Yak backbone, so the preferred target is architecture-dependent. Our contributions are:
•
We propose JAM, a single recipe for a pretrained visual backbone and an action expert in which recorded future observations enter only as frozen prediction targets, and the foresight branch is discarded after training.
•
We show through fixed-architecture comparisons that foresight can replace visual generation while preserving or improving success. Future-offset targets are more effective than current-offset targets, and the best target depends on the backbone: a plain VAE suffices for the Wan video backbone. With targets cached, JAM reduces the estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by
73.0

•
We apply the same objective to generative, self-supervised, and vision-language backbones, with the strongest generative and vision-language instantiations achieving comparable control performance, showing that strong performance with foresight is attainable using either a generator-initialized or a vision-language backbone.

3.3
Instantiations across pretraining families
We instantiate JAM with backbones from three pretraining families. In the cross-backbone comparison in Table
3
, each future anchor is a frozen copy of the corresponding backbone. Our matched FastWAM and ImageWAM experiments additionally evaluate VAE-direct future anchors.
Generative backbones.
FastWAM pairs a Wan2.2-5B video backbone with an action expert of the same depth, and ImageWAM (Ovis-U1) pairs the pretrained Yak18 image-editing backbone with an 18-block action expert of matching width
(
Team Wan et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
. Their generative objectives denoise future video latents and generate a future image. Under JAM, the backbone sees only the clean current frame, and the policy architecture and action-expert initialization are unchanged. Two further targets isolate what the frozen generator contributes: the same backbone with random initialization, which keeps the architecture but removes the pretrained features, and the frozen VAE tokenizer alone, which removes the target transformer and predicts lifted latent-patch features.
Self-supervised backbones.
DINOv2 is an image encoder with no language input and no generative head
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
. The action expert mirrors the backbone’s transformer blocks, and a separate text encoder supplies instruction features to the action expert, but not to the visual backbone.
Vision-language backbone.
Qwen3.5-2B is a vision-language model that already reads images and text together
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
. The action expert mirrors the backbone’s blocks and reads the backbone’s tokens through causal token mixing over image, text, and action tokens, so it is a VLA trained with an additional foresight loss.

Our study has two stages. First, we replace visual generation with foresight within fixed policy architectures and deployment paths, examining target offsets and future anchors. Second, we apply the common objective to backbones from different pretraining families. We also compare the resulting policies with published systems and evaluate training cost.

Conclusion
JAM bridges vision-language-action and world-action models by separating backbone initialization, supervision on future observations, and the modules retained at inference. It trains a pretrained visual backbone and an action expert with action and foresight losses, using frozen future representations as targets and discarding the foresight branch after training. With the policy architecture fixed, replacing visual generation with foresight yields higher success rates than the corresponding generative baselines on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the largest gains on LIBERO-Plus; RoboTwin 2.0 success is similar or slightly higher. With cached targets, JAM reduces online FLOPs per sample per update by
73.0
%
73.0\%
relative to FastWAM and
36.8
%
36.8\%
relative to ImageWAM. With the recipe fixed, the same supervision applies to generative, self-supervised, and vision-language backbones, and the best generator-initialized and vision-language policies achieve comparable performance. These results show that effective foresight training is possible with either pretraining family, while the cross-backbone comparison does not isolate the effect of pretraining alone. Both families can be trained as Just Action Models that learn from recorded futures without visual generation during policy training or additional inference machinery.

Ethics statement
This study evaluates robot manipulation policies in simulation using public models, code, and datasets. Experiments use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 and involve no human participants or personal data. Relevant risks include failures under distribution shift and unsafe deployment of simulation-trained policies without physical validation.

Qwen3.5-2B.
The 24-layer backbone encodes each view separately alongside the instruction, without a separate text encoder. Its action expert copies compatible weights from 18 GatedDeltaNet and six full-attention blocks and adds action input, output, and flow-time modules. Causal token mixers process the current image–text prefix before action tokens, preventing actions from influencing the prefix. The frozen future anchor reads the instruction, current views, and 16-step future views in one causal sequence. Future-image features supervise current-image features at the same layer; future views never enter the policy prefix.
DINOv2-B/L.
Each encoder processes views separately. Its action expert matches its depth and width, copies normalization, attention, and MLP weights, and adds action input, position, flow-time, AdaLN, and output modules. Action queries attend to the text prefix, same-layer patch keys and values from both views, and action tokens; visual queries never attend to text or actions. The text prefix contains 512 cached tokens from frozen Qwen3-4B, projected to the action width. A frozen DINOv2 copy encodes each future view into final-layer patch targets for the corresponding policy layer.

article.headline: JAM：用未来表征预测替代视觉生成的统一配方
article.lede: 论文把 VLA 与 WAM 的差异拆成三个可分离选择，提出动作损失加未来表征预测损失的统一配方，在 LIBERO 与 L
article.problem: 视觉-语言-动作模型（VLA）从视觉语言模型继承预训练知识，世界-动作模型（WAM）则从图像或视频生成器出发、在学动作的同时学预测未来画面，两派争论哪种范式更好。但这一分歧实际上捆绑了三个本可分开的选择：骨干初始化、施加在未来观测上的目标函数、以及推理时是否保留该未来损失的机制，因此仅比较成功率无法判断究竟是哪一项在起作用。
article.method: 作者提出 Just Action Model（JAM）：一个预训练视觉骨干加一个动作专家，训练时同时优化动作流匹配损失和一个「预见损失」。预见损失让当前观测特征去回归冻结未来锚（frozen future anchor）对记录未来帧的编码，用余弦距离、梯度不回流到目标；预测头与锚分支只在训练时存在，部署时直接丢弃，训练和推理都不做图像或视频生成。由于目标固定，未来表征可预先计算并缓存，骨干可以是生成式 DiT、自监督编码器或视觉语言模型。
article.results: 在固定策略架构下替换目标函数：FastWAM 换用预训练 Wan 目标的预见损失后，LIBERO 从 97.00% 升到 97.45%、LIBERO-Plus 从 55.31% 升到 55.58%；ImageWAM（Ovis-U1）则从 92.90%/65.27% 升到 96.75%/79.95%。为 Wan 改用冻结 VAE 直接目标时 LIBERO-Plus 达 64.54%，对应 RoboTwin 2.0 上 JAM(Wan) 为 91.4%、FastWAM 为 91.2%，JAM(FLUX.2) 为 93.1%。跨骨干方面，JAM(Ovis-U1)、JAM(DINOv2-L)、JAM(Qwen3.5-2B) 在 LIBERO-Plus 上分别为 79.95%、70.39%、81.14%（Qwen3.5-2B 仅用动作损失时为 77.03%）。缓存目标后，每样本每次更新的在线训练估计 FLOPs 从 FastWAM 的 15.52 TFLOPs 降到 4.19 TFLOPs，降幅 73.0%；相对 ImageWAM 从 5.81 降到 3.67 TFLOPs，降幅 36.8%。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明从记录的未来帧中学习并不需要视觉生成目标：只要把未来当作冻结的表征目标，就能在保持原有部署路径不变的前提下超过对应的 WAM 基线，并省掉生成分支的训练开销。这也让生成式骨干与视觉语言骨干可以放在同一套监督配方下比较，而不必先站队。
article.limitations: 全部实验都在 LIBERO、LIBERO-Plus 和 RoboTwin 2.0 仿真基准上完成，没有真机验证，论文自己也把分布偏移下的失效列为风险。跨骨干比较因架构与动作接口不同，无法单独隔离预训练本身的影响；最优未来锚还依赖架构（Wan 偏好冻结 VAE、Ovis-U1 偏好预训练 Yak），且训练预算缩到 10k 更新时 JAM(Wan) 的 LIBERO-Plus 仅 48.47%，低于 20k 更新 FastWAM 的 55.31%。

page_papers.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
page_papers.abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

article.headline: 十个AI代理自主后训练，接受人类反馈
article.lede: 十个前沿模型扮演训练代理，六天内各自用1000 GPU小时打造助手，再依据人类反馈继续改进。
article.problem: 递归自我改进的关键一问是：AI代理能否自主完成数据选择、训练流程实现与检查点挑选，训练出有用的语言模型，并利用用户反馈自我改进。现有讨论多为概念推演或封闭评测，缺少可审计、可复现的过程记录与统一对照。
article.method: 作者搭建 RSI Arena 两阶段研究：十个前沿模型各作为训练代理，起点统一为 NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base。第一阶段为期六天，每个代理在共享的 64 GPU 集群上拥有 1,000 GPU 小时和 300 美元 API 额度，自主选数据、写训练流程、挑检查点，随后用 20 个基准和盲测人类评估打分。第二阶段把涉及各自 Stage 1 模型的对比记录与投票反馈给代理，再给三天额外训练时间，并以 NVIDIA Instruct 作为两轮评测的公共参照。
article.results: 十个代理全部产出了可用的助手模型。最强模型由 GPT-6 Astra 训练，在 12 个能力基准上中位缩小了基座到 Instruct 之间 76% 的差距；在对回答长度和格式做统计调整后，其人类偏好评分接近 NVIDIA Instruct。第二阶段中，十个模型里有八个的风格调整后相对评分较第一阶段有所提升。但基准提升幅度不大，且与偏好提升没有清晰关联；部分代理倾向于鼓励更长回答，有一个模型在 StrongREJECT 上的有害顺从增加。预算使用也无法预测结果：Gemini 3.8 Flash 在 12 小时、19 GPU 小时后即停止，其模型的人类评分却高于各用掉约 1,000 GPU 小时的 Muse Spark 1.3 和 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「AI 自主训练 AI」这一模糊命题放进带成本上限、过程留痕、统一基座与盲测人类评估的可审计沙盒，让人类反馈能否引导自主模型开发成为可测量的经验问题。
article.limitations: 能力基准提升有限，且与偏好提升缺乏清晰关联，说明偏好信号可能更多奖励表面风格（如更长回答）而非真实能力；此外仅一个基座模型、单一集群、两阶段共约九天，向更大规模与更长周期自我改进的外推仍存疑。

page_papers.title: Not Just a Subject: Capturing Adaptive Scene-Specific Variance for Visual Storytelling
page_papers.abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly improved text-to-image generation, enabling their application to visual storytelling, where coherent image sequences are generated from narrative prompts. However, existing methods primarily focus on identity preservation and often fail to adapt to diverse scene variations, resulting in semantic misalignment and structural inflexibility. We propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework that harmonizes identity consistency with scene-specific adaptation across text and vision spaces. In the text space, we decouple the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts to prevent information dilution, but this leaves the scene without access to appearance cues. To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which softly injects a phrase-level appearance residual into the scene's <EOS> embedding. In the vision space, we find that scale mismatch between identity and scene subjects causes a few identity tokens to be repeatedly transferred, producing structural artifacts. We address this with Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors identity features at the scene-specific scale (Identity Anchoring) and integrates them via Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate performance under varied spatial compositions, we extend the Consistory+ benchmark with diverse framing scenarios (Consistory+_+). Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance on both benchmarks.

Notably, improvements from CCB are primarily reflected in text-related metrics, whereas Adaptive Identity Preservation contributes more prominently to identity-related scores such as CLIP-I.
This complementary trend indicates that each module effectively targets its intended objective, enabling more balanced control over textual fidelity and identity consistency.
While configuration (7) achieves higher CLIP-I, our full method, EOS-Story, outperforms in both CLIP-T and DreamSim.
We also compare results with and without subject size matching (
Fig.
10
b,
Tab.
5
).
Without size aligning, scale discrepancies between identity and scene representations often lead to misaligned identity transfer, resulting in distorted subject proportions.
In contrast, size-aware alignment ensures that identity features are referenced at an appropriate spatial scale, promoting more coherent subject integration.
5
Conclusion
In this work, we propose
EOS-Story
, a training-free framework that adaptively models scene-specific variance in visual storytelling across text and vision spaces. We introduce
Cross-Contextual Bridging
, which decouples the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts and bridges the resulting semantic gap by injecting phrase-level appearance residuals into the scene’s
⟨
\langle
EOS
⟩
\rangle
embedding. To complement this with structural adaptation, we further propose
Adaptive Identity Preservation
, which anchors subject features at the scene-specific scale and refines integration through Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate scene adaptability, we extend Consistory+ with diverse framing variations (Consistory+_+).
Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance in both prompt fidelity and structural adaptability.

Appendix 0.B
Consistory+_+ & Framing Evaluation Details
The ShotBench
[
15
]
includes a wide range of framing phrases across eight categories (
Tab.
7
).
To ensure a focused and rigorous evaluation of scene-specific structural variance, we intentionally restricted the scope to three primary categories, excluding the remaining five based on the following methodological criteria: (1) Prompt Redundancy: Shot Framing descriptors (e.g., “single”, “2 shot”) primarily specify the number of characters, which is already inherently defined by the subject phrases in the storyboard prompts; (2) Redundancy Mitigation: Lens Size phrases (e.g., “wide lens”) are largely redundant as they are semantically encompassed by the Shot Size category (“wide shot”); (3) Domain Incompatibility: Camera Movement is inherently applicable to temporal video sequences and is thus irrelevant to static image generation; and (4) Task Relevance: Lighting-related categories fall outside the scope of our work, as they primarily focus on stylistic or artistic variations rather than the structural and compositional elements that define scene-specific variance.
Framing Phrase Filtering.
Although SDXL generally produces textually well-aligned images, it sometimes struggles to accurately reflect specific framing phrases.
Before incorporating these phrases into our benchmark extension, we first evaluate how well they are captured by the base SDXL model using the ShotBench evaluation mechanism.
To quantitatively assess phrase reflection, we construct approximately 90 diverse scene prompts and append each framing phrase at the end (e.g., “A photo of a woman baking cookies, close-up shot”).
We generate images for 10 random seeds per phrase and compute the top-1 and top-3 accuracy, along with standard deviations, as shown in
Fig.
16
.
For example, in the “shot size” category with 7 phrase options, this results in a total of 6,300 images (90 scenes × 7 phrases × 10 seeds).
We filter out framing phrases whose top-1 accuracy is zero (e.g., “extreme wide shot”), as these are not reliably reflected in the generated outputs from SDXL.
Consistory+_+
With the remaining framing phrases, we extend the original Consistory+ benchmark using GPT-4o.
Since these phrases are visually meaningful primarily for animate subjects, we first guide GPT-4o to determine whether the subject in each prompt is animate.
Then, the model is instructed to append the most appropriate framing phrase for the given scene, resulting in Consistory+_+.
Framing Accuracy Evaluation.
Following the evaluation protocol in
[
15
]
, we provide the generated image along with the corresponding framing category (e.g., shot size) and prompt the model with a multiple-choice question.
For instance, for shot size evaluation, we prompt the model with a multiple-choice question such as
“What is the shot size of this shot?” and provide predefined options (e.g., wide shot, medium shot, close-up shot).
The predicted category is compared against the framing phrase specified in the text prompt, and accuracy is reported.

Although our model effectively balances prompt and subject coherence, several limitations remain.

article.headline: 免训练故事生图：让角色随场景变形
article.lede: 免训练框架用 EOS 残差注入外观、按场景尺度对齐身份特征，Consistory+ 文本对齐指标升至 0.9042。
article.problem: 现有的视觉故事生成方法大多只关注主体身份一致性，把叙事提示当成一个整体编码，长提示中的动作、环境等场景细节容易被稀释，导致语义错位。视觉侧又常用与空间无关的特征注入方式，无视每个场景的构图与主体尺度差异，造成姿态僵硬、结构重复。
article.method: 作者提出免训练框架 EOS-Story，分文本与视觉两条路径处理场景差异。文本侧 Cross-Contextual Bridging 把叙事拆成身份与场景子提示，用「身份 EOS 减风格-主体 EOS」得到短语级外观残差，再加到场景的 ⟨EOS⟩ 嵌入上，避免外观信息稀释又不拉长提示。视觉侧 Adaptive Identity Preservation 先按场景主体尺寸重采样身份特征（Identity Anchoring），再用相似度阈值 μ+σ 过滤不可靠匹配，最后通过 Identity-Aware Self-Attention 让场景特征有选择地关注主体特征。
article.results: 在 SDXL-base-1.0、50 步去噪、λ=0.55、第 9 步切换 IA 与 IASA 的设置下，Consistory+ 上 CLIP-T 为 0.9042（1P1S 0.8871、StoryDiffusion 0.8985），DreamSim 0.2005 为对比中最低，Aesthetic 6.1764、ImageReward 1.1680 均为最高，CLIP-I 0.8850 略低于 IP-Adapter 的 0.9398。扩展基准 Consistory+_+ 上 CLIP-T 0.8998、CLIP-I 0.8787、DreamSim 0.2146、ImageReward 1.3217，均优于对比方法。20 名被试、40 个故事板的用户研究中，52.8% 的样本首选该方法；生成 5 个故事占用 47777 MB 显存、耗时 118.570 秒，显存略高于基线但延迟相当。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明故事生图的关键不只是「保住这张脸」，还要允许主体在尺度、视角上随场景变化；而 ⟨EOS⟩ 嵌入可作为短语级语义控制点，为免训练个性化提供了一种轻量接口。
article.limitations: 方法沿用交叉注意力图作为主体掩码，作者承认掩码偶尔会圈错区域，导致生成错位，且底层 SDXL 本身有时完全画不出某些概念（如 faun）。此外，Cross-Contextual Bridging 依赖 CLIP 的 ⟨EOS⟩ 汇总特性，无法直接迁移到 T5 或 LLM 文本编码器，FLUX 实验只用了视觉侧的 AIP 模块。
article.figure_caption_zh: EOS-Story 流程：文本侧跨上下文桥接把外观残差写入场景的 ⟨EOS⟩ 嵌入，视觉侧先按场景尺度锚定身份特征，再用身份感知自注意力融合。

page_papers.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
page_papers.abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

Abstract
Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction.
However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity.
A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements.
We therefore introduce
The Trinity
, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver.
Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree.
We introduce
Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real
: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer.
Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology.
The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a
Capability-Aware Harness Router
that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree.
Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

This approach is suitable when tasks share similar capability requirements, but can lead to Harness overfitting and poor generalization across heterogeneous tasks.
Conversely, a global Harness struggles to accommodate conflicting task demands, including performance–efficiency trade-offs in embodied tasks, limiting its efficiency and adaptability.
A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements.
For example, although ARC-AGI-3
[
36
]
and Micromouse
[
